It appears that the central point of neurobehavioral change in schizophrenia is based on changes in the activities or release of neurotransmitters such as dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, acetylcholinesterase, adrenaline, aspartate, glycine, GABA and GABA-T ( , , , , , ). The severity of schizophrenia depends in part on oxidative stress and the level of neurochemical imbalance affecting neural circuits in several brain structures such as the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and striatum ( , ). The results of this study confirm those of previous research showing that repeated administration of ketamine causes positive symptoms, negative symptoms, and cognitive symptoms or disorders ( , ). Ketamine is an antagonist of NMDA glutamate receptors. When ketamine binds to NMDA receptors, an imbalance occurs between the release of dopamine, glutamate, and GABA. Inhibition of NMDA receptors leads to stereotypical behaviors and locomotor hyperactivity. Blocking NMDA receptors located on GABAergic interneurons reduces their inhibitory activity; GABAergic interneurons are known to exert an inhibitory role on glutamatergic neurons through the release of GABA. The reduction in the activity of these GABAergic interneurons leads to excessive release of glutamate, which in turn stimulates the mesolimbic circuits to release more dopamine, causing delusions and hallucinations ( , ). The literature has shown that in addition to causing a state of NMDA receptor hypofunction, ketamine also activates D 2 receptors. Stereotypy is used to diagnose the positive symptoms of ketamine-induced schizophrenia in mice ( , ). These symptoms are a series of repetitive movements and gestures with no apparent purpose: head movements, intense licking, chewing, and intermittent sniffing ( ). Previous studies have shown that the increase in the time and number of escalations is due to an increase in dopaminergic and glutamatergic activity in the cortical areas of the brain, which results in repetitive behaviors ( , ). The aqueous lyophilisate of F. mucuso (25, 50, and

a state of NMDA receptor hypofunction, ketamine also activates D 2 receptors. Stereotypy is used to diagnose the positive symptoms of ketamine-induced schizophrenia in mice ( , ). These symptoms are a series of repetitive movements and gestures with no apparent purpose: head movements, intense licking, chewing, and intermittent sniffing ( ). Previous studies have shown that the increase in the time and number of escalations is due to an increase in dopaminergic and glutamatergic activity in the cortical areas of the brain, which results in repetitive behaviors ( , ). The aqueous lyophilisate of F. mucuso (25, 50, and 100 mg/kg) had a consistent calming effect on the time to climb and the number of climbs between 10 and 65 min. The reduction in the time and number of escalations reflects the simplification of the positive symptoms of schizophrenia. F. mucuso appears to have a stimulating effect on GABA receptors, which promotes a decrease in neuronal excitation by lowering dopamine levels ( ). However, F. mucuso reduced ketamine-induced repetitive behavior between 10 and 65 min. Our results are consistent with those obtained for Morinda citrifolia ( ), Terminalia ivorensis ( ), Scopoletin and Rutin ( ), and Terminalia macroptera ( ), which reduced stereotypy in mice, demonstrating their antipsychotic effects. Ketamine-induced hyperlocomotion is partly attributed to the blockade of NMDA receptors in the mesolimbic regions, leading to disinhibition and a consequent increase in neuronal excitation ( ). In addition, ketamine acts as an indirect dopamine agonist, which explains the behavioral stimulation ( ). The aqueous lyophilisate of F. mucuso (25, 50 and 100 mg/kg) attenuated the increase in locomotor activity by significantly reducing ( p < 0.001) the number of lines crossed and the time spent moving. Consequently, F. mucuso is likely to be used in the treatment of the positive symptoms of schizophrenia. This is because it lifts the blockage of NMDA receptors on the inhibitory GABAergic system, often considered to be associated with the behavioral hyperactivity of schizophrenia ( ). F. mucuso acts as GABA agonist, preventing the excessive release of dopamine in the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and striatum. Our results are consistent with those of ( , ), who showed that extracts that reduce the number of lines crossed and increase immobility time are effective in reducing positive symptoms. Negative symptoms of schizophrenia are a crucial feature of this disorder ( ). Frequently present at the onset of the disease, they persist throughout its course, even during periods of remission. The increase in immobility induced by ketamine in the forced swim test in mice is a negative symptom (behavioral despair) characteristic of schizophrenia ( , , ). Previous studies have reported the involvement of the 5-hydroxytryptaminergic (5-HT) system in the negative symptoms of schizophrenia ( , ). The work of ( ) indicates that increased immobility in forced swimming is caused by the blockade of 5-HT2A receptors. Similarly, the work of ( ) showed that increased which showed that an increase in extracellular glutamate concentration causes hyperactivation of serotonin 5-HT2 receptors, responsible for the increase in immobility time induced by ketamine. The aqueous lyophilisate of F. mucuso (25, 50 and 100 mg/kg) significantly reduced ( p < 0.001) immobility time in mice. The reduction in immobility in the forced swim test by the plant suggests the existence of antidepressant properties. Consequently, the lyophilisate acts as a 5-HT2A receptor antagonist and may have antipsychotic effects. Our results and observations are supported by previous studies conducted on Terminalia ivorensis ( ), Philenoptera cyanescens ( ), Terminalia macroptera ( ), Cissampelos owariensis ( ), and Diosgenin ( ), which have shown that reduced immobility is a sign of reduced despair and negative symptoms in schizophrenia. The Y-maze was developed to study learning and short-term memory functions in mice ( ). Cognitive disorders, such as deficits in attention, language, executive functions, and working memory, are fundamental cognitive symptoms in schizophrenia ( ). Ketamine-induced memory impairment is linked to antagonism of glutamatergic and acetylcholine neurotransmission and to stimulation of oxidative stress in the brain ( , ). Increased acetylcholinesterase activity in the brain also confirms memory deficits in schizophrenia ( ). Administration of F. mucuso lyophilisate (25, 50 and 100 mg/kg) reduced cognitive function impairments, as indicated by an increase in the number and percentage of correct alternations. Previous studies have reported improvements in cognitive deficits with antipsychotic drugs and plant extracts ( , , , ). Mechanistically, learning is associated with phosphorylation by calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (Ca 2+ /CaMK II). Inhibition of the NMDA receptor, which is a ligand-activated Ca 2+ channel, decreases this phosphorylation, which could explain the cognitive deficits induced by ketamine due to the disruption of long-term potentiation ( ). Previous studies have reported improvements in cognitive deficits with antipsychotic drugs and plant extracts ( , , , ). Mechanistically, learning is associated with phosphorylation by calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (Ca 2+ /CaMK II). Inhibition of the NMDA receptor, which is a ligand-activated Ca 2+ channel, decreases this phosphorylation, which could explain the cognitive deficits induced by ketamine due to the disruption of long-term potentiation ( ). In the early stages of memory formation, ketamine also inhibits acetylcholine and antagonizes the α-7nAchR nicotinic acetylcholine receptor ( ). Therefore, F. mucuso lyophilisate improves cognitive impairment through its ability to enhance working memory by stimulating the synthesis of acetylcholine and glutamate. The hypofunctionality of dopaminergic neurotransmission in the prefrontal cortex is thought to be partly responsible for schizophrenia. This is due to the blockade of NMDA receptors in the ventral tegmental area, which leads to a reduction in cortical dopamine release. Ketamine is known to influence dopamine transmission and receptor activation via multiple mechanisms ( ). It is important to note that ketamine has two major effects in the brain: it increases dopamine release in the striatum and inhibits its uptake in the same organ ( ). In addition, one mechanism by which ketamine produces undesirable behavioral effects is related to the blockade of NMDA receptors located on GABAergic inhibitory neurons in the limbic and subcortical regions of the brain ( ). This disinhibitory action would increase neuronal activity and cause excessive dopamine release in the limbic and striatal regions following dysfunction of the striatum, prefrontal cortex, and hippocampus, likely resulting in hyperdopaminergic and glutamatergic signaling in schizophrenia ( , ). NMDA receptor antagonists are associated with increased dopamine and glutamate release, leading to reduced cortical inhibition. The accumulation of cytosolic dopamine can lead to neurotoxicity, a detrimental effect on neuron survival ( , ). Ketamine induced an increase in dopamine levels in the brain ( , , ). Administration of the aqueous lyophilisate (25, 50 and 100 mg/kg) normalized dopamine levels in the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and striatum by significantly reducing ( p < 0.01; p < 0.001) dopamine levels. Our results corroborate previous studies ( , ) which indicated that hypoglutamatergia is responsible for the decrease in cerebral dopamine. F. mucuso may have acted through the mechanism of dopamine regulation and therefore as an antagonist of D1 and D2 receptors. Numerous studies have examined the neural circuits responsible for functional brain networks and cognitive processes ( ). Several studies have shown that, in addition to alterations in dopaminergic and cholinergic transmission ( ), the 5-HTergic system may also be a key factor primarily linked to negative symptoms in schizophrenia ( ). Negative symptoms have been associated with an increase in serotonergic transmission dependent on 5-HT2A/2C receptors ( ). Indeed, increased 5-HT2A receptor regulation is linked to exacerbated GABAergic phosphorylation, increased dopamine release, and glutamatergic excitotoxicity in the striatum ( , ). Consequently, these disturbances could be the cause of behavioral abnormalities. Exposure to ketamine caused an abnormal increase 5-HT concentration in the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and striatum ( , ). Previous studies have shown that the sustained loss of GABAergic interneurons induced by ketamine was linked to an upregulation of the enzyme responsible for the synthesis of superoxide radicals, which are responsible for stereotypical behaviors and depression ( , ). However, administration of the aqueous lyophilisate of F. mucuso (25, 50 and 100 mg/kg) significantly decreased ( p < 0.05; p < 0.01; p < 0.001) serotonin concentration in the striatal, prefrontal cortical, and hippocampal regions of the mouse brain. A decrease in 5-HT could be caused by an increase in the activity of the enzyme glutamate decarboxylase. The latter plays a role in regulating the synthesis of GABA from glutamate, suggesting an increase in GABAergic neurotransmission ( , ). The improvement in negative deficits would be significantly influenced by the reduction in serotonin in the PFC, HPC and ST and therefore the plant would act as a 5-HT antagonist through its modulatory activity on the 5-HTergic system. Alteration of glutamatergic neurotransmission pathways or inhibition of glutamate reuptake has been considered a determining factor in the severity of schizophrenic symptoms ( , ). This hypothesis is supported by previous studies showing altered expression and function of glutamate transporters on astrocytes or calcium-dependent signaling in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia ( ). This suggests that elevated levels of glutamate in certain brain regions or increased glutamate reuptake may contribute significantly to schizophrenia ( , ). Impaired calcium-dependent glutamate release by glutamatergic neurons has been associated with disturbances in plasma membrane calcium ATPase ( ). In addition, ketamine induces a state of hypofunction of the NMDA receptor and its downstream signaling pathways, leading to disruption of

factor in the severity of schizophrenic symptoms ( , ). This hypothesis is supported by previous studies showing altered expression and function of glutamate transporters on astrocytes or calcium-dependent signaling in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia ( ). This suggests that elevated levels of glutamate in certain brain regions or increased glutamate reuptake may contribute significantly to schizophrenia ( , ). Impaired calcium-dependent glutamate release by glutamatergic neurons has been associated with disturbances in plasma membrane calcium ATPase ( ). In addition, ketamine induces a state of hypofunction of the NMDA receptor and its downstream signaling pathways, leading to disruption of glutamate activity toward other receptors, which is linked to mitochondrial dysfunction causing hyperstimulation ( , ). Ketamine can therefore cause excessive calcium influx into the cytosol and glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity ( ). A significant flow of glutamate has been observed in the prefrontal cortex and a decrease in the hippocampus and striatum, leading to dysfunction of the cortical and striatal pathways ( , , ). Administration of aqueous lyophilisate of F. mucuso (25, 50 and 100 mg/kg) led to a decrease in glutamate levels in the hippocampus and striatum, and the opposite effect in the prefrontal cortex. Our results corroborate those of ( ). This shows that the plant has antipsychotic properties. Research has established that the positive, negative, and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia have one thing in common: neurotransmitter imbalance and disruption of connectivity between the hippocampus, striatum, and cortex ( ). Abnormalities in cholinergic transmission have been identified as being associated with the cognitive impairment observed in schizophrenia ( , ). These involve increased acetylcholinesterase concentration in the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and striatum ( , , ). This abnormality has been observed during chronic administration of ketamine ( ). Acetylcholinesterase hyperactivity causes cognitive symptoms such as memory and learning disorders ( ). This further confirms ketamine ability to influence α7nAChR receptors and other regulatory molecules essential for learning and memory ( ). Ketamine causes an increase in cholinesterase levels in the hippocampus, which leads to the suppression of acetylcholine and glutamate and causes cognitive symptoms in mice. The imbalance in cholinergic neurotransmission related to cognitive function is the result of dysregulated acetylcholinesterase activity ( ). Ketamine treatment increased AchE flow in the HPC, PFC and ST and reduced Ach concentration, thereby attenuating cholinergic transmission and suppressing nicotinic and muscarinic receptor activities. The aqueous lyophilisate of F. mucuso (25, 50, and 100 mg/kg) reversed this effect by significantly reducing ( p < 0.001) AchE activity, clearly suggesting an increase in the hippocampal, cortical, and striatal cholinergic system. Furthermore, low AchE levels are linked to cholinergic improvement. The ability of F. mucuso to reduce AchE activity, which is responsible for the degradation of acetylcholine, suggests increased cholinergic neurotransmission in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. Our results are consistent with the work of ( , , ), which showed that the improvement in memory functions is due to a reduction in AchE levels in the brain. Ketamine-induced NMDA receptor blockade causes GABAergic inhibition, leading to a decrease in gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) levels and an increase in neuronal activity, resulting in excess dopamine and serotonin in schizophrenia ( ). The administration of ketamine to mice resulted in a reduction in GABA release and, therefore, an increase in GABA-T activity and dopamine release, which stimulates stereotypy and hyperlocomotion, which are positive symptoms ( , ). This enzyme decreases the level of GABA in the brain and at the same time increases the level of the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate, causing hyper-excitation of neurons ( ). Increased GABA levels and decreased GABA-T activity after administration of different doses (25, 50 and 100 mg/kg) of the aqueous lyophilisate of F. mucuso were observed in different regions of the brain. These findings suggest a close interaction between the lyophilisate and GABAergic neurotransmission. These results show that the lyophilisate may be capable of restoring and maintaining the balance between the inhibitory system by downregulating dopamine in the prefrontal cortex. The plant acts as a GABA receptor agonist and GABA-T antagonist, inhibiting voltage-dependent sodium channels and increasing GABA concentration in the synapses, thereby facilitating GABAergic neurotransmission. F. mucuso appears to act as a tranquilizer. Our results are consistent with those obtained for Lippia multiflora ( ) and Cissus quadrangularis ( ). obtained for Lippia multiflora ( ) and Cissus quadrangularis ( ). Under normal conditions, the human body has an oxidative system and an antioxidant defense system, both of which are in dynamic equilibrium. In abnormal situations, free radicals that are not eliminated from the body can react with normal tissue cells, damaging cell structure and causing cell dysfunction. Oxidative stress occurs when the body is subjected to various internal and external environmental stimuli, leading to an imbalance between oxidative and antioxidant processes ( ). Moderate oxidative stress is necessary for normal physiological functioning of the body, while excessive oxidative stress can have deleterious effects. The main targets of oxidative stress damage are DNA, lipids and proteins ( ). Ketamine administration induced a state of NMDA receptor hypofunction, causing glutamate activity to shift to other receptors, resulting in hyperstimulation ( ). It causes excessive cytosolic Ca 2+ influx and glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity ( ). The brain accounts for 2% of total body weight but consumes about 20% of the body oxygen. Compared to other organs, it consumes more oxygen, generates more free radicals, and has lower levels of antioxidants, making it more susceptible to damage from oxidative stress ( ). Social isolation, vitamin D deficiency, chronic stress during adolescence, perinatal infections, inflammation, etc. all ultimately lead to the oxidative stress observed in schizophrenia ( ). Various studies have established a link between impaired glutamate metabolism and the oxidative stress observed in the brains of schizophrenics. Glutamate is converted to GSH via a two-step enzymatic process requiring ATP (glutamate-cysteine ligase and GSH synthase) and metabolized by the enzyme glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) to GABA, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter ( ). Thus, alterations in the GAD biosynthesis pathway and GSH synthesis are associated with redox imbalance, as evidenced by elevated MDA concentrations ( , ). This corroborates several previous studies showing that repeated administration of ketamine in mice increased lipid peroxidation (MDA) and reduced SOD, GSH and CAT activity ( , , , ). Similarly, ketamine causes an increase in nitrite levels, associated with nitrergic stress. The increase in nitrite concentration in the brain was associated with an increase in dopamine and glutamate release through upregulation of calcium-induced nitric oxide synthesis mediated by NMDA receptors ( , ). However, treatment with the aqueous lyophilisate of F. mucuso reversed these changes in the hippocampal, striatal, and cortical areas by increasing GSH levels and SOD and CAT activities. Nevertheless, F. mucuso reduced markers of lipid peroxidation (MDA) and nitrergic stress (NO) in the HPC, PFC and ST. Risperidone also increased antioxidant levels and decreased pro-oxidant levels ( , ). Oxidative stress is recognized as a pathological pathway involved in the alteration of NMDA receptor response due to changes in GSH biosynthesis ( ). It should be noted that the increase in GSH concentration may reflect a modulatory action of neurotransmitters, due to the components of GSH (glutamate, glycine, and cysteine). Our results corroborate those of ( , , ), which showed that reduced levels of MDA and NO and increased levels of CAT, SOD and GSH in the HPC, PFC and ST reflect a reduction in ketamine-induced oxidative stress. The plant acts through the oxidative pathway, protecting the brain against excitotoxicity and alteration of neuronal structure. Brain alterations were observed in microphotographs of the HPC, PFC and ST, confirmed by neuronal loss due to leukocyte infiltration, cytolysis, and necrosis in schizophrenic mice. Necrosis, hyperchromatic cells and cell degeneration were observed in CA1 and CA3. Pyknosed cells, degeneration of the pyramidal and radiatum layers, and cell death due to the action of endocellular enzymes were observed in CA1. Necrosis of the polymorphic, granular, and molecular layers was observed in the dentate gyrus. All of the above explains the neurodegeneration and neuronal death due to oxidative stress and neurochemical alteration induced by ketamine. F. mucuso (25, 50 and 100 mg/kg) restored neuronal integrity in CA1, CA3, and GD in the HPC, ST and PFC. 13 Conclusion This study evaluated the antipsychotic effects of the aqueous lyophilisate of F. mucuso bark on behavioral disturbances, oxidative stress, neurochemical deficits, and neurodegeneration induced by ketamine in mice. The results as a whole demonstrate the role of the aqueous lyophilisate of F. mucuso in managing stereotypy, hyperlocomotion, despair, and memory loss in schizophrenia. The reversal of behavioral disorders in schizophrenia by F. mucuso is mediated by the modulation of neurochemical transmission and the mechanism of oxidative and nitrergic stress inhibition. The plant repaired brain damage by restoring the integrity of neuronal cells in the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and striatum in mice. In addition, it stimulated the production of new cells. All these observations confirm the use of F. mucuso as an antipsychotic for the management of schizophrenia.

documents.title: Eating Disorders Treatment

chunks.content: Feeding Disorders Children with Pediatric Feeding Disorders (PFD) and their families experience high levels of stress and require specialized treatment to address the multiple factors that impact their feeding as well as the impairment that the feeding problems cause. In most cases, the etiology of feeding is considered complex and likely multifactorial, consisting of some combination of developmental, psychosocial, oral-motor, sensory, medical, nutritional, and /or emotional factors that may impact each other. In the proposed consensus definition, PFD “is defined as impaired oral intake that is not age-appropriate, and is associated with medical, nutritional, feeding skill, and/or psychosocial dysfunction” ( ). Without treatment, children diagnosed with pediatric feeding disorders are at risk for medical and emotional complications, such as anxiety, social isolation, and challenges to the caregiver-child relationship. Caregivers also frequently report high levels of stress (e.g., ). Prevalence and Etiology Significant feeding difficulties appear in 3–10 % of children with developmental disabilities ( ; ), up to 87% of children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD; Diolordi et al., 2016; ; Malhi et al., 2016), and 40–70% of children with chronic medical concerns (see , for review). Children may be hypersensitive, hyposensitive, or have a mix of sensitivity to certain aspects of food and/or eating (see for details). Children with ASD often experience rigidity or sensory sensitivities, which can make it challenging to eat foods, which often lack predictable tastes and textures (e.g., ). Mental health can be impacted when children may persistently and frequently become anxious, sad, angry, or frustrated during mealtime. Broadly, we posit that children may avoid eating when they have learned to pair eating with unpleasant experiences, whether the discomfort is due to medical, oral motor, sensory, or emotional experiences. For example, children who have had medical problems (e.g., history of reflux, eosinophilic esophagitis, dental pain, diarrhea) can develop anxiety around eating and negatively associate eating with pain. Both children and their caregivers can develop anxiety and high levels of stress around mealtimes that lead to maladaptive behaviors. Children with developmental and oral-motor delays may have learned that eating is challenging or frustrating. Feeding is often seen as a crucial component of nurturing children. Child-caregiver relationship disturbances and psychological problems may also contribute to feeding ( ). Children’s feeding challenges can thus negatively impact caregivers’ own sense of effectiveness and disrupt the caregiver-child relationship. Because feeding and mealtimes take place multiple times per day, challenges with feeding can be particularly disruptive to both caregivers and children. There has been a relative gap in literature focused on (1) treatments that address the cognitive and emotional components to feeding that may contribute to the feeding behaviors and caregiver stress, (2) outpatient treatment for feeding, and (3) treatments for children with comorbidities that are frequently used in clinical outpatient settings. First, there is a gap in intervention research focused on treatments that target the thoughts and feelings of children with PFD. In line with learning and cognitive behavioral theory, we hypothesize that thoughts, feelings, and behaviors impact each other. We posit children’s feeding behaviors are related to their thoughts and feelings about eating that stem from negative learning experiences, rather than representation of intentional noncompliance. In particular, anxiety, anger, frustration, or sadness as well as negative thoughts about the food are likely also contributing to the behavior of rejecting or not eating particular foods. However, most published research focuses on operant conditioning behavioral interventions (see systematic reviews by , and ). These treatments often focus on children’s compliance behaviors (e.g., bites eaten) as the outcome, without focus on the cognitive and emotional factors that may lead to the behaviors or the family systems that may be impacted by the PFD. The published studies tend to use a combination of operant conditioning strategies such as use of rewards or escape extinction models. For example, with rewards, a child may be required to perform a specific task (e.g., eat 20 bites) to earn a particular reward. With the escape extinction model, a nonpreferred or novel food may be placed on a spoon in front of a child’s mouth or in their mouth and remain there until a child complies with eating it. The theory behind the strategy is that children will eventually stop escaping the demand if they are not reinforced and allowed to avoid the food. Many previous studies have examined the efficacy of escape extinction, both with and without other behavioral techniques such as positive reinforcement ( ; ). However, in both inpatient and outpatient settings, use of escape extinction strategies can pose difficulties for some children and families. By using behavioral strategies such as nonremoval of the spoon and reward for eating bites, children must ignore their own hunger cues if they are already satiated. Children may become flooded and distrust the caregiver around the mealtime situation. In

eventually stop escaping the demand if they are not reinforced and allowed to avoid the food. Many previous studies have examined the efficacy of escape extinction, both with and without other behavioral techniques such as positive reinforcement ( ; ). However, in both inpatient and outpatient settings, use of escape extinction strategies can pose difficulties for some children and families. By using behavioral strategies such as nonremoval of the spoon and reward for eating bites, children must ignore their own hunger cues if they are already satiated. Children may become flooded and distrust the caregiver around the mealtime situation. In addition, it is not a natural way for a child to eat and can be disruptive to a family meal. For example, it may be stressful for families to spend the focus of meals on the child’s eating behaviors. These strategies tend to give children little control and may create power dynamics at the table. Escape extinction such as nonremoval of the spoon can be aversive for the parent to implement, child to experience, and negatively impact caregiver-child interactions. Promising cognitive behavioral approaches that deviate from traditional operant conditioning behavioral approaches are emerging. A pilot study by using a multifamily group cognitive behavioral approach with 11 participants ages 8–12 with ASD with IQ at or higher than 80 showed high participant satisfaction. completed a feasibility study on a cognitive behavioral therapy approach to target avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder, with clinicians rating 85% of the 17 participants who completed the study as much or very much improved. However, both of these approaches focused on older children with a cognitive level capable of engaging in more complex tasks such as monitoring their thoughts, feelings, and /or sensations and engaging in aspects of cognitive restructuring. Alternative approaches are still needed for younger children or individuals with lower developmental levels. A second gap is the relative lack of studies focused on outpatient treatments for feeding; those that exist have small sample sizes. The majority of published studies have focused on day treatment and inpatient treatments ranging from 11 to 46 intervention days (see ). While they are associated with positive outcomes, there are challenges. Day treatment program and inpatient hospitalizations are expensive, disrupt family life ( ), and may present challenges when trying to generalize behavioral techniques to the home setting. Given the intensive nature of inpatient and day treatment programs, there may be longer waitlists since only a few patients can be treated at one time. It is also unclear whether these programs can reduce the stress families feel around feeding, especially once they return to home settings. With behavioral approaches, strategies used may be specific for the client and difficult to take a universal approach with all children in the family. Among studies focused on outpatient feeding treatment, study sizes are small. For example, used an escape extinction technique by continuously placing a small amount of food on a child’s lips or inside of his mouth every 5–10 seconds. A second randomized controlled study of 21 patients found that the 73% of patients who completed the study were all able to transition from tube to oral feeding after undergoing a 6-month interdisciplinary outpatient feeding program ( ). A third study that specifically focused on children with ASD found decreased parental stress but no changes to mealtime behavior during the 8-week intervention ( ). showed decreased parental concern and increased enjoyment of food by participants in a group treatment but the study size was small ( n = 20). Further studies that incorporate parental experiences with larger sample sizes are needed. A third gap in the literature is the lack of research on the outcomes of clinical treatment approaches that are commonly used in clinical practice and offer an alternative to escape extinction and operant conditioning compliance approaches. For example, the Sensory Oral Motor Sequences (SOS) Approach ( ) to feeding is grounded in the use of systematic desensitization and learning and has been used in multiple clinical settings. The SOS Approach breaks the feeding process into 32 steps, starting with step 1, tolerating being in the same room as the food, to step 32, chewing and swallowing the food independently (Toomey). Play and social interactions are considered the incompatible relaxation responses and play is also used as a tool for learning ( ). There are few outcome studies of this approach despite its wide usage. As cited by , there is an unpublished manuscript by Creech (2006) that focused on 10 children who showed increased positive mealtime behaviors, such as smiling and positive interactions with caregivers; a different study examining 37 children showing an increase repertoire of foods (Boyd, 2007; as cited in ); and a conference presentation indicating that children who had not been gaining weight prior to treatment had increased

and social interactions are considered the incompatible relaxation responses and play is also used as a tool for learning ( ). There are few outcome studies of this approach despite its wide usage. As cited by , there is an unpublished manuscript by Creech (2006) that focused on 10 children who showed increased positive mealtime behaviors, such as smiling and positive interactions with caregivers; a different study examining 37 children showing an increase repertoire of foods (Boyd, 2007; as cited in ); and a conference presentation indicating that children who had not been gaining weight prior to treatment had increased in weight and height following treatment ( n = 46) (Toomey). This latter presentation presented some preliminary feasibility data including cost of treatment and outcomes. These pilot studies are promising, although two of them are unpublished. Of note, a significant difference between the SOS Approach and traditional behavioral approaches is that in the SOS Approach, children are in charge of how much they engage in the systematic desensitization whereas in traditional behavioral approaches, children typically obey and follow commands. Thus, the SOS Approach was chosen as the basis of the Picnic Group intervention as it offers a classical conditioning strategy for addressing feeding. Further, its focus on using playful interactions as tools for learning are in line with child development. This approach allows for intrinsic motivation around learning. The approach also allows for positive child-caregiver interactions and a return to a trajectory where children learn that mealtimes are a positive shared social experience. Another frequently used and understudied approach is the Get Permission Approach (Klein; www.getpermissionapproach.com ). This approach helps guide caregivers to read children’s cues and support them while helping their children learn to become “happy, self-directed eaters who enjoy eating, are confident in their eating skills and are internally motivated to eat enough” (Klein). Aspects of this approach were also chosen to be used in the Picnic Group as it helps caregivers feel successful. The approach changes the dynamics of the parent-child relationship in feeding such that both parties may change their thoughts, feelings, and behaviors around mealtime. In the , exposure as a form of learning is also used to help children learn to experience joy and confidence in eating. In Satter’s model, meals are considered the repeated neutral exposure to learn to enjoy foods, provide emotional and social reassurance, and social experience ( ). In brief, in the Division of Responsibility, Satter posits it is the adult’s responsibility to choose what is served, where it is served, and when it is served while it is the child’s responsibility to choose whether and how much food is eaten. This level of control that children have is similar to that of the SOS Approach. This approach signifies a significant deviation from behavioral approaches that focus on compliance based on number of bites eaten and focuses instead on children learning how to have positive relationships with feeding. However, the other components of the SOS Approach and Get Permission Approach were felt to be necessary to include in treatment with children with PFD so that children and their caregivers had systematic approaches to exploring novel or not-yet-preferred foods that could be causing them anxiety or other negative feelings. Food chaining ( ) is another strategy that is commonly used but understudied. There is one retrospective study available with 10 participants ( ), and more are needed. Food chaining links a preferred food to a new or nonpreferred food by changing one sensory property of the food at a time. For example, food chaining can be used to progress a child who only eats applesauce to raw apple slices, by modifying one aspect of the food at a time, waiting for habituation or pleasurable associations to the new variation, and then changing another aspect of the food the next time the child is working on exposures (see for sample). More research is needed on feeding protocols that may address the multiple factors that impact eating (e.g., anxiety, mechanics, sensory aversions, skill deficits), as well as the broader areas of a child’s life that are impacted by feeding problems (e.g., caregiver-child interactions during mealtime, negative associations with mealtime). Current Study This paper examines the clinical outcomes of an interdisciplinary outpatient family group outpatient treatment program that integrates principles of cognitive behavioral therapy with commonly used but understudied approaches such as the SOS Approach ( ), Get Permission Approach (Klein, www.getpermissionapproach.com ), and Satter’s Eating Competence Model and Division of Responsibility ( , , 2023), and Food Chaining ( ). These components were chosen as they help children learn how to enjoy food through a habituation and systematic desensitization model, reframe mealtimes, and foster more natural child-caregiver interactions around feeding. The current study focuses on a retrospective review of outcomes of the children who were treated by an interdisciplinary outpatient group program that uses alternative techniques to more limited escape extinction models. The Picnic Group draws from cognitive behavioral principles, the SOS Approach to Feeding ( ), the Get Permission Approach (Klein, www.getpermissionapproach.com ), , , 2023), Food Chaining ( ), and traditional oral sensory techniques. The Picnic Group used in this study has been used in our clinical setting for 15 years with children with a variety of medical and developmental disorders who have commercial and public insurance, which suggests the program is feasible to implement in a pediatric hospital outpatient setting. Our clinical impression is that this integrative method is useful for decreasing parental stress and improving children’s abilities to tolerate and enjoy a wider range of foods, but this has not been examined quantitatively. Our patients consist of a diverse group of children with isolated feeding problems as well as children with comorbid medical or developmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorders. Advantages of our program include that it is easier for caregivers to implement, it has a broader focus, addresses parental stress and parent-child relationships, and taps into the children’s intrinsic motivation to interact with food. This has improved generalizability and sustainability of treatment benefits. Picnic Group Intervention Program At our large regional pediatric hospital, our 12-week Picnic Group uses an interdisciplinary treatment approach that draws from cognitive behavioral principles and sensory integration principles. A theoretical model of the approach has been illustrated in . Techniques focus on changing the negative associations children and caregivers have built around mealtime through: classical conditioning (e.g., by increasing pleasurable interactions with each other, using playful systematic desensitization approaches to decrease anxiety and aversion to the food); addressing the impact of sensory needs on feeding; addressing caregivers’ automatic thoughts, behaviors, and feelings around their children’s feeding; addressing the impact of feeding on the family system; and using peer modeling for social learning and support for both the children and parents/caregivers. Medical providers, dietitians, speech-language pathologists, and psychologists diagnose and treat the medical, nutritional, motor, sensory, and behavioral components of feeding problems seen in our population. Participants attend the hour-long group sessions once weekly for a total of 12 weeks. Children participate in a child’s group while caregivers participate in a caregiver group that is held simultaneously in a room with a one-way mirror. Child Approach Theoretically, in our view children’s nondesired behaviors occur in part because they have negative automatic thoughts and feelings about food or feeding, rather than misbehavior (see ). For example, when they see a nonpreferred food, they may have thoughts like “I hate dinner” or “This is going to be horrible” or “I can’t do it.” They may have feelings such as “This is scary.” Their behaviors may look like hiding, tantrumming, crying, or saying things like “I won’t eat it” or “This is yucky.” To target children’s negative automatic thoughts and feelings, children’s food selectivity is addressed through a cognitive behavioral lens, which includes aspects of the SOS Approach to Feeding ( ), the Get Permission Approach (Klein, www.getpermissionapproach.com ), , , 2023), and Food Chaining ( ). The cognitive behavioral strategies are based on classical conditioning, systematic desensitization, and habituation. The group modeling is based on social learning theory. Caregiver Approach Caregivers receive psychoeducation, cognitive behavioral therapy, family systems interventions, and parent-to-parent support to help facilitate generalization of feeding progress to the home environment, increase predictability of mealtimes, increase child-caregiver interactions during mealtime, and increase the enjoyment of family mealtime. Our approach differs from traditional operant conditioning models in most feeding treatment research that tend to rely more exclusively on operant conditioning strategies that emphasize aversive escape extinction and consistent rewarding of each bite. It also reduces the need for the caregiver to act as an authoritative disciplinarian during the meal. Instead, the caregiver can focus instead on enjoying the food and mealtime with their child rather than count how many bites the child takes. In addition, our services are provided in a group format to capitalize on peer modeling, which is also different from most published studies on feeding treatment. Hypotheses In this paper, we compare ratings between Week 12 of intervention and baseline. This study examined three primary hypotheses: Hypothesis 1: Our hypothesis is that there were fewer feeding problems and negative feeding behaviors posttreatment than at baseline. Rationale: We think children were displaying problematic feeding behaviors due to their thoughts and feelings related to feeding stimuli, rather than noncompliance or misbehavior. This hypothesis is based on research on factors that impact anxiety, development, learning, and preliminary data that make up components of the Picnic Group. By focusing on the feelings, habituation, reframing, and strategies to pair positive interactions with foods, children will have decreased anxiety about the food and therefore show fewer problematic behaviors. Hypothesis 2: Our hypothesis is that the number of foods children are willing to engage with at Week 12 is higher than the number of foods at Week 1. Rationale: We think that children are more likely to engage with food when they learn strategies to approach new or not-yet-preferred foods and practice habituating to each step while interacting with the food in a pleasurable way. This hypothesis is based on research on learning, intrinsic motivation, and the role of habituation in anxiety treatment. Hypothesis 3: Our hypothesis is that caregivers’ own strain related to oral feeding concerns will be lower at Week 12 than at Week 1. Rationale: Our program addresses caregiver feelings and provides caregivers with tools to address their own automatic thoughts, perspectives, and feelings. Based on cognitive behavioral therapy, when changing someone’s behaviors and automatic thoughts, we expect to see a change in their feelings which, in this situation, we are examining as caregiver strain. Methods Participants Between January 1, 2004 and August 31, 2014, 93 children ages 30 months to 11 years ( ) were seen by the Feeding Team for group treatment. We received approval from the hospital Institutional Review Board for conducting a retrospective analysis on these patients’ measures. Patients all exhibited feeding problems. Some children had isolated feeding problems. Other children also had comorbid medical or developmental disorders. These diagnoses include developmental delay, cystic fibrosis, ASD, craniofacial abnormalities, gastro esophageal reflux, eosinophilic esophagitis, food allergies, anxiety, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder inattentive subtype, hyperactivity/impulsivity subtype and combined subtypes, genetic syndromes such as Down Syndrome and DiGeorge syndrome, cardiac defects, history of prematurity, sensory integration disorder, and short gut syndrome. Approximately 45% of the sample had an ASD. Although there is considerable heterogeneity of underlying diagnoses as well as overall severity of feeding problems, the children were similar in the phase of intervention required and were included because they were representative of the clinic population that consists of varying diagnoses. Some children were utilizing nasogastric or gastric tubes for nutritional and/or hydration needs at the time they attended group. All children could separate from their caregivers, attend to motivating, tabletop activities for 30–40 minutes without one-to-one support from an adult, and were judged clinically to have potential benefit from peer modeling, based on caregiver or therapist reports. Patients were not selected randomly. All patients received the same topics in treatment with some variability in order of topics. All patients who received treatment and completed pre- and post-intervention assessments are included in the review. Groups consisted of children with Latinx/Hispanic, Asian, Black/African-American and White backgrounds ( ). Non-English-speaking children and/or families participated in our groups through interpretation. Most participants were boys (73/93 or 78%). Patient characteristics are presented in . Patients all had feeding problems, although some children with swallowing problems or predominantly oral motor problems were typically referred to individual treatment to better address those difficulties. Some participants had previously participated in individual or group feeding therapy with an occupational therapist or speech-language pathologist or had had consultations with a gastroenterologist, registered dietitian or behavior therapist. Feeding History Survey This questionnaire was created to gather information from families about the child’s feeding problems and experiences starting at birth. The data collected from this survey yields the number of feeding problems indicated by the caregiver from a checklist of possibilities. The feeding problems on this measure are specific to the child and are considered negative behaviors. The caregiver indicates whether the behavior is present. Children’s Eating Behavior Inventory This measure asks caregivers to record the frequency of different eating and mealtime behaviors. Caregivers also indicated whether the behavior was problematic to them. Although normative data is reported in the article accompanying the inventory, for our purposes, we recorded the number of behaviors reported as a problem by the caregivers ( ). The types of behaviors on this measure range from positive to negative and include other family members in addition to the child. The caregiver completing this measure is asked to report the frequency of all behaviors and whether the behavior constitutes a problem from their perspective. Feeding Caregiver Strain Questionnaire This measure was adapted from the Caregiver Strain Questionnaire ( ) that was originally intended to measure the impact that living with a child with emotional and behavioral problems had on the family and caregiver. For most items, “emotional or behavioral problem” was replaced with “feeding difficulties.” For our purposes, caregivers were asked to focus on the past 6 weeks instead of past 6 months. We reported the total score for this instrument, reversing the value of one item. Bites Swallowed A trained assistant tracked and documented the level of interaction with food items as they were presented at each treatment session, and whether each food item reached the swallowing stage at that session. These results were reviewed and confirmed by one of two clinicians who were present throughout the treatment sessions. A standard test menu with foods from different food groups and with different textures is offered at both Week 1 and Week 12 to facilitate comparison. Statistical Methodology We reported the median and range for both baseline and 12-week measurements ( ). To compare outcomes between baseline and the 12-week follow-up, we used the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test. Each p -value was adjusted for multiple comparisons via the Bonferroni method. Hedges’s g is reported as a general effect size measure for differences in measurements, with rough interpretation of Hedges’s g as small (0.2), moderate (~0.5), and large (~0.8) ( ). Spearman correlations were calculated to assess the association between demographic and diagnoses with treatment outcomes. A linear regression was also conducted to examine whether demographics or diagnoses were associated with differences in outcomes. Procedures On average, each family in the group brings in two foods per week for all children in the group to share, with one food that is already familiar or preferred, and another food that is new, in progress, or not yet preferred. To start changing the children’s automatic thoughts on food with ones they like versus dislike, each week revolves around a particular theme based on shape (e.g., foods that can be cut into triangles), color (e.g., foods that are green), or taste (e.g., citrus or sour foods). This allows both children and caregivers to start discussing foods with other characteristics other than like or dislike and allows for nonjudgmental descriptive words for various foods. During these sessions, children typically engage in exposures with 8 to 10 foods per week in session, depending on group size or attendance. Caregivers are also instructed to expose their children to new, in progress, and not-yet-preferred foods at mealtime at home. New foods are ones that children have not been exposed to before. In-progress foods are those that children have started engaging in exposures with. Not-yet-preferred foods are foods that children have tried but may not like yet. Families are generally guided to have 75% of the meal consist of familiar or preferred foods, and 25% of the meal consisting of a new, in progress, or not-yet-preferred food. Families are generally guided to have 75% of the meal consist of familiar or preferred foods, and 25% of the meal consisting of a new, in progress, or not-yet-preferred food. During the classical conditioning approach exposure technique, instead of having an immediate expectation to consume a new food, children are presented with multiple intermediate steps in a fear hierarchy, such as smelling the food, touching the unfamiliar food, or kissing the food. Children have control over the pace of moving through the hierarchy using play and exploration until children are habituated and not as fearful of eating the new food, based on their affect or behaviors. The process lets them build positive associations with the food. While the majority of interactions are based on classical conditioning principles, the approach also incorporates aspects of operant conditioning at times, such as intermittent use of social rewards such as verbal encouragement to reinforce approximations to the goal. For example, a child may hear “Great job touching the carrot” or receive a “High Five.” At times, children may receive other rewards for their efforts. For example, if a family is having challenges with motivation in the home setting, they may track the number of times a child engages with a step on a fear hierarchy such as smelling a food or making teeth marks in the food. A predetermined reward may have been discussed with the family, such as reading an extra book at bedtime. Broadly, however, the goal is for children and families to be trained to enjoy exploring food such that the positive experience (e.g., play) is presented simultaneously with the food in a classical conditioning presentation, rather than to eat for the purposes of receiving rewards. Thus, in our program, the food is considered the stimulus and presented simultaneously with pleasurable experiences. Most sessions are facilitated by an occupational therapist and a speech-language pathologist, with occasional psychologist participation. From the moment children arrive, the emphasis is on creating the positive association between mealtime routine and pleasure. When transitioning from the waiting room to the clinic room, clinicians already engage in pleasurable activities such as blowing bubbles or singing songs to decrease stress and increase regulation. The session begins with a 10-minute sensory warm-up activity such as smelling various food odors and guessing the item or using hands to paint with shaving cream. We often read a story related to food or eating and the children are encouraged to participate by filling in words or turning pages. This activity is followed by hand-washing and oral warm-ups utilizing an oral motor tool. Children then go to the mealtime table. At the table, children engage in a routine that is also intended to keep children feeling regulated before engaging more in exposures. Children follow a routine of examining and passing each food item around. Each child takes some of the food item onto his, her, or their plate, typically with their hands or utensil. Children, the speech-language, and occupational therapists then playfully interact with the food using a systematic desensitization and hierarchical approach. In keeping with the tenets of the SOS Approach ( ), children are encouraged to slowly increase level of interaction with the foods, such as touching the food with their fingers, smelling the food, bringing food close to mouth, blowing food near mouth into an “all done” or “bye-bye” bowl, touching the food to lips or “kissing” the food, licking the food, making teeth marks into the food, taking a bite of food and spitting it into the “all-done” bowl, taking a bite of food and chewing it before spitting it into the “all-done” bowl, or chewing and then swallowing the food. Children and adults at the table are encouraged to be as creative and silly as they would like as they engage in their food exploration, emphasizing the pleasurable quality of the food interaction. For example, if the step they are working on is bringing the food closer to their mouth, they might place the food on the back of their hand and blow it off. If they are working on bite pressure, they might hold the food between their teeth like a puppy holds a bone and make barking noises. Therapists encourage increased interaction with the food based on the child’s responses, peer modeling, and giving some autonomy. For example, a therapist might say, “Should we touch the food to our chin or our lips next?” The children move onto the next step if they have habituated to the step they are on and

For example, a therapist might say, “Should we touch the food to our chin or our lips next?” The children move onto the next step if they have habituated to the step they are on and are enjoying that level of interaction. Children are never forced to progress to a particular step. If they have an aversive reaction to a step, they go back to the previous step until they have fully habituated and ideally, can enjoy that step. The child’s level of interaction with the food item is monitored and tracked. Children’s automatic thoughts are addressed by focusing on reframing comments like “I don’t like it” to “I’m not used to it yet” and “I’m learning about this food.” Similarly, instead of viewing food dichotomously as like/dislike, children are taught to think about foods on multiple dimensions (e.g., crunchy versus soft), and what they can do with the food instead of just “I can’t eat it.” At the end of the therapeutic meal, children are expected to engage in an end routine. They kiss or blow their remaining food into the “all done” or “bye-bye” bowl. They then clear their plates, wash their hands, and receive the “report card,” which details their achievements during the session. Parents are encouraged to continue food explorations throughout the intervening week, also engaging in a beginning, middle, and end routine to the mealtime with emphasis on pleasurable interactions with foods that may fall within the theme of the week, or other food the family is eating. They do not need to be the exact same foods as the ones practiced in the clinic session. The focus is on employing food exploration strategies in as many meals as possible so that children learn to generalize the process for engaging in new foods, rather than specific food themselves. On most weeks, while children are in the session with an occupational therapist and speech-language therapist, parents are in their own group in an adjacent room and can watch their children participate in the group. The psychologist provides cognitive behavioral strategies and family systems–based group therapy. The psychologist discusses behavior management, including learning the antecedents and consequences associated with desired and undesired behaviors and links these to potential thoughts and emotions. The group explores changing familial patterns of behaviors at mealtimes, monitoring caregivers’ emotions and feelings that emerge during mealtimes, learning adult coping techniques during mealtime stress, reframing negative cognitions (automatic thoughts) during mealtime, reducing parent-child conflict related to food and improving family systems functioning during mealtime to facilitate carry-over from hospital to home environments. Parents are taught to recognize and understand symptoms of anxiety and sensory aversions, SOS, the Satter Eating Competence Model, and Food Chaining ( ) approaches, and systematic desensitization techniques to address their children’s anxiety and sensory aversions. See for a sample list of topics. The order of topics may shift depending on provider availability. In terms of addressing automatic thoughts, if parents have an automatic thought such as, “She would never eat that” or “He doesn’t eat fish,” they may be guided to formulate an alternate thought, such as, “She is still learning to accept jicama” or “He doesn’t eat fish YET.” If a parent personalizes or overgeneralizes a situation, such as “He won’t eat for me,” parents may be guided to reframe the situation as “He is nervous and is working on eggs” or “He is not eating this yet.” To reframe fear of a food with a child, they might say, “We’re still learning about apples. We’re learning about how it looks, how it smells, etc.” “It’s small and white and hard. For example, a parent may state “I’m a bad parent” as a result of negative messages from others and themselves that their children’s weight and eating issues are their fault. During group sessions, the clinicians and other parents help the parent reframe these thoughts and gain self-compassionate insight. In terms of behavior, parents are guided to offer preferred food along with nonpreferred food to emphasize the idea that both foods are pleasurable, increase likelihood children will eat something at the meal and reduce refusal behaviors, and reduce parental stress about how much the child eats. Summary of Picnic Group Progress Ana expanded both her repertoire and intake of foods by the end of Picnic Group. She gained 0.20 kg and grew 1 cm over the course of 12 weeks. Since the first session, she stopped using two cans of Pediasure by gtube, and was on track to being weaned entirely from the gtube 2 months after the end of group. She attended 10 out of 12 sessions. At the end of group, she tolerated a variety of textures and tastes. She was also taking bigger bites and consuming more. Overall, she made excellent progress in the feeding group program. She made the most improvements in the areas of willingness to try new foods, oral motor skills, and use of communication during mealtimes. She added many new foods to her repertoire, including small tastes of yogurt, chicken, fruits, and vegetables. She continued to struggle with limited volume. However, over time and with practice, it was expected that she would expand the volume taken. Behavior was often exemplary, and she improved in her ability to verbally communicate wants and needs during mealtimes. She only demonstrated negative behaviors at mealtime when she felt pressured to eat, when she anticipated food being fed directly to her, or if there were too many non-preferred foods on her plate. On all primary measures, significant changes were noted between first and last visit. Fewer feeding problems were endorsed on the Feeding History Survey at Session 12 (median = 5) than at Session 1 (median = 6; p = 0.012). Specifically, children were reported to have one less type of feeding problem at the end of 12 weeks. Caregivers also reported fewer specific types of eating and mealtime problematic behaviors on the Child Eating Behavior Inventory between Session 12 and Session 1 ( p < 0.001). There was a moderate effect size in all cases ( ). Children’s mealtime behaviors in session also shifted. Children tended to be able to work up the food hierarchy for more types of foods per session. At baseline, children worked up the food hierarchy to biting and swallowing approximately 3 test menu foods during the session (median reported), while they could work up to the biting and swallowing step for 5 of 9 test menu foods presented at the 12 th session ( p < 0.001). At the family systems level, caregivers reported a reduction in the impact of feeding problems on the caregivers and family ( p < 0.001). Results of the evaluation indicated that age, gender, and race were not associated with treatment outcomes. However, whether a child had a medical versus developmental diagnosis was associated with a difference in the extent to which feeding created strain in the family ( p = 0.010). Caregiver strain decreased overall and caregivers of children who had a developmental diagnosis showed greater decrease in strain. A child’s diagnosis was associated with the degree to which caregiver strain decreased between Week 1 and Week 12. Caregivers of children with a developmental disability showed greater decrease in caregiver strain. Discussion This study had several primary findings. This study takes a first step at examining the

Caregiver strain decreased overall and caregivers of children who had a developmental diagnosis showed greater decrease in strain. A child’s diagnosis was associated with the degree to which caregiver strain decreased between Week 1 and Week 12. Caregivers of children with a developmental disability showed greater decrease in caregiver strain. Discussion This study had several primary findings. This study takes a first step at examining the potential impact of a 12-week interdisciplinary treatment program that involves both children and caregivers. Consistent with hypotheses, results of this study suggest children in Picnic Groups showed symptom improvement during the 12-week course and caregivers report less caregiver strain. Caregivers of children with developmental disabilities indicate the greatest decrease in caregiver strain by Week 12. This study has several strengths. The study addresses the gap in literature by examining the use of a treatment program that addresses the potential thoughts, feelings, and learning needed to enjoy food. The program uses classical conditioning strategies such as systematic desensitization and habituation by increasing pleasurable food and mealtime experiences, while still incorporating aspects of operant conditioning to reward efforts, and cognitive behavioral principles to target family functioning and the negative thoughts that are associated with mealtime. In contrast, many other studies to date have focused more exclusively on operant conditioning techniques such as aversive escape extinction approaches and eating to receive rewards (e.g., see review by ). With respect to the reported feeding-related problems, types of problems that were improved upon include tolerance of the sight or smell of non-preferred foods on the table, as well as willingness to touch, smell, or lick novel or non-preferred food items. In this manner, children are progressively desensitized to these foods, allowing them to gradually work towards biting, chewing, and swallowing the food items while maintaining autonomy for what they put inside their mouth. This study found increased ability to work up the food hierarchy. While there is sometimes concern that children may not reach the eventual goal of biting and chewing food if they were not forced to, our participants were able to reach the stage of biting and chewing foods at the 12 th session. A potential benefit of this progressive hierarchical approach is that “trying” new foods can feel more manageable and predictable to both children and caregivers when they can progress through the same intermediate steps each time. In addition, smaller incremental changes (e.g., being able to tolerate the food on the same plate or touching their skin) can increase children’s sense of mastery and increase caregivers’ ability to feel effectual. The program also is unique in its approach in ensuring families provide modeling for food behaviors to make mealtimes more natural, rather than focused on child compliance or bites swallowed. This feeding program appeared to decrease caregiver-reported feeding stress, as intended. One strength of this feeding program is that it addresses the family system impacted by feeding problems and not just the specific feeding mechanics and behavior of the child. Consistently using an escape extinction model and rewards system or operant conditioning model at each meal with children, as in many other types of feeding interventions, has the potential to be difficult to maintain over time ( ). In our intervention, the goal is focused more on meeting a child where they are, keeping interactions enjoyable and fun, stopping at the food hierarchy level when they have reached the upper limit of tolerance for that meal, and revisiting the food through additional exposures at another time until the child is habituated and even enjoying that level of exposure. The family focuses on positive modeling and increased conversations during mealtimes that are more naturalistic, rather than focus on just the child with feeding problems. This approach has the potential to decrease the extent to which feeding problems impact the family. The results of our analyses suggest that this approach is related to decreases in caregiver stress and the negative impact of feeding problems on the family. It is particularly interesting that caregivers of children with developmental disabilities reported a significant decrease in caregiver strain, a highly desirable outcome given the multiple demands these caregivers are faced with. Family mealtimes are often the only times during a family’s day that the entire family is in the same place, at the same time. Conversations can help increase children’s vocabulary, and family mealtimes have also been linked to positive mental health and academic benefits ( ; ; ). By decreasing the need for meals to focus on compliance, families can focus more on these joyful types of conversations and playful interactions that can foster positive

of children with developmental disabilities reported a significant decrease in caregiver strain, a highly desirable outcome given the multiple demands these caregivers are faced with. Family mealtimes are often the only times during a family’s day that the entire family is in the same place, at the same time. Conversations can help increase children’s vocabulary, and family mealtimes have also been linked to positive mental health and academic benefits ( ; ; ). By decreasing the need for meals to focus on compliance, families can focus more on these joyful types of conversations and playful interactions that can foster positive child-parent interactions. This study is also unique in reporting results on the use of a group treatment format and use of peer modeling as a component to treatment. Children often learn from each other and it was hypothesized that it could be beneficial for children to see other children also sharing similar struggles with food and to be able to practice the steps to eating together. Group treatment also has the advantage for caregivers. Many caregivers with children with feeding disorders experience stress and social isolation (e.g., ). The group format allows caregivers to share their experiences with other caregivers who understand the level of stress and strain children’s feeding problems can cause. Another strength of this study is its inclusion of children with diverse medical and diagnostic backgrounds. Approximately 45% of the participants have an autism spectrum disorder. Children with autism spectrum disorders can sometimes have difficulties with unstructured periods at school such as lunchtime, and selective eating and feeding problems may exacerbate difficulties at lunchtime. This treatment approach allows these patients the experience of meal periods that include other children. In addition, most children eat some meals with other children in the school setting such that the feeding group could imitate the experience of eating with peers and help with generalizability. Additionally, this study begins to address some of concerns regarding numbers of subjects, use of caregiver questionnaires, description of maladaptive behaviors, and social validation. This study utilizes a multimethod, multireported approach. Both caregiver reports, as well as objective behavioral measurements in sessions, were recorded and compared. Limitations and Future Directions This retrospective research design has limitations. First, this study would have been strengthened by being conducted first as a feasibility study that gathered feasibility measures to be in line with the NIH Stage Model for Behavioral Intervention Development ( https://www.nia.nih.gov/research/dbsr/nih-stage-model-behavioral-intervention-development ). There are several aspects that suggest the program would be feasible. The SOS Approach, a component of the Picnic Group, has reported on costs of running the SOS Approach program ( ). The program has offered courses and workshops to providers for decades, which suggests acceptability to providers and the ability to disseminate the intervention. The Get Permission Approach, another component of the Picnic Group, similarly offers workshops and courses to providers, suggesting acceptability and dissemination possibilities ( www.getpermissionapproach.com ) . A retrospective study of 10 participants in a Food Chaining intervention showed efficacy in the community setting ( ). Another intervention component was Satter’s Division of Responsibility and Eating Competence Model, which also trains other professionals and offers continuing education credits, suggesting acceptability and ability to disseminate the intervention ( https://www.ellynsatterinstitute.org/ ). Further, a feasibility study examining an adaptation of Satter’s work showed the adaptation was acceptable and feasible ( ). While this study did not collect feasibility data, it provides significant value. First, one of the main reasons to start with a feasibility study is that some interventions may require too many resources to be implemented in real-world settings ( https://www.nia.nih.gov/research/dbsr/nih-stage-model-behavioral-intervention-development ). At our pediatric hospital outpatient setting, groups typically run 3 times a year and this study examines groups over a 10-year period. This history suggests this program can be implemented in a real-world community setting with community-level therapists to work with patients who had a mix of commercial and public insurance, as well as a breadth of diagnoses. This history suggests that adequate resources were available to implement the program, as occupational therapists, speech language pathologists, dietitians, and psychologists were able to implement the program during this period and the program is sustainable. Another reason to initially conduct feasibility studies is that it can be difficult to generalize a treatment from a research study to the community setting, and treatment outcomes may weaken in community setting with community providers ( ). The positive outcomes of this retrospective study in a real community setting with community providers is promising, as one might expect a study conducted under more robust research conditions with a higher level of fidelity may yield stronger outcomes. This current study provides a first step to suggesting this type of group treatment can be implemented and yield positive outcomes when implemented in a community-based setting with community-based providers. This pilot

it can be difficult to generalize a treatment from a research study to the community setting, and treatment outcomes may weaken in community setting with community providers ( ). The positive outcomes of this retrospective study in a real community setting with community providers is promising, as one might expect a study conducted under more robust research conditions with a higher level of fidelity may yield stronger outcomes. This current study provides a first step to suggesting this type of group treatment can be implemented and yield positive outcomes when implemented in a community-based setting with community-based providers. This pilot data has value for providing support for planning a more formalized prospective feasibility study in a research context that then follows the NIH Stage Model for Behavioral Intervention Development. A second limitation is this study was retrospective, rather than prospective. Patients were not randomized, there was no control group, and raters were not blinded. This study takes a first step at examining the potential impact of an interdisciplinary group format using systematic desensitization in a playful social setting and a family-centered and classical conditioning approach by increasing pleasurable food experiences to increase food repertoire. Future studies should gather feasibility data. They can compare progress of children in the group setting to children on a waitlist to examine impact of intervention versus natural maturation. Future studies might also compare long-term outcomes between randomized groups where children underwent this current interdisciplinary group with systematic desensitization, and group where children underwent a more operant conditioning and escape extinction model. Several articles have discussed the need for randomized, controlled trials for therapeutic approaches to address pediatric feeding difficulties ( ; ). Future studies could examine long-term follow-up and further analyze cost-effectiveness of this program. Third, this study’s outcome measures were broad, such that it is hypothesized that decreased caregiver stress was related to increased emphasis on positive experiences of food at mealtimes, changes to the conceptualization of the responsibility of caregivers at mealtime, change of their roles from command enforcers, and targeted strategies to address cognitions, emotions, and behaviors of the caregivers. The study also examined children’s tolerance of new foods. However, specific item outcomes were not directly compared. Further studies can examine outcomes such as tube dependency, variety of food repertoire, oral motor skills, as suggested by . In addition, future studies can directly examine factors that potentially mediate or moderate the impact of treatment, such as parenting style, other concurrent interventions, and patient medical status to help elucidate what works for whom the best, and which specific components of the treatment are most robust. This study provides promising outcomes of an alternative approach to feeding treatment.
