The majority (57.4%) had already undergone at least 1 (up to 5) previous treatments, mainly for panic disorder: 31.5% had received at least 1 inpatient treatment, 29.6% outpatient psychotherapy, and 7.5% had been exclusively treated with medication. At intake, 22.2% of patients were on antidepressants, 9.3% each were on anxiolytics or herbal sedatives, and 27.8% took other medication. At follow-up, remission was achieved by PFPP in 50.0%, and by CBT in 55.6% (χ 2 = 0.15, df = 1, P = 0.78). Scores on the PDSS, the primary outcome measure, declined from pre- to posttreatment and from posttreatment to follow-up. Corrected ESs for PFPP were d = 1.28 and 1.03, respectively. These were d = 1.81 and 1.28, respectively, for CBT (uncorrected ESs in ). A total of 5 (13.2%) participants of the completer sample (3 from PFPP, 2 from CBT) sought additional psychotherapy during follow-up (4 outpatient and 2 inpatient psychotherapy). Two patients from the CBT condition received additional CBT. Two PFPP patients sought inpatient treatment—1 owing to a relapse, 1 after severe psychosocial stress (10-year-old daughter was missing)—1 began a new CBT. shows the results of the regression analyses on the changes of the PDSS score, from pre- to posttreatment and from pretreatment to follow-up. LEAS baseline, PDSS baseline, and CGI were predictors explaining 65% of variance of the change of the PDSS score, from pre- to posttreatment. Only PDSS baseline was a predictor from pretreatment to follow-up. Treatment group was not a significant predictor of outcome. Secondary Outcomes Both treatments had large effects on global functioning (as measured by the CGI) and on general anxiety (as measured by the HARS); CBT also had a strong effect on depression (as measured by the HDRS, but not the BDI) and distress at follow-up. The other ESs were small to moderate ( ). Regarding secondary outcomes, there were moderate ES differences favouring CBT for HARS and HDRS at termination and small ES differences favouring CBT at follow-up (CGI, HDRS, and SCL-90-R). Discussion Overall, our study showed that PFPP can be effectively implemented as a short-term treatment for panic disorder, with and without agoraphobia, into routine care in Germany by psychoanalysts who had been trained in and used a long-term PFPP treatment model. Two thirds of our sample had comorbid Axis I or II diagnoses. Most of our patients also suffered from comorbid medical conditions and had undergone previous psychiatric treatment, highlighting the severity of the diagnoses. Based on ITT analysis, 47.2% of the patients who were randomized to PFPP achieved response and 44.4% achieved remission at termination. While not statistically significant, there were small-to-moderate ES differences favouring CBT (response 72.2%, remission 55.6%). At termination, ESs for the PDSS, our primary outcome, were large for both groups (PFPP: d = 1.15; after correcting for initial LEAS scores d = 1.28; CBT: d = 2.26; d = 1.81 after correction). We also demonstrated large treatment effects in both conditions on general anxiety and on psychosocial functioning. PFPP also had moderate effects on depression (HDRS) and small-to-moderate effects on distress. CBT had strong effects on depression (HDRS), moderate-to-large effects on distress, and small-to-moderate effects on the BDI score. At 6-month follow-up, PFPP continued to be effective as evidenced by stable response and remission (50%) rates, which were comparable to CBT (55.6%). ESs at follow-up were large in both treatments (1.03 for PFPP and 1.28 for CBT). Thus small-to-moderate ES differences of our primary outcome (scores and response and [or] remission rate) at termination favouring CBT were no longer present. PFPP posits that termination constitutes a

psychosocial functioning. PFPP also had moderate effects on depression (HDRS) and small-to-moderate effects on distress. CBT had strong effects on depression (HDRS), moderate-to-large effects on distress, and small-to-moderate effects on the BDI score. At 6-month follow-up, PFPP continued to be effective as evidenced by stable response and remission (50%) rates, which were comparable to CBT (55.6%). ESs at follow-up were large in both treatments (1.03 for PFPP and 1.28 for CBT). Thus small-to-moderate ES differences of our primary outcome (scores and response and [or] remission rate) at termination favouring CBT were no longer present. PFPP posits that termination constitutes a crisis in treatment enabling the patient to work through issues of separation, which may account for a slightly lower response and (or) remission at termination, while long-term effect on panic symptoms are comparable to CBT. Limitations We performed an effectiveness study to determine the feasibility of implementing PFPP into clinical practice in a different language from the one in which it was developed, and in the context of a different health care system. We chose to compare it with gold standard treatment, CBT with exposure therapy as performed by experts in this modality, to evaluate whether dynamic clinicians used to a long-term treatment model could adapt their style effectively to this symptom-focused, time-limited psychoanalytic intervention. The 2 CBT therapists had been trained and routinely practiced the manualized study treatment. The most effective CBT therapist carried the highest caseload ( n = 12); the high ESs exceeded previous CBT trials with comparably high rates of comorbidity. The psychoanalysts in the study were experienced in performing long-term treatments (with high and low frequency), applying short-term psychotherapy only to patients in acute crisis and to determine indication for long-term treatment. They had neither a background in symptom-focused, time-limited treatment nor in PFPP. Future comparative trials will need to strive for better therapist matching. As psychoanalysts in Germany do not routinely perform manualized, short-term training treatments, it will be advisable to have them perform pilot cases before entering patients into a clinical trial. Owing to limited funding, we were restricted to small sample sizes. As our focus was on implementation of a new treatment, randomization was performed in a 2:1 ratio. The study was not powered for detection of nonequivalence of the 2 treatments. The LEAS reliably and validly assesses different levels of implicit and explicit affect processing, and has been used extensively and standardized in the German population. , For patients experiencing panic seemingly out of the blue, we considered the LEAS a potentially important patient variable. Indeed, baseline LEAS had a strong effect at treatment termination. As we found a significant baseline difference favouring the CBT condition, we took LEAS into account in our statistical analyses. While an interesting finding in itself, however, its effect on outcome was not our primary hypothesis. While most ESs were comparable, several ESs between groups were slightly to moderately larger for CBT at termination, levelling out to follow-up. Note that, in our conservative analysis, as in many CBT trials, over 40% of patients did not respond in the long run to either intervention. Regardless of treatment condition, at follow-up, 13.2% of the sample sought additional treatment. Thus there may be a need for longer treatment interventions in this highly comorbid sample. Stratifying patients by LEAS may be a promising strategy to be tested in future studies.

chunks.content: Note on terminology Following a discussion among the guideline development group and our expert-by-experience collaborators, we agreed to use the term “female” in this guideline to refer to both women and girls whose biological sex at birth was female. Introduction The median age of onset of psychosis is 20 years, however, symptom onset is often later in females, with a second peak after age 50. Psychotic disorders are recognized among the most severe and debilitating health conditions. , Early intervention at first onset of symptoms is considered the gold standard of care as reducing the duration of untreated psychosis can improve clinical, functional, and social outcomes. , Early intervention services offer psychological, social, occupational, and educational interventions, alongside antipsychotic medicines as a primary treatment for first-episode psychosis. Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) support the translation of research evidence into clinical practice. Several CPGs exist for the management of first-episode psychosis. Except for clozapine (not first-line), evidence suggests minimal differences in efficacy between second-generation antipsychotic medicines in first-episode psychosis. Therefore, current guidelines recommend selection of first medicine as a shared decision incorporating clinician opinion, medicine availability, and individual preferences regarding benefits and side-effects. , Approximately half of those presenting with first-episode psychosis are treated in community settings where there is an opportunity to offer the medicines with the most favorable side-effect profiles. Some CPGs favor second-generation antipsychotic as first-choice due to their more acceptable side-effects, particularly considering neurological side-effects. , Others recommend avoiding olanzapine first-line (especially for younger individuals) due to the significant risk of metabolic side-effects and weight gain. , A specific guideline for females is needed to enhance current CPG recommendations and ensure that outcomes that are critically important to females are considered in the recommendation process. Given the large number of available antipsychotic medicines, it is not considered feasible to comprehensively discuss the benefits and side-effects of all options within a single clinical encounter, especially with those who have no prior exposure to antipsychotic medicines. International prescribing data consistently show that antipsychotic use in first-episode psychosis is concentrated among a small number of medicines, namely olanzapine, risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride, quetiapine and aripiprazole. In some countries, olanzapine remains the most frequently prescribed first-line agent. , , , However, evidence indicates that removing olanzapine as a first-line option within CPGs is associated with reduced prescribing. Similarly, medicine-specific recommendations delivered through shared decision-making are associated with improved prescribing quality and better clinical outcomes compared with non-directive guidance to prescribe any second-generation agent. Rather than restricting choice, these approaches aim to organize medicines into categories and highlight preferred options to support informed shared decision-making. Overall, while CPGs broadly support the use of any second-generation antipsychotic, prescribing practice remains narrowly focused, and greater specificity within guidelines appears to improve care. Current CPGs remain limited in their ability to account for biological variability, particularly sex differences, including how females experience side effects and what they consider most important in the decision-making process. Due to the historical under-representation of females in preclinical and clinical trials, existing CPGs are primarily based on studies conducted in predominantly male populations and do not provide sex-specific recommendations. Consistent with this, sex-differences in antipsychotic efficacy remain insufficiently studied to guide medicine choice. A recent systematic review reported only limited evidence of superior efficacy of olanzapine in females, with no consistent sex-based efficacy differences identified for any other antipsychotic medicines. Current CPGs also fail to consider the overlap between peak age of onset of psychosis and peak fertility in females. Additionally, sex differences in pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics may influence antipsychotic tolerability and safety. , As early treatment experiences strongly influence adherence and outcomes, antipsychotic medicines optimization for females experiencing first-episode psychosis is vital. Hyperprolactinemia occurs with many antipsychotic medicines with both symptomatic and asymptomatic consequences. Although evidence for sex-differences in prevalence is mixed, females consistently experience greater magnitudes of prolactin elevation than males. Adolescents appear particularly vulnerable to this side-effect. For females, symptomatic consequences include amenorrhea, galactorrhea, sexual dysfunction, and infertility, which are reported among the most subjectively distressing antipsychotic side-effects and are associated with loss of the feeling of femininity and reduced quality of life. The asymptomatic consequences of antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia are understudied. Large cohort studies have reported decreased bone mineral density (impaired attainment of peak bone mass in <25 years), increased risk of osteopenia, osteoporosis, and fractures in females exposed to prolactin-raising agents as well as severely increased breast cancer odds (20% after 1-4 years and 47%-56% after ≥5 year). , Additionally, as high prolactin levels suppress estrogen production, hyperprolactinemia may also worsen psychotic symptoms and cognition in females. While cardiometabolic side-effects do not appear more common in females overall, sex differences in antipsychotic-induced weight gain remain inadequately explored. Qualitative studies show weight gain is highly distressing for females, undermining body image, self-esteem and adherence and a preference for more

density (impaired attainment of peak bone mass in <25 years), increased risk of osteopenia, osteoporosis, and fractures in females exposed to prolactin-raising agents as well as severely increased breast cancer odds (20% after 1-4 years and 47%-56% after ≥5 year). , Additionally, as high prolactin levels suppress estrogen production, hyperprolactinemia may also worsen psychotic symptoms and cognition in females. While cardiometabolic side-effects do not appear more common in females overall, sex differences in antipsychotic-induced weight gain remain inadequately explored. Qualitative studies show weight gain is highly distressing for females, undermining body image, self-esteem and adherence and a preference for more proactive strategies to prevent antipsychotic-induced weight gain has been expressed. Concerns about long-term cardiometabolic health as a result of weight gain have also been reported which are valid given the significant contribution of weight gain to cardiometabolic risk and all-cause mortality. , In light of these sex-specific risks and subjective side-effect burdens, we developed a CPG to inform first-choice antipsychotic medicine for females experiencing first-episode psychosis. Methods This guideline is an adaptation of existing recommendations to consider patient important outcomes for females when assessing the balance of risk and benefit in choice of antipsychotic treatment for first-episode psychosis. The GRADE-ADOLOPMENT process was followed. The manuscript has been written using the RIGHT-Ad@pt checklist for reporting adapted healthcare guideline recommendations and with reference to the AGREE II and AGREE-REX standards for CPGs. A summary of the guideline development process mapped to the AGREE II criteria is outlined in Table S1.1. Scope and Purpose The purpose of this CPG is to provide evidence-based recommendations for the choice of antipsychotic medicine for females experiencing a first-episode of psychosis. Key health questions were devised ( ). We aim to provide accessible information to clinicians, service users, and caregivers to support shared decision-making and implementation of the recommendations. The recommendations are for young females aged 13-17 years and adults 18 years and older. Recommendations apply to inpatient and community settings. An individual perspective is taken and therefore the judgments are based on the balance of expected benefits and harms, the certainty of the evidence, and acceptability, preferences, and values of those to whom the recommendations apply. Population level considerations such as equity, feasibility, and resource utilization were considered, particularly in relation to availability of newer medicines. The Guideline Development Group The guideline development group (GDG) consisted of international researchers and clinicians with expertise in women’s health, adult psychiatry, child and adolescent psychiatry and early intervention psychosis programs. All guideline group members practice in high income countries. We used the EVOLVE framework to ensure the meaningful involvement of our experts-by-experience at the optimum stages of guideline production and to routinely embed their preferences and values within the CPG. Our experts-by-experience panel were involved in identifying the topic for guideline consideration, identifying important outcomes, generating recommendations, iteratively reviewing and developing the resulting algorithm and co-designing information videos to support guideline implementation. Conflicts of interest disclosures were gathered and reviewed by the guideline chair (BOD)— . No action was required to manage conflicts of interest. Source Guideline Identification A previously published systematic review of guidelines for the pharmacological treatment of first-episode psychosis in adults was partially updated with a search of guideline repositories in February 2025 (Table S1.3A). A separate systematic search was conducted to identify source guidelines for the pharmacological treatment of psychosis in young people <18 years (Table S1.3B). All guidelines were reviewed for currency, quality, and development approach. Guidelines were assessed for quality using the AGREE II criteria by 2 independent reviewers and a third reviewer resolved any disagreement (DK, CHR, and AC). Only guidelines that scored 60% or more on “Domain 3: Rigor of Development” were considered as source guidelines. Guidelines with a full evidence synthesis, compatible with GRADE and structured Evidence to Decision approach were preferred as they are most useful in the GRADE-ADOLOPMENT process. , Data extracted from current guidelines included the method of development and the findings for the key health question of antipsychotic choice for females experiencing first-episode psychosis. Development of Guideline Recommendations Patient important outcomes from existing guidelines were reviewed by the GDG. A working group (CHR, DK, AC, BOD, FMCN, YH) reviewed the recommendations from existing guidelines, adapted the Evidence to Decision Framework ( ) and summarized the information in an algorithm for presentation to the GDG. Decisions were made by consensus. All panel members agreed on the final recommendations, the strength of the recommendations ( ) and algorithm. The guideline was field tested by members of the GDG at several stages throughout the process to elicit feedback and gauge acceptability. This field testing was carried out among consultant psychiatrists working in both inpatient and outpatient settings, advanced specialist mental health pharmacists working in an inpatient setting and the experts-by-experience panel. A final external review was conducted by two

All panel members agreed on the final recommendations, the strength of the recommendations ( ) and algorithm. The guideline was field tested by members of the GDG at several stages throughout the process to elicit feedback and gauge acceptability. This field testing was carried out among consultant psychiatrists working in both inpatient and outpatient settings, advanced specialist mental health pharmacists working in an inpatient setting and the experts-by-experience panel. A final external review was conducted by two psychiatrists. Results Female-Specific Recommendations in Existing CPGs On reviewing existing CPGs, we determined that there were no female-specific recommendations regarding choice of first antipsychotic medicine (Tables 1.3A and 1.3B). Guideline Recommendations Patient Important Outcomes Up to 80% of those with first-episode psychosis respond to their first antipsychotic medicine. Evidence indicates that there is no one agent with significant superiority in terms of efficacy in this population. CPGs therefore recommend that the choice of first antipsychotic be based on the individual preferences regarding side-effects. , , , The GDG agreed that the critically important patient outcomes of hyperprolactinemia and cardiometabolic side-effects, particularly weight gain, should be prioritized in the Evidence to Decision Framework. Existing CPGs already address neurological side-effects by preferentially recommending second-generation over first-generation antipsychotic medicines, reflecting evidence that strong D2 receptor blockade is associated with extrapyramidal symptoms. While these outcomes have been extensively considered, hyperprolactinemia has been less consistently prioritized. The GDG therefore designated hyperprolactinemia and cardiometabolic side-effects, particularly weight gain, as critically important outcomes in the Evidence to Decision Framework. Other side-effects, including anticholinergic and sedative effects, were considered but assigned lower priority based on relative subjective burden and potential for physical harm. The evidence of harm associated with antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia—specifically the increased risk of fractures and the increased risk of breast cancer—is of low certainty ( ). However, the GDG considered the link with patient important outcomes, including amenorrhea, galactorrhea, sexual dysfunction, infertility, increased risk of fractures due to osteoporosis, and increased risk of breast cancer, to be sufficiently established to use raised prolactin levels as a surrogate measure. According to the GRADE handbook, when important outcomes are relatively infrequent or emerge over long periods of time, surrogate markers are acceptable but may lead to a rating down of the certainty of the evidence. A judgment was made in consultation with our experts-by-experience that most females would choose to avoid medicines with a high certainty of raised prolactin or cardiometabolic side-effects. Recommendation 1: For females experiencing a first-episode of psychosis we do not recommend the following medicines as first-choice antipsychotic due to a relatively higher risk of extrapyramidal, cardiometabolic and hormonal side effects: first-generation antipsychotics, clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride. (Strong recommendation against) High Risk Cardiometabolic Side-Effects in Adults Clozapine and olanzapine are consistently associated with the highest risk of weight gain in adults with quetiapine, risperidone, and paliperidone having a lower but still significant potential to cause clinically significant increases in weight. , Clozapine and olanzapine are also associated with the highest risk of glucose dysregulation in adults. While both, along with quetiapine also carry the highest risk of dyslipidaemia. High Risk Cardiometabolic Side-Effects in Adolescents For adolescents, weight gain was more common with olanzapine, quetiapine, clozapine, risperidone, and paliperidone than with other antipsychotic medicines. Glucose and lipid alterations were greater for children and adolescents with quetiapine and olanzapine than with other antipsychotic medicines. , High Risk Prolactin-Elevating Side-Effects in Adults Multiple network meta-analyses have evaluated the risk of antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia in adults with amisulpride, risperidone, paliperidone, and first-generation antipsychotics consistently demonstrating the highest risk. , , High Risk Prolactin-Elevating Side-Effects in Adolescents Among adolescents, risperidone and paliperidone ranked highest in terms of associated prolactin elevation. , Olanzapine also carries a high risk of prolactin elevation in those under aged 18 years. , Of note, there have been no trials of amisulpride or sulpiride in adolescents. Recommendation 2: For females experiencing a first-episode of psychosis, we recommend aripiprazole as the preferred medicine. For adult females, brexpiprazole and cariprazine* are also recommended with brexpiprazole an option for females aged 13-17 years. Lurasidone, asenapine and ziprasidone are the preferred dopamine antagonists with lurasidone an option for females aged 13-17 years. (Choice may be guided by availability/accessibility/affordability). *Highly effective (user independent) contraceptive methods are recommended during treatment with cariprazine and for at least ten weeks following the last dose of cariprazine. Aripiprazole Aripiprazole is a partial D2 agonist and 5-HT2A antagonist that poses the lowest risk for cardiometabolic difficulties and raised prolactin in both adolescents and adult populations. , , , , It is considered the safest treatment option for females experiencing first-episode psychosis. The safety and effectiveness of aripiprazole has been established in both adults and

are the preferred dopamine antagonists with lurasidone an option for females aged 13-17 years. (Choice may be guided by availability/accessibility/affordability). *Highly effective (user independent) contraceptive methods are recommended during treatment with cariprazine and for at least ten weeks following the last dose of cariprazine. Aripiprazole Aripiprazole is a partial D2 agonist and 5-HT2A antagonist that poses the lowest risk for cardiometabolic difficulties and raised prolactin in both adolescents and adult populations. , , , , It is considered the safest treatment option for females experiencing first-episode psychosis. The safety and effectiveness of aripiprazole has been established in both adults and adolescents ( ). Aripiprazole has a long half-life of >75 h and may take longer to reach steady state (approximately 2 weeks) resulting in a longer time-to-effect. This longer half-life, along with the partial D2 agonist properties, are an important advantage to aripiprazole. They contribute to the significantly lower relapse rates as compared to other antipsychotic medicines when aripiprazole is gradually discontinued by guided gradual tapering. Another benefit of aripiprazole is its availability in both oral (daily) and long-acting injectable formulations (monthly or 2-monthly). , Long-acting injections are associated with a 32% lower risk of relapse and re-hospitalization. Brexpiprazole and Cariprazine Brexpiprazole and cariprazine are both partial agonists at dopamine D2 receptors and antagonists at serotonin 5-HT2A. They are associated with a low risk for both prolactin-elevation and cardiometabolic side-effects albeit not as low as aripiprazole. , , The safety and effectiveness of brexpiprazole and cariprazine has been studied in both adult and adolescent populations although cariprazine has only recently been approved for use in adolescents in the United States only ( ). Similar to aripiprazole, brexpiprazole and cariprazine have long half-lives (>91 h and >48 h, respectively) with cariprazine having 2 active metabolites with even longer half-lives (effective half-life for total cariprazine is 1 week). , Asenapine, Lurasidone, and Ziprasidone Asenapine, lurasidone, and ziprasidone are antagonists at dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors and have a different pharmacological profile to the partial agonists (aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, and cariprazine). They have shorter half-lives resulting in shorter time-to-effect. Their risk profiles are outlined in . The safety and effectiveness of asenapine, lurasidone, and ziprasidone have been studied in adults. While the safety of both asenapine and ziprasidone has been established in adolescents, the efficacy of these medicines for adolescents with psychotic illness has not been demonstrated ( ). Lurasidone, on the other hand, has demonstrated both safety and efficacy in this population in both short and longer-term studies. Summary Multiple meta-analyses have examined the risk of both prolactin-elevating and cardiometabolic side-effects with second-generation antipsychotic medicines in adolescents and adults. Based on this information, we have identified 6 medicines that are associated with a low or low-to-medium risk of either/both side-effects in adults and 3 medicines in adolescents. As aripiprazole was the only antipsychotic medicine to show either no change or an improvement, across both prolactin-elevating and cardiometabolic parameters, it should be offered as a first-choice. Brexpiprazole and cariprazine also demonstrated a more favorable profile with regard to prolactin-elevating and cardiometabolic parameters in adults and could therefore be offered as an alternative to aripiprazole. However, cariprazine has only recently been approved for use in individuals under 18 years of age in the United States, and comparative tolerability data in children and adolescents remains limited. As a result, until cariprazine is more widely available, brexpiprazole should be offered to adolescents according to local availability/accessibility/affordability. Lurasidone, asenapine, and ziprasidone, while not completely risk-free, are in the low-to-medium risk category when it comes to susceptibility to cause prolactin-elevating/cardiometabolic side-effects and should be available to adults in whom a partial agonist is not appropriate with lurasidone only being offered to adolescents. Practical Considerations in Developing the Algorithm Half-Life The D2 partial agonists/5HT2A antagonists (aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, and cariprazine) have longer half-lives which means that time to steady state is approximately 2 weeks. The D2/5HT-2A antagonists, in contrast, have shorter half-lives and result in a shorter time-to-effect. This may be relevant for the choice of antipsychotic in different contexts where time to onset of action is a key consideration. Dose Escalation The manufacturers do not differentiate between males and females when it comes to antipsychotic dose initiation and subsequent titration. , , , As females have smaller organs, more fatty tissue and lower blood volume, their volume of distribution is different to males taking the same dose of antipsychotic medicine. Premenopausal females also have an estimated 10%-15% greater blood flow to the brain, which makes it easier for antipsychotic medicines to reach their target receptors. The activity of CYP1A2 has been found to be lower in premenopausal females than in males. , While this results in wide sex-differences in metabolism of clozapine and olanzapine, it does not affect the medicines we recommend as first-choice options. We examined the evidence

titration. , , , As females have smaller organs, more fatty tissue and lower blood volume, their volume of distribution is different to males taking the same dose of antipsychotic medicine. Premenopausal females also have an estimated 10%-15% greater blood flow to the brain, which makes it easier for antipsychotic medicines to reach their target receptors. The activity of CYP1A2 has been found to be lower in premenopausal females than in males. , While this results in wide sex-differences in metabolism of clozapine and olanzapine, it does not affect the medicines we recommend as first-choice options. We examined the evidence on sex-related differences in our Evidence to Decision Framework ( ) and found the evidence on sex-related changes for aripiprazole of low certainty. However, the manufacturer recommended starting dose of 10 mg was determined to be too high by the GDG. A starting dose of 5 mg for adult females is therefore recommended. This lower starting dose aligns with that recommended in the recently published INTEGRATE guidelines. Brexpiprazole, cariprazine, and asenapine are understudied and studies on ziprasidone and lurasidone have not been able to demonstrate any sex-related differences. , The starting dose and subsequent dose titration for these medicines were therefore not adjusted. The doses and titration schedules are suggestions and may be adjusted according to setting and clinical presentation. The dose may also require adjustment in relation to age/life stage, for example, post-menopause. Side-Effects To facilitate the shared decision-making process in the clinical setting, the most common subjectively unpleasant side-effects are described in the algorithm for each medicine in line with the manufacturers’ summary of product characteristics. , , , Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Contraceptive Advice A summary of the details of the available data on the safety of each recommended medicine during pregnancy and while breastfeeding is described in this section of the algorithm along with specific contraceptive advice. Of note, there are no clinically significant drug–drug interactions between aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine, lurasidone, asenapine, ziprasidone, and any oral or other contraceptives. , , , , Medicine safety during pregnancy and when breastfeeding are important considerations when treating females of childbearing potential. The evidence base for second-generation antipsychotic medicines in pregnancy and breastfeeding relies largely on observational cohorts, registries, and pharmacovigilance, and is therefore limited. Across recent systematic reviews/meta-analyses, second generation antipsychotic medicines as a class (including aripiprazole, ziprasidone, and lurasidone but not brexpiprazole, cariprazine, or asenapine) are not supported as major teratogens. They appear to carry a low risk of congenital malformations with observational evidence suggesting possible increased risks of preterm birth and neonatal morbidity. However, heterogeneity and residual confounding limits causal inference. Among the 6 medicines recommended (3 for adolescents), aripiprazole has been studied the most and human data suggests low risk for major congenital malformations, pregnancy loss, or adverse neonatal outcomes above background population risk. There is limited human data of the safety of aripiprazole in breastfeeding but doses of up to 15 mg are reported to produce low levels in milk. As aripiprazole can lower serum prolactin, poor milk supply and lactation cessation have also been reported. Available safety data on lurasidone and ziprasidone is limited and as a result both carry potential risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. , Although there is no evidence of teratogenicity with ziprasidone, the manufacturer recommends an “appropriate” method of contraception during treatment. , Lurasidone is more than 99% bound to plasma proteins, so it is unlikely that it would be excreted into milk in sufficient amounts to affect a breastfed infant. , Nonetheless, data on its safety in breastfeeding is insufficient to make any specific recommendations. As there is little published experience with ziprasidone during breastfeeding potential toxicity cannot be ruled out. , According to a recent systematic review exploring the use of dopamine partial agonists in pregnancy and lactation, there are no formal studies specifically examining brexpiprazole or cariprazine. However, the manufacturers of cariprazine specifically advise against its use during pregnancy or in women of childbearing potential not using effective contraception. Highly effective contraceptive methods are recommended during treatment and for at least 10 weeks following the last dose of cariprazine. There are no formal studies on asenapine safety during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Overall, medicine-specific risk estimates remain limited for the 6 medicines (3 for adolescents) recommended in this CPG and the “safest” medicines are more often the ones with the most data on their use in pregnancy. Information Videos Each antipsychotic medicine recommended in the guideline has a QRcode linking to one of 2 corresponding information videos—one for adults and one for adolescents. The videos were co-designed by pharmacists, psychiatrists, nurses, experts-by-experience, and youth representatives and outline important information associated with the medicine in an accessible way. for the 6 medicines (3 for adolescents) recommended in this CPG and the “safest” medicines are more often the ones with the most data on their use in pregnancy. Information Videos Each antipsychotic medicine recommended in the guideline has a QRcode linking to one of 2 corresponding information videos—one for adults and one for adolescents. The videos were co-designed by pharmacists, psychiatrists, nurses, experts-by-experience, and youth representatives and outline important information associated with the medicine in an accessible way. Monitoring As antipsychotic medicines are associated with specific physical health monitoring recommendations, details of the baseline monitoring along with frequency of repeat monitoring is outlined. The monitoring is in line with international recommendations but may be adapted according to the local setting. , Those prescribing antipsychotic medicines should play a central role in both monitoring and managing side-effects that negatively impact physical health or subjective experience. Given that individuals who are antipsychotic-naïve are more susceptible to side-effects, ensuring that baseline and early repeat monitoring is carried out is imperative to ensure early detection and/or preventative interventions. In relation to side-effects that cannot be measured objectively, the use of a validated rating scale is recommended with suggested tools including the GASS (Glasgow antipsychotic side-effects scale)—a 22-question self-rating scale for detecting both frequency and distress associated with second generation antipsychotic side-effects and the BARS (Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale)—a 4-question objectively rated clinical tool designed to assess the presence and severity of akathisia. , As sexual side-effects are among the most distressing associated with antipsychotic medicines, exploring these using other relevant assessment tools may be appropriate. Cautions Details of potential drug–drug interactions are highlighted, specifically those that prolong QTc interval and those that inhibit or induce the enzymes involved in the metabolism of the recommended antipsychotic medicines CYP2D6 (aripiprazole, brexpiprazole), CYP3A4 (aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine, lurasidone), and CYP1A4 (asenapine). , , , , Review Advice on next steps are provided for those who have a good response and good tolerance, those who have good response and poor tolerance and those who have poor response. A recommendation to start planning for clozapine from the time of first presentation is also detailed. Final Guideline Algorithm The final guideline algorithm ( ) outlines the core recommendation to offer 1 of 6 antipsychotic medicines that are associated with a low or low-to-medium risk of prolactin-elevation and/or cardiometabolic side-effects to adults or 1 of 3 antipsychotic medicines to adolescents. Separate versions for adults-only and adolescents-only are also available ( and ). Results of Field Testing and External Review Members of the GDG reported that using the guideline algorithm was intuitive, helped with a shared understanding of the decision-making process and supported service user engagement. The experts-by-experience panel found the guideline flow to be helpful and especially liked the list of most common side-effects and the QR codes to the co-designed medicines information videos. The 2 external reviewers highlighted that the guideline algorithm may be used differently in different contexts, for example, acute inpatient versus outpatient settings. However, acknowledged that many females experiencing a first-episode of psychosis would be seen first in the outpatient setting. Update Plan This is a focused recommendation unit of a suite of guidelines for females. We plan to review and update the guidelines in 3 years. Discussion Main Findings We describe robust methods using GRADE-ADOLOPMENT methodology for the development of a guideline on first-choice antipsychotic medicine for females with first-episode psychosis. We recommend 6 (3 for adolescents) specific agents that are associated with a low/low-to-medium risk of prolactin-elevating and cardiometabolic side-effects for females from age 13+ years. Aripiprazole is selected as first-choice given its low effects on prolactin-related and cardiometabolic side-effects and relative safety during guided gradual tapering. Clinical Significance This is the first female-specific CPG on the choice of antipsychotic medicine for adolescent and adult females experiencing first-episode psychosis. Evaluations of the efficacy of antipsychotic medicines have not demonstrated superiority for any individual agent for those experiencing a first-episode of psychosis. , The choice of medicine should therefore be guided by a shared decision based on individual preferences, beliefs and values and the treatment options offered by the clinician. , Given the number of available antipsychotic medicines, it is not feasible to discuss all options within a single clinical encounter and treatment options must be limited to a manageable subset to support shared decision-making. Real-world prescribing in first-episode psychosis remains concentrated among a limited number of agents, particularly olanzapine. Evidence that olanzapine restriction within guidelines and medicine-specific recommendations improve prescribing quality and outcomes highlight the benefits of greater specificity in CPGs. , Females, however, are not specifically accounted for in existing CPGs. within a single clinical encounter and treatment options must be limited to a manageable subset to support shared decision-making. Real-world prescribing in first-episode psychosis remains concentrated among a limited number of agents, particularly olanzapine. Evidence that olanzapine restriction within guidelines and medicine-specific recommendations improve prescribing quality and outcomes highlight the benefits of greater specificity in CPGs. , Females, however, are not specifically accounted for in existing CPGs. Sex-differences in antipsychotic efficacy are insufficiently studied and the available evidence on pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic sex differences in our review was of low/very low certainty, precluding their use as reliable determinants of antipsychotic medicine choice at present. Additionally, females experience a second peak in first-episode psychosis around the menopausal transition which is characterized by declining estrogen levels and increased vulnerability to bone and cardiometabolic disease. There is an association between prolactin-raising antipsychotic medicines and osteoporosis, fracture risk, and break cancer. However, due to the distal relationship between the 2 factors, causality is challenging to demonstrate which is reflected in the certainty of the evidence in our review. Regardless, these potential long-term risks could be reduced by choosing prolactin-sparing medicines. Based on sex-specific physiological differences and subjective experiences of certain side-effects (hyperprolactinemia and cardiometabolic) along with potential negative implications for physical health, the GDG judged that the balance of benefit and harm favors an initial choice of 6 (3 for adolescents) preferred medicines with one medicine of first-choice. This decision is supported by psychological research demonstrating that having too many options to choose from can result in information overwhelm, decreased motivation, an inability to choose, decision-related anxiety, dissatisfaction, and worse outcomes in healthcare. In simplifying the antipsychotic medicine options available, we hope to improve the shared-decision making process for a vulnerable group of antipsychotic-naive individuals. Limitations Effective guideline development and implementation is associated with inherent limitations. This includes the potential biases of the GDG that may influence decision-making. As well as the low certainty evidence on which recommendations may be made. However, we endeavored to adhere to an evidence-based guideline development process according to AGREE II standards and using an Evidence to Decision Framework. One key limitation associated with implementation of this guideline is the variability in local contexts around antipsychotic medicine licensing and availability. Medicines licensing is the formal process by which regulatory authorities assess and approve a medicine for public use. A medicine receives a marketing authorization (the conditions under which the medicine can be prescribed, including approved indications, dosage, and target population) after rigorous evaluation of its safety, quality, and efficacy, supported by data from clinical trials. The antipsychotic medicines recommended in this guideline are not all licensed in every locality for psychosis from age 13+. Additionally, even where medicines are licensed, they still may not be available as a result of local prescribing restrictions or if the medicine is not marketed in the country in question. However, to overcome this barrier, the GDG has begun the process of engaging with policy makers to improve equity of access to these antipsychotic medicines. Lumateperone (Caplyta®), xanomeline/trospium chloride (Cobenfy®), and cariprazine for adolescents were discussed by the GDG. Due to their absence from comparative studies and availability in only one jurisdiction (United States) they were excluded from the guideline algorithm (cariprazine is recommended for adults only) but may be considered for future versions. Another barrier to the implementation of this guideline relates to changing prescribing practices of the target users of the guideline. Prescribers may be less familiar with newer medicines. It is expected that our shared decision-making resources—the guideline algorithm and the medicines information videos—will serve as educational material to both individuals with first-episode psychosis as well as the clinicians caring for them. We also acknowledge that there will be situations where our preferred medicines may not be deemed appropriate and other medicines may be offered. In line with the definition of a “strong recommendation” using the GRADE approach, our recommendations will apply to “most” but not all individuals. As the purpose of this guideline is not to restrict prescribing but rather to highlight options preferred by “most” individuals, we have also developed shared decision-making resources (medicines information videos) for other medicines including olanzapine, paliperidone, risperidone, and quetiapine—available at www.progressresearch.org/resources . We make a definitive case for choosing antipsychotic medicines with a lower risk of prolactin-raising and cardiometabolic side-effects for females experiencing first-episode psychosis which reflects a deliberate focus on the critically important patient outcomes. Earlier and established CPGs have primarily focused on neurological side-effects, presenting second-generation antipsychotics as a therapeutic advance on the basis of reduced long-term extrapyramidal risk. We acknowledge that by extending the set of critically important outcomes to include hyperprolactinemia and cardiometabolic side-effects, we assigned lower priority to other side-effects, including anticholinergic and sedative effects. While not deemed to be of critical importance, we appreciate that these outcomes

make a definitive case for choosing antipsychotic medicines with a lower risk of prolactin-raising and cardiometabolic side-effects for females experiencing first-episode psychosis which reflects a deliberate focus on the critically important patient outcomes. Earlier and established CPGs have primarily focused on neurological side-effects, presenting second-generation antipsychotics as a therapeutic advance on the basis of reduced long-term extrapyramidal risk. We acknowledge that by extending the set of critically important outcomes to include hyperprolactinemia and cardiometabolic side-effects, we assigned lower priority to other side-effects, including anticholinergic and sedative effects. While not deemed to be of critical importance, we appreciate that these outcomes may be important on an individual level. As a result, we have included a list of the most commonly reported side-effects associated with each antipsychotic medicine option in the guideline algorithm. Of note, the 6 medicines recommended (3 for adolescents) are also associated with a lower risk of anticholinergic and sedative effects. We also acknowledge that while offering antipsychotic medicines with a lower risk of prolactin-elevating and cardiometabolic side-effects, they may not be entirely risk-free. Adolescents are more susceptible to antipsychotic side-effects, especially weight gain, which can even occur with medicines such as aripiprazole. We recommend regular physical health monitoring at baseline and appropriate intervals to ensure that side-effects such as weight gain, should they occur, are identified promptly. Appropriate interventions may then be put in place to mitigate against further risk, for example, initiation of metformin for those who have gained >3% weight at any time during the first year of treatment (adults) or >3% weight outside expected growth trajectory (adolescents). Finally, as this is a CPG on the first-choice of antipsychotic medicine for females with first-episode psychosis, we have not considered those with affective symptomatology which is a limitation of the guideline. However, certain antipsychotic medicines that we recommend have demonstrated efficacy for both psychotic and manic/affective illness and are licensed for these indications as outlined in . These medicines may therefore be preferred for those whose illness has an affective component. We have also included a prompt in the “Review” section of the guideline algorithm to “consider affective component” for those who have had a poor response to their first-choice medicine. Future Research This is the first recommendation unit in a suite of guidelines addressing care for females experiencing psychosis across the lifespan. Future research will look at the effective implementation of this guideline and the associated medicines information videos as shared decision-making resources in the clinical setting. The guideline algorithm is an effective tool for shared understanding with service users as it provides a list of (6 for adults, 3 for adolescents) medicines along with the rationale as to why they are being offered. Other clinical supports, such as Psymatik, are also useful in clinical practice to allow clinicians search the latest meta-analytic evidence on side-effects to inform discussions. Particularly when choosing a second antipsychotic medicine should the individual experience side-effects with the initial choice. As CPGs support research translation, they are essential in reducing the 17 years it takes for research evidence to reach day-to-day clinical practice. A CPG on the choice of first antipsychotic medicine for males experiencing a first-episode of psychosis is a top priority for future research. Additionally, other CPGs on the pharmacological management of acute agitation and distress for those experiencing psychotic symptoms and a CPG on the management of antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia should also be considered for future guideline development. Sex-differences in medicine pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics are variable and profound, and still have not been thoroughly investigated. The available evidence on pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic sex differences related to the antipsychotic medicines recommended in this CPG is limited ( ). Future research should therefore look at the impact of sex differences in first-choice antipsychotic medicine absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion as well as the biochemical and physiologic effects of these medicines. While this is a guideline on first-choice of antipsychotic medicine for first-episode psychosis in females, future guidelines should consider subsequent antipsychotic medicine options for females where a first-choice medicine is ineffective or poorly tolerated. Risperidone, amisulpride, olanzapine, and especially clozapine have demonstrated superior efficacy in those with multi-episode schizophrenia. However, these medicines carry a higher risk for either prolactin elevation, cardiometabolic side-effects or both. Additionally, strong effects of sex and estrogen have been reported for medicines such as olanzapine and clozapine via CYP1A2 metabolism. , As a result, further research on how to optimize these second/third line antipsychotic medicines in females is crucial to ensure both safety and tolerability. Conclusion This guideline represents an important advancement in personalized mental healthcare by providing recommendations for the choice of the initial antipsychotic medicine for females experiencing first-episode psychosis. Developed using a robust and transparent methodology through the GRADE-ADOLOPMENT and AGREE II frameworks, it provides clear, evidence-informed recommendations. Additionally, strong effects of sex and estrogen have been reported for medicines such as olanzapine and clozapine via CYP1A2 metabolism. , As a result, further research on how to optimize these second/third line antipsychotic medicines in females is crucial to ensure both safety and tolerability. Conclusion This guideline represents an important advancement in personalized mental healthcare by providing recommendations for the choice of the initial antipsychotic medicine for females experiencing first-episode psychosis. Developed using a robust and transparent methodology through the GRADE-ADOLOPMENT and AGREE II frameworks, it provides clear, evidence-informed recommendations. While challenges remain in ensuring consistent availability of the recommended medicines—due to differences in licensing, marketing, and prescribing practices—the development group has initiated efforts to address these barriers through policy engagement and clinician education. Future research will focus on the implementation of the guideline and the effectiveness of its accompanying shared decision-making resources, ensuring the recommendations translate into improved patient outcomes and more informed, collaborative prescribing decisions in clinical practice. chunks.content: Schizophrenia is a severe mental illness with serious consequences for the majority of patients and their families, and for society at large, even though many patients have a favorable course. – Despite the establishment of early detection and intervention services and the development of new psychosocial interventions, 40% to 50% of patients with first-episode schizophrenia (FES) have symptoms at 10 years of follow-up. , Studies examining the 1-year outcome in FES, show highly variable remission rates ranging from 17% to 81%. , Antipsychotic medication remains the most effective treatment for positive symptoms in schizophrenia. Clozapine has been shown to be the most efficacious drug in this drug class. Moreover, clozapine is effective in about one third of patients not responding to 2 trials with nonclozapine antipsychotics, hereafter termed the treatment-resistant patients. The antipsychotic treatment algorithms incorporated in the guidelines for the treatment of schizophrenia are outlined in Figure . – The algorithms generally recommend 2 trials with different antipsychotic drugs of adequate dosing and duration before clozapine is indicated. However, the initiation of clozapine may not match the time frame given in guidelines. The profile of adverse effects for clozapine may increase this delay in the treatment of FES patients, who are generally more vulnerable to antipsychotic adverse effects such as weight gain and the metabolic syndrome. However, clozapine has achieved favorable results in the treatment of FES patients. One study examined the use of clozapine in a cohort of consecutive FES patients with a 2-year follow-up. Although patients who received clozapine had more positive and negative symptoms at baseline, they managed to reach rates of remission and recovery similar to those who had never received clozapine, indicating additional effects of clozapine for FES. Another study showed a robust response to clozapine for FES patients who had not responded well to initial trials of second-generation antipsychotic drugs. The use of clozapine as a second-line antipsychotic for FES-spectrum disorders has also achieved favorable results. Given the serious long-term sequences of nonremission in FES, optimization of the antipsychotic treatment with thorough consideration of clozapine and skillful long-term specialist follow-up are of outmost importance in this patient group. We aimed to study the 1-year remission rate and the antipsychotic treatment for a cohort of consecutively recruited FES patients. The prescribed antipsychotic treatment was compared with treatment guideline recommendations. METHODS The sample is drawn from the TIPS (Early Treatment and Intervention in Psychosis) 2 cohort study that included all first-episode psychosis patients admitted to either outpatient clinics or hospital. – The study was carried out within the publicly funded specialist psychiatric catchment area services in Rogaland County, Norway, with a total of 370,000 inhabitants. The study comprises data from the time of inclusion until 1-year follow-up. All patients were assessed within a week of contact with the psychiatric services and assigned to the standard treatment program consisting of an antipsychotic medication algorithm, multifamily group work, and supportive psychotherapy. All patients entering the study gave written informed consent. The project received ethical approval from the Regional Committee for Medical Research Ethics Health Region West, Norway (015.03). Participants This study included all eligible participants with FES recruited to the TIPS cohort study during the period January 2002 to August 2013. The inclusion criteria were the following: living in the catchment area in Rogaland County, Norway; age 15 to 65 years; meeting the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (Fourth Edition) ( DSM-IV ; American Psychiatric Association, 1994) criteria for schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, or schizophreniform disorder, described further on as core schizophrenia; being actively psychotic, as measured by the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) score of 4 or more on at least 1 of the Positive subscale items: 1 (delusions), 3 (hallucinatory behavior), 5 (grandiosity), 6 (suspiciousness/persecution), or General subscale item 9 (unusual thought content); not receiving previous adequate treatment for psychosis (defined as antipsychotic medication of more than 3.5 haloperidol equivalents for 12 weeks or until remission of the psychotic symptoms); having no neurological or endocrine disorders with relationship to the psychosis; having no contraindications to antipsychotic medication; understanding and/or speaking a Scandinavian language; having an IQ score of higher than 70. From the total cohort, 122 had a core-schizophrenia diagnosis (FES). From this group of 122 FES patients, 78 completed the 1-year follow-up, as shown in Figure . Design The study was an observational cohort design with a 1-year follow-up. Participants were categorized as remitted or nonremitted according to their remission status, as per the Remission in Schizophrenia Working Group criteria (see hereinafer), at the 1-year follow-up. Participant characteristics at baseline and 1-year follow-up were compared, and the pharmacological treatment was assessed in detail. The algorithm used in TIPS was recommended as a standard hospital policy and was a modification of the Norwegian treatment guidelines. Assessments For the TIPS cohort, patients were assessed

Participants were categorized as remitted or nonremitted according to their remission status, as per the Remission in Schizophrenia Working Group criteria (see hereinafer), at the 1-year follow-up. Participant characteristics at baseline and 1-year follow-up were compared, and the pharmacological treatment was assessed in detail. The algorithm used in TIPS was recommended as a standard hospital policy and was a modification of the Norwegian treatment guidelines. Assessments For the TIPS cohort, patients were assessed at baseline, 3 months, and 12 months. For this study, only the baseline and 12 month assessments were used. Assessment teams were clinically experienced and trained research personnel. Raters were trained by rating preprepared case notes and audio/videotapes. Good interrater reliability was achieved on major parameters in the research group. The Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV Axis I disorders was used for diagnostic purposes. Symptom levels were measured by the PANSS. For the PANSS, we calculated the total and the positive, negative, excitative, depressive, and cognitive component scores. Other characteristics were also assessed, such as suicidality and duration of untreated psychosis (DUP). Presence of suicidality was defined as having suicidal thoughts, plans, or attempts. The DUP was measured as the time from onset of psychosis until the start of adequate treatment. Onset of psychosis was defined as the first week with positive psychotic symptoms corresponding to a PANSS score of 4 or more on Positive subscale items 1, 3, 5, or 6 or on General subscale item 9. In cases with long DUP, all available data sources were used to ascertain the length of this period to the best achievable level, including semistructured personal interviews with patients and relatives. Adequate treatment was defined as the start of structured treatment with antipsychotic medication, start of hospitalization, or the start of outpatient clinic psychotherapy designed to manage psychotic symptoms. Global functioning was measured by the Global Assessment of Functioning scale with scores calculated for symptom and function subscales. Misuse or dependence of alcohol and drugs was measured by the Clinicians Rating Scale. Remission Remission was defined in accordance with the Remission in Schizophrenia Working Group standardized symptom remission criteria. The Remission in Schizophrenia Working Group is a panel of experts from the United States, who developed in 2004 a consensus definition of remission applied to schizophrenia. The proposed criteria were also supported by international field experts and were published in 2005. These criteria consist of no score of 4 or higher for the past 6 months on any of the following PANSS items: P1 (delusions), P2 (disorganized thought), P3 (hallucinatory behavior), N1 (affective flattening), N4 (passive social withdrawal), N6 (lack of spontaneity), G5 (bizarre posture), or G9 (unusual thought content). Patients were categorized as nonremitted if they reported any relapse, defined as deterioration of symptoms with score of >4 on the relevant PANSS subscales during the previous 6 months. Remission status at the last available observation was based on the assessment at the 1-year follow-up. Pharmacological Treatment At 1-year follow-up, we examined the pharmacological strategies applied for patients by assessing adherence to the algorithm using patient files. The algorithm described 3 drug alternatives with clozapine being the third drug of choice, as shown in Figure . The first author (P.D.) read all the patient files and clinical descriptions (Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV and PANSS) to ascertain whether participants had remitted or relapsed during the first year of follow-up. Clinical descriptions were scrutinized and assessed for indications for a switch to clozapine. Pharmacological treatment was assessed in detail. The total duration of antipsychotic treatment, as well as the number of periods with antipsychotic treatment, was calculated using the patient files. The different antipsychotics used as first, second, third, or fourth choice were also assessed. In addition, the first author performed a digital search in all the medical files of the patients in the hospital data system, with index “clozapine,” “klozapin” (the Norwegian term for clozapine), and “Leponex” (the brand name for clozapine in Norway). Unclear cases were discussed with one of the coauthors (T.K.L.). Whenever possible, we sought to identify the reasons for clozapine not being considered or offered to patients. Data Analysis Analyses were performed using the SPSS Statistical Program Package version 20.0 (IBM, Armonk, NY). Participants were classified according to remission status (yes/no) at the 1-year follow-up. Categorical variables were presented in cross tables and analyzed using χ 2 or Fisher exact test as appropriate. All group comparisons of continuous and ordinal data were analyzed using the nonparametric Mann-Whitney U test because of nonnormality as assessed with visual inspection of histograms. RESULTS Sample Characteristics and 1-Year Remission Characteristics of the remitted and nonremitted groups are outlined in Table . A total of 78 patients were included in the sample, and the majority (68%) were nonremitted at the 1-year follow-up. All of the nonremitted patients (n = 53) scored 4 or more on at least 1 of the positive symptoms included in the remission criteria, whereas this was the case for 43 patients (81% of the nonremitted) regarding the negative and general symptoms. Both groups comprised mostly young men (mean age of 27 and 26 years, respectively, for the remitted and nonremitted group; 64% and 72%, respectively, were men). At baseline, there were no significant differences between the remitted and nonremitted group for sex, age, years of education, symptom, and function profile (Global Assessment of Functioning scale, PANSS), misuse or dependence of alcohol and drugs, and suicidality. We found a trend for DUP being longer in the nonremitted group, but this was not statistically significant (median of 40 weeks compared with 16 weeks, P = 0.054). Antipsychotic Treatment in the Remitted and the Nonremitted Groups The average number of periods of treatment with any antipsychotic drugs and the total duration of treatment during the first year were not significantly different between the 2 groups, as shown in Table . Two patients (8%) in the remitted group and 4 patients (7%) in the nonremitted group had no trials of antipsychotic drugs during the study period. The majority in both groups, 17 patients (68%) of the remitted and 30 patients (57%) of the nonremitted, received 1 type of antipsychotic drug during the first year. Four remitted patients (16%) and 8 nonremitted patients (15%) were treated with 2 different antipsychotic drugs. There were no significant group differences for no use of antipsychotic drugs, use of 1 antipsychotic drug, or use of 2 or more antipsychotic drugs. Regarding the first-choice antipsychotic drug, there were no significant group differences. The most frequently prescribed antipsychotic drugs were olanzapine, risperidone, and quetiapine. Olanzapine was the first used antipsychotic drug for 48% of the remitted patients and 45% of the nonremitted (remitted, 11; nonremitted, 22 patients). Three (6%) of the nonremitted patients were offered, and 2 (4%) received treatment with clozapine. For 1 patient, this was a second-choice drug, and for the other one, this was a fourth choice. There was no information that indicated an evaluation of clozapine for any of the other patients in the sample. The vast majority of patients were treated with second-generation antipsychotic drugs. None of the remitted patients was treated with first-generation antipsychotic drugs. Of the nonremitted patients, 8% were treated with a first-generation antipsychotic as a first-choice drug. Three of the 4 patients were switched to second-generation antipsychotic drugs only. The fourth patient was switched first to olanzapine and then to levomepromazine, which is a first-generation antipsychotic drug. Two more patients were treated with a first-generation antipsychotic as a second-choice drug. The first one switched from risperidone to haloperidol and had no further switches during the first year. The second patient switched from olanzapine to haloperidol, then switched from haloperidol to perphenazine (another first-generation antipsychotic drug), and finally from perphenazine to risperidone. Psychiatric Treatment The majority of patients were in contact with the health care system during the study period, with around two thirds in each group having at least 1 inpatient admission at the psychiatric department. There were no significant group differences in the duration of inpatient admissions, as shown in Table . DISCUSSION A major finding in this study is the 1-year remission rate of 32% for FES patients. Results from other studies for this patient group vary considerably. In a review of remission in schizophrenia with 27 studies included, the rate of remission in FES ranged from 17% to 78%, whereas another study showed a remission rate of 81%. The variability of the reported remission rates may be a result of the heterogeneity among the studies. Contributing factors to the heterogeneity include selection bias and low representativeness of the studies, the definition of remission, and the frequency and duration of follow-up. The stringent criteria used in this study, such as a core-schizophrenia diagnosis, FES, and both dimensions of the proposed remission criteria —symptom reduction and duration, are likely to have contributed to the relatively low remission rate. However, treatment

the rate of remission in FES ranged from 17% to 78%, whereas another study showed a remission rate of 81%. The variability of the reported remission rates may be a result of the heterogeneity among the studies. Contributing factors to the heterogeneity include selection bias and low representativeness of the studies, the definition of remission, and the frequency and duration of follow-up. The stringent criteria used in this study, such as a core-schizophrenia diagnosis, FES, and both dimensions of the proposed remission criteria —symptom reduction and duration, are likely to have contributed to the relatively low remission rate. However, treatment factors vary between studies and are likely to influence remission rates. We found that all of the nonremitted patients had at least 1 positive symptom during follow-up. These results indicate the use of antipsychotics in all of the nonremitted patients in our study, given that antipsychotics are most effective in the treatment of positive symptoms of schizophrenia. It is possible that these patients may have remitted, had they received a more intensified treatment with antipsychotics according to the guidelines. A proportion of these patients should probably be evaluated for treatment with clozapine. These results also underline, however, that even with optimal antipsychotic effect on positive symptoms, there would be a proportion of patients still not achieving remission, because of the presence of negative symptoms. The second major finding of our study is a low exploitation of treatment options of antipsychotic treatment in the nonremitted group. For this group, 7% did not use any antipsychotic drug during the 1-year follow-up, and a further 57% were treated with one antipsychotic drug only. Contrary to the guidelines, the majority of the nonremitted FES patients (64%) did not commence the second step of the algorithm. Fifteen percent of the nonremitted patients received 2 antipsychotic drugs, 1 of these was prescribed clozapine, and the others were not further switched to clozapine despite nonremission and therefore did not pass the second step of the guideline algorithm. Altogether, only 2 patients were offered clozapine, one as a second choice and the other as a fourth choice. In both cases, the recommended guidelines were not followed. The 7% nonuse together with 57% of patients receiving 1 antipsychotic drug only in a cohort of nonremitted patients with schizophrenia must be regarded as nonadherence to well-known national and international treatment guidelines. The nonuse of antipsychotics is a major concern. We have not explored other reasons for not taking any antipsychotic, such as patients' unwillingness, and therefore, it is not possible to conclude that the clinicians did not follow the guidelines for schizophrenia treatment in all of these cases. There are many factors shown to influence nonadherence to consensus-based guidelines by treating clinicians. The applicability of clinical practice guidelines in psychiatry has been studied during recent years, including trying to identify barriers to guideline adherence. – Some proposed barriers are physician related, such as lack of awareness or familiarity, lack of agreement and concerns about control over professional practice. There are also patient-related barriers such as nonadherence and reluctance, clarity and complexity of guidelines, and environmentally related barriers such as resources and facilities. , However, clinicians in our study performed good clinical practice in prescribing mainly second-generation antipsychotic drugs, and first-generation antipsychotic drugs were used in only a few cases. For example, the United Kingdom NICE guidelines recommend treatment with at least 1 nonclozapine second-generation antipsychotic drug for treatment-resistant patients. The Texas Medication Algorithm Project algorithm for schizophrenia provides some recommendations for treatment of FES. In the 2003 version, clinicians could choose either a first-generation antipsychotic drug or clozapine after 2 inadequate trials with second-generation antipsychotics. In the 2007 update, first-generation antipsychotics were an option at the second step of the algorithm and after a trial of a second-generation antipsychotic at the first step. The third step included the use of clozapine only. By contrast, the Norwegian guidelines do not differentiate the 2 types of antipsychotic drugs in terms of timing of treatment. In general, the wide use of second-generation antipsychotic drugs by clinicians in our study does not come in conflict with the contemporary national and international guidelines for treatment of FES. The finding of similar rates of nonuse of antipsychotics between the remitted and the nonremitted groups may be indicative of the heterogeneity of schizophrenia. It would be valuable to follow the course of these patients with respect to the course of illness, diagnosis, and future antipsychotic treatment. Our finding that 2 patients remitted without using antipsychotics may challenge the general recommendation for continuous antipsychotic treatment in the first year of FES. It would be valuable to follow the course of these patients with respect to the course of illness, diagnosis, and future antipsychotic treatment. Our finding that 2 patients remitted without using antipsychotics may challenge the general recommendation for continuous antipsychotic treatment in the first year of FES. Regarding clozapine treatment and its limited use, various barriers have been investigated. – Studies show that most practitioners are familiar with the guidelines and the effectiveness of clozapine but are reluctant to prescribe the drug because of the risk of fatal adverse reactions such as agranulocytosis. , Lack of knowledge of the current evidence for clozapine may be contributing to this finding because very few patients on clozapine progress from neutropenia to agranulocytosis, and other antipsychotics also pose a risk of agranulocytosis. This small risk of agranulocytosis is, in our opinion, outweighed by a reduced mortality associated with clozapine treatment. For the proportion of nonremitted patients with at least 2 antipsychotics trials (19/53), several reasons could explain the possible low use of clozapine. First, we are not sure if this sample can be regarded as treatment resistant because we did not explore if the previous treatment periods were of adequate duration and if the antipsychotics were given in adequate doses. This is crucial to define treatment resistance, and clozapine is only recommended once treatment resistance is demonstrated. Second, patients may have been offered but refused the suggested treatment because of the comprehensive blood-monitoring associated with clozapine use, or refused for other reasons. Third, medical contraindications for the use of clozapine may apply. However, we found no written evaluation of indications of clozapine in the medical files. Adherence to guidelines could be enhanced through regular training sessions for physicians on the implementation of the guidelines and including information on the current evidence base for the management of treatment with clozapine. Concerns by patients about clozapine could be addressed by providing them with information on the advantages of clozapine and the adoption of shared decision-making methods by clinicians. In addition, the facilities and infrastructure of the psychiatric institutions should be improved to allow an easier and more user-friendly follow-up for those receiving clozapine but also other antipsychotic drugs. Some clozapine clinics have been established, and it is possible that these facilities increase the quality of antipsychotic treatment and the remission rate in schizophrenia. Future research is needed on how to optimize implementation of evidence-based guidelines for the treatment of schizophrenia in the early stages because this may be imperative for improving outcome for these patients. Strengths and Limitations The strengths of our study include a robust design, whereby all the consecutive FES patients in a catchment area were assessed and followed up for 1 year. The study had access to the medical files of all patients and thus information on treatment over the 1-year follow-up. The stringent inclusion criteria ensured homogeneity in terms of diagnosis. Our study, however, was limited by the lack of assessment of the attitudes or behavior of patients toward treatment by medication. We are unable to determine whether nonadherence to guidelines is underpinned by patients refusing to receive antipsychotics including clozapine. Second, the attitudes of clinicians toward clozapine were not explored in our study. Given the lack of written considerations of clozapine use in the medical files, we cannot exclude that clinicians may have considered clozapine and refused prescribing for acceptable medical reasons. CONCLUSIONS Our study is one of the first to examine the adherence to guidelines for the pharmacological treatment and the 1-year remission rate for FES patients using stringent criteria. The quality of care given to patients is often correlated to the degree to which the clinicians follow the guidelines. Guidelines suggest a clinical practice that influences good patient outcomes. Therefore, adherence to guidelines is crucial for providing effective and evidence-based treatment. Given the finding of low adherence to the guidelines and insufficient pharmacological treatment for the FES patients in our study, a more evidence-based practice could be achieved by increasing guideline awareness and training in their implementation among the clinicians.
