chunks.content: Introduction Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are a group of conditions first manifesting early in childhood, characterised by impairments of personal, social, academic or occupational functioning. Examples of NDDs include autism spectrum disorder (ASD), global developmental delay (GDD), intellectual disability (ID), learning disability (LD) and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). NDDs have a combined prevalence of ~17% in children aged 3–17 years, making them the most common chronic medical conditions encountered in paediatric primary care. Given their clinical and aetiological heterogeneity, the cause of NDDs can be challenging to diagnose. Comprehensive clinical care includes investigations aimed at elucidating the underlying cause, such as brain imaging and laboratory tests, including genetic testing. Identifying the genetic aetiology of an NDD is of clinical and personal utility. Increasingly, accurate genetic diagnosis can lead to tailored therapy (and may provide information about prognosis that in turn can guide medical care and therapy. Definitive diagnosis may avoid unnecessary testing or treatments, enable surveillance for known comorbidities and help families access additional disease-specific support. Accurate diagnosis of the cause of NDDs facilitates genetic counselling and informs recurrence risks that guides reproductive decision making and enables prenatal diagnosis. When an inherited aetiology is identified, this can provide diagnoses to other family members with NDD. Finally, by ending the diagnostic odyssey for families, identifying an aetiology can also provide psychological benefits (eg, alleviation of guilt, acceptance, closure, empowerment) and improve parental quality of life. The diagnostic process begins with a thorough clinical assessment of the patient, which includes a medical, developmental and family history with physical examination. The presence or absence of certain clinical features may provide clues as to the underlying cause and therefore direct the appropriate investigations. If a known genetic condition is recognised, targeted testing should be done first. For example, if a 2-year-old girl presents with classical features of Rett syndrome, it is prudent to do MECP2 sequencing prior to other investigations. However, it is more often the case that the clinical presentation is non-specific, and thus there are a large number of potential genetic aetiologies. It is therefore important to broaden the testing approach, which could result in earlier diagnosis. When a known syndrome is not readily apparent, there are a variety of testing options, including chromosomal microarray (CMA), fragile X syndrome (FXS) testing, testing for a range of inherited metabolic diseases (‘metabolic testing’) and tests that use next-generation sequencing such as multigene panels and exome sequencing (ES). Professional organisations from a range of disciplines recommend CMA as a first-tier test for children with GDD, ID and ASD. While fragile X testing is generally recommended as a first-tier test for these NDDs, criteria for testing are inconsistent. Recommendations vary considerably for metabolic testing, while the use of gene panels and ES is relatively new and typically not included in recommendations aimed at non-geneticists. Not surprisingly, a recent survey of Canadian genetic and metabolic physicians found that CMA and fragile X testing are the most often used tests for patients with NDDs, while the use of metabolic tests, gene panels and ES was highly variable. Therefore, Canadian recommendations for genetic investigation of NDDs are urgently needed. Definitions Clinical definitions ADHD: a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development. ASD: an NDD characterised by persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction and the presence of restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities. May be diagnosed with or without accompanying intellectual or language impairment. Dysmorphic features: visible morphological findings that differ from those commonly seen in the general population or same genetic ancestry. GDD: an NDD characterised by significant delay (at least two SD below the mean using standardised testing) in achieving at least two developmental domains, including gross or fine motor, speech and language, cognition, social and personal functioning, and activities of daily living. A diagnosis of GDD applies to individuals under the age of 5 years who are too young to participate in standardised testing to assess intellectual functioning. IMDs: genetic disorders that result in metabolic defects due to deficiency of enzymes, membrane transporters or other functional proteins. ID: an NDD characterised by deficits in intellectual and adaptive functioning. Intellectual functioning includes reasoning, problem solving, planning, abstract thinking, judgement, academic learning and experiential learning. Adaptive functioning are the skills needed to live independently and responsibly and include communication, social skills, personal independence at home or in the community and school or work functioning. LD: also known as specific learning disorder; an NDD characterised by deficits in the ability to learn or use foundational academic skills (reading, writing or arithmetic), which is not better accounted for by ID. NDD: a group of conditions manifesting early in development, characterised by impairments of personal, social, academic or occupational functioning. Syndromic: for an individual with an NDD, refers to the presence of additional

academic learning and experiential learning. Adaptive functioning are the skills needed to live independently and responsibly and include communication, social skills, personal independence at home or in the community and school or work functioning. LD: also known as specific learning disorder; an NDD characterised by deficits in the ability to learn or use foundational academic skills (reading, writing or arithmetic), which is not better accounted for by ID. NDD: a group of conditions manifesting early in development, characterised by impairments of personal, social, academic or occupational functioning. Syndromic: for an individual with an NDD, refers to the presence of additional clinical features such as dysmorphisms, congenital malformations, medical comorbidities etc, which may suggest an underlying genetic cause (refer to ). Technical definitions Next-generation sequencing (NGS): high-throughput sequencing technology used to determine nucleotide sequences and genome dosage at numerous loci simultaneously. Genome-wide sequencing (GWS): sequence analysis of all or a large part of the genome performed by NGS; includes exome and ES. ES: an NGS approach that determines the DNA sequence of most of the protein-coding exons found in the genome of an individual. As of 2022, this test is available in most provinces for patients meeting specific clinical criteria. Genome sequencing (GS): an NGS approach that determines the sequence of most of the DNA content encompassing the entire genome of an individual. As of 2022, this test is only available on a research basis or through clinical pilots within Canada. Multigene panel: simultaneous sequencing of multiple genes associated with a specific clinical presentation. First-tier test: a laboratory test or other diagnostic investigation that should be pursued prior to all others. Second-tier test: a laboratory test or other diagnostic investigation that should be pursued if first-tier tests are negative or inconclusive. Metabolic testing: blood and/or urine tests that measure analytes (such as amino and organic acids) in order to identify patterns indicating an inherited metabolic disease. Methods To develop recommendations, the Canadian College of Medical Geneticists (CCMG) formed an NDDs working group of physicians and clinical scientists from medical genetics and genomics, developmental paediatrics, paediatric neurology, biochemical genetics, cytogenetics and molecular genetics. The CCMG is a Canadian organisation responsible for certifying medical geneticists and clinical laboratory geneticists and for establishing professional and ethical standards for clinical genetics services in Canada. The working group considered laboratory tests currently clinically available in Canada to investigate the aetiology of NDDs, organised into three subgroups: (1) CMA and FXS testing, (2) metabolic testing and (3) NGS-based testing including ES and multigene panels. Each subgroup, in consultation with the broader working group, identified key questions, conducted a literature search, reviewed and discussed the evidence and drafted recommendations based on quality and level of evidence. The working group reviewed all draft recommendations and reached consensus. The draft manuscript was reviewed by subcommittees of the CCMG (laboratory practice, clinical practice and metabolics committees). It was then circulated for comment to the CCMG membership-at-large and, following incorporation of feedback, approved by the CCMG Board of Directors. This position statement was also circulated for comment to the Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities committee of the Canadian Pediatric Society. Considerations Target audience and scope These recommendations apply to patients with NDDs for whom no specific aetiological diagnosis is suspected after a thorough history and physical examination. If a specific genetic disorder is suspected with a high degree of clinical certainty, targeted testing should be done first, and if negative, then one should proceed with the testing recommended in this position statement. If no diagnosis is reached after the recommended investigations, periodic re-evaluation of the patient by a geneticist is recommended, as testing technology and genomic knowledge is rapidly evolving. The time interval for re-evaluation is specific to the patient’s unique situation (eg, age and testing done) and should be determined by the geneticist. We acknowledge that the demand for genetic consultation is high, and waitlists are often long for non-urgent referrals. Thus, we provide recommendations for first-tier testing that primary care and/or non-genetic specialist clinicians can order while the patient awaits a clinical genetics or metabolic assessment to ensure faster access to genetic testing. The non-geneticist should have a good understanding of the benefits and limitations of first-tier tests and should obtain informed consent for testing from the patient or their guardian(s). Should first-tier testing be abnormal, a referral to the appropriate specialist is indicated, and many genetic/metabolic clinics will expedite consultation for patients referred with an abnormal result. We also provide guidance as to which patients should be referred to genetics if first-tier testing is not diagnostic. The role of the geneticist is to determine whether second-tier testing is indicated to ensure that the patient and family have an opportunity to discuss the test results and to make recommendations for follow-up care if a diagnosis is made. Should first-tier testing be abnormal, a referral to the appropriate specialist is indicated, and many genetic/metabolic clinics will expedite consultation for patients referred with an abnormal result. We also provide guidance as to which patients should be referred to genetics if first-tier testing is not diagnostic. The role of the geneticist is to determine whether second-tier testing is indicated to ensure that the patient and family have an opportunity to discuss the test results and to make recommendations for follow-up care if a diagnosis is made. The evidence reviewed for the development of this position statement applies specifically to patients with GDD, ID and/or ASD. The existing evidence was highly heterogeneous with respect to the clinical phenotypes of the patients studied, so it was not possible to make separate recommendations for patients with and without syndromic features, for patients with different severities of impairment or for patients in different age groups (paediatric or adult). Evidence was also reviewed for patients with other NDDs (eg, ADHD and LD), but there are no high-quality studies that enable distinction between patients with and without comorbid GDD or ID. Therefore, until such evidence emerges, we do not recommend genetic investigations for patients without GDD, ID or ASD unless there are other clinical features suggestive of a genetic (‘syndromic’; see ) or metabolic aetiology. The recommendations herein apply to probands of all ages. The urgency of testing is typically higher for younger children, particularly if the parents are planning a pregnancy. This does not preclude testing and/or genetic/metabolic specialist referral for adolescents and adults, particularly if the patient has not been tested or evaluated in 5 years or more. The recommendations herein also apply to probands with ID regardless of severity, as there was insufficient evidence to exclude probands from such testing based on level of disability. Further studies addressing this are required. There may be specific clinical scenarios that demand a different approach to that suggested herein, so clinicians should always use their judgement as to whether the recommended investigations are appropriate. Patient and family preferences should always be considered. This position statement is not intended to be a comprehensive guide to the medical investigation of individuals with NDDs, and as such, we do not make recommendations regarding neuroimaging or health surveillance (eg, thyroid screening, vision assessment, etc). The Canadian context Canada’s population of nearly 39 million is concentrated in the southern parts of Ontario, Quebec and Alberta, with relatively sparse population density in the rest of the country. Twenty-one per cent of the population lives in rural or remote areas with limited access to specialist medical care (Canadian Medical Association Policy Statement, 2014). The Canada Health Act stipulates that all Canadians should have universal insurance coverage for medically necessary healthcare service. Healthcare is a provincial and territorial responsibility, and nationwide there is variability regarding the types of genetic and metabolic tests that are publicly funded. There is also some variability in the conditions screened for by newborn screening. The most expensive and resource-intensive genetic tests, such as ES, are not always accessible due to provincial healthcare insurance exclusions or limited access to specialists qualified to order and interpret this testing. The working group has taken these inequities into consideration, and where possible, we have offered alternatives, such as recommending multigene panel testing when ES is not available. Limitations The working group formulated the recommendations using the best available evidence at the time of writing (2022). The quality of the evidence, however, generally falls at a level II–IV (moderate) based on the GRADE system, so these recommendations should be considered conditional on completion of higher quality studies. Expert opinion was used to fill in the gaps where evidence was lacking. It was beyond the scope of the working group to conduct an independent cost-effectiveness analysis as part of the development of this position statement. Recognising that resources are finite, these recommendations attempt to strike a balance between avoiding over-testing and the risk of missing a diagnosis that may have treatment or recurrence risk implications for the patient and their family. Finally, input from patients and their families was not solicited in the development of these recommendations, but for future iterations of this statement, this will be an important addition. The sections further will briefly summarise the evidence for each test modality and list recommendations for use of the test as first or second tier for patients with NDDs. It should be understood that first tier tests are, for the most part, able to be ordered by any qualified clinician and therefore should generally be done prior to (or at the same time as) referral for genetics consultation. summarises the recommendations and provides guidance as to when a patient should be referred to genetics

Fragile X testing (<italic toggle="yes">FMR1</italic> CGG repeat analysis) FXS) is an X-linked condition caused by the unstable expansion of a CGG repeat in the 5′UTR of the FMR1 gene and subsequent hypermethylation, preventing gene expression. It is a common monogenic cause of NDDs, with a prevalence of 1.4 per 10 000 males and 0.9 per 10 000 females. FXS testing is widely available and can be ordered by a variety of clinicians. FXS cannot, at this time, be diagnosed by CMA or ES. The ‘classic’ FXS phenotype in males includes moderate-to-severe ID, macro-orchidism and distinctive facial features (long face, large ears and prominent jaw). Common comorbid conditions include ASD, anxiety and hyperactivity. Deviation from the classical phenotype is influenced by age and sex (with females and prepubescent children manifesting fewer physical characteristics) and the presence of DNA methylation or repeat size mosaicism. The phenotype in females is highly variable, with IQ ranging from normal to moderate ID, likely due to the effects of random X-inactivation. FXS has a high recurrence risk in families, as children with a full mutation have mothers with a premutation that confers a risk for expansion in the oocyte, or with a full mutation. If the diagnosis of FXS is delayed, parents may not have the opportunity to have prenatal diagnosis in subsequent pregnancies, which may result in multiple affected children. For these reasons, a variety of professional organisations recommend FXS testing as a first-line diagnostic test (concurrent with CMA) for GDD, ID and ASD. These recommendations were largely based on expert opinion and/or published prior to publication of larger studies examining the diagnostic yield of NGS-based testing for NDDs. The diagnostic yield of fragile X testing varies between studies, based on the study design and characteristics of the study population. Taken together, the sex-specific prevalence of FXS in individuals with NDD is 2.2%–2.5% for males and 1.3%–1.6% in females. Retrospective reviews of laboratory databases demonstrate a diagnostic yield of 0%–2.5% for FXS testing. The diagnostic yield of FXS testing increases (9.5%–17%) when inclusion criteria are restricted to males with NDD and characteristic physical and behavioural features or family history suggestive of FXS. Use of a diagnostic ‘checklist’ to determine likelihood of FXS in males generally has high sensitivity, but only if a low threshold is used. There is insufficient data to determine whether this approach yields a higher diagnostic rate in females with NDDs. No studies have evaluated the cost-effectiveness of selective FXS testing based on clinical criteria. Recommendations for fragile X testing FXS testing is recommended as a first-tier diagnostic test for individuals presenting with: GDD, ID or ASD and a clinical presentation or family history suggestive of FXS (see ). Any NDD and a family history of FXS or other FMR1 -related disorder. FXS testing is not recommended for individuals with GDD or ID who do not meet the above criteria and have a complex clinical presentation that is not consistent with FXS (eg, multiple congenital anomalies, profound neurological impairment). Chromosomal microarray CMA uses comparative genomic hybridisation or SNP array to detect gains and losses of chromosomal material, known as CNVs. SNP-based arrays are also able to detect areas of long contiguous stretches of homozygosity, which may suggest parental consanguinity or uniparental disomy. While CMA can detect CNVs as small as approximately 20–50 kb, resolution varies depending on the technology used and density of DNA probes. CMA is widely available and can be ordered by a variety of clinicians. CNVs can be classified as pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain significance, likely benign or benign. CNVs of uncertain significance require interpretation from a clinical geneticist and may warrant additional investigations. CMA may detect ‘susceptibility CNVs’: recurrent CNVs with variable expressivity and/or incomplete penetrance. The phenotype resulting from these CNVs is variable and likely influenced by other genetic and environmental factors. Detection of these variants in an individual with a neurodevelopmental disorder may not entirely explain the observed phenotypes, so additional investigations may be warranted; however, this is not well studied. The phenotype resulting from these CNVs is variable and likely influenced by other genetic and environmental factors. Detection of these variants in an individual with a neurodevelopmental disorder may not entirely explain the observed phenotypes, so additional investigations may be warranted; however, this is not well studied. A variety of professional organisations recommend CMA as a first-tier test for individuals with GDD, ID or ASD, based on its high diagnostic yield compared with standard karyotype. In general, the diagnostic yield of CMA is lower in studies in which the probands have mild ID (12%–19% vs 20%–30% for moderate to severe ID ) or ASD without syndromic features (4%–5% for non-syndromic ASD vs up to 25% for those with syndromic features ). There are no studies that investigate the diagnostic yield of CMA for isolated speech or motor delay or LD. Although three studies report a detection rate of 8%–9% for rare CNVs in individuals with ADHD, they lack sufficient clinical information about the probands to determine whether ADHD was isolated or associated with GDD/ID or syndromic features. Furthermore, in these studies, many of the detected rare CNVs were inherited and the pathogenicity and clinical impact of these CNVs were unclear. Another study found that children with isolated ADHD had similar detection of rare CNVs compared with controls. There is strong evidence for the utility of CMA as a first-tier test for individuals with GDD, ID or ASD. There is insufficient evidence for the utility of CMA as a first-tier test for other NDDs such as ADHD without GDD, ID or ASD unless there are other clinical features suggestive of a syndromic aetiology (see ). Recommendations for CMA testing CMA is recommended as a first-tier diagnostic test for individuals presenting with: GDD, ID or ASD. Other NDDs when syndromic features are present (see ). Metabolic testing Inherited metabolic disorders (IMDs) comprise a group of genetic conditions that can present with NDDs as part of the clinical spectrum. Metabolic testing can detect the presence or absence of biochemical markers that lead to a diagnosis of IMD. While individually rare, there can be clinical value in diagnosing IMDs: for some disorders, early identification and treatment can improve outcomes, and most of the conditions are autosomal recessive and therefore have a high recurrence risk. According to a systematic literature review, over 100 IMDs with ID as a major feature have potential treatments. Examples of IMDs causing NDD that have disease-modifying treatments are urea cycle disorders, maple syrup urine disease, homocystinurias, including cobalamin-related conditions, and some creatine disorders including guanidinoacetate methyltransferase deficiency. Some authors suggest that all individuals presenting with GDD/ID/ASD should be screened for IMDs, while others recommend screening only for individuals with additional clinical features suggestive of an IMD. There is also a lack of consensus among experts as to which metabolic investigations comprise a comprehensive screen for IMDs. Indeed, there is wide variability in Canadian clinical practice. Both the Canadian Pediatric Society and the American Academy of Pediatrics reference a systematic literature review as the rationale to screen for treatable IMDs in all children presenting with GDD/ID; however, the diagnostic yield of this approach was unknown at the time. The protocol suggested by the Treatable Intellectual Disability Endeavor (TIDE) ( www.tidebc.org ) is extensive; yet, not all the tests in this protocol are widely available, and clinical utility and cost-effectiveness have not been evaluated. The reported diagnostic yield of metabolic testing for patients with NDDs can vary depending on the population studied. However, using the best evidence available (more recent publications in populations with expanded newborn screening, larger case series with clear case definitions), the overall diagnostic yield of metabolic testing for patients with NDDs is 0.25%–0.42% for GDD/ID in non-consanguineous populations. Retrospective reviews of the medical records of patients with diagnosed IMDs show that most of these patients have clinical features suggestive of an IMD in addition to GDD/ID. In a prospective study by Campistol et al in 2016, an IMD diagnosis was rarely identified in children with non-syndromic ASD. A review of the pilot implementation of the TIDE protocol for patients with GDD/ID, with and without suggestive neurological features, demonstrated no significant increase in diagnoses of IMD during time periods before and after implementation despite a greater than fourfold increase in test volumes. Metabolic testing early in the diagnostic process should theoretically improve ‘time to diagnosis’ and clinical outcomes for IMDs not detected by newborn screening; however, this has not been rigorously studied. Reviews, commentaries and guidelines that quote diagnostic yields of metabolic investigations for NDDs as high as 5% should be interpreted with caution. Metabolic testing early in the diagnostic process should theoretically improve ‘time to diagnosis’ and clinical outcomes for IMDs not detected by newborn screening; however, this has not been rigorously studied. Reviews, commentaries and guidelines that quote diagnostic yields of metabolic investigations for NDDs as high as 5% should be interpreted with caution. Literature examining the diagnostic yield of metabolic testing for patients with NDDs is generally of low quality due to lack of peer review, small sample sizes, variability in tests performed and lack of robust case definitions. Furthermore, some publications pre-date the expansion of newborn screening to detect more treatable IMDs. Although most children with treatable IMDs are now diagnosed by routine provincial newborn screening programmes in Canada, newborn screening cannot detect all treatable IMDs, neonatal screening programmes vary among provinces/territories and false-negative screens are possible. For children with NDDs, most IMD diagnoses are made in those with clinical features such as regression or plateauing of development, acute encephalopathy or altered level of consciousness, movement disorders, intractable seizures, multisystemic involvement, specific ophthalmological findings, organomegaly and/or features suggestive of a storage disease. Patients with such ‘red flags’ should be referred for specialist consultation without delay. provides guidance on additional investigations that should be ordered, where possible, for patients with these features while they await consultation. Given its very low yield, routine metabolic testing is not recommended for patients with GDD/ID/ASD without suggestive clinical features listed in . Rarely, a treatable IMD may be missed by not performing metabolic testing for such patients; for example, patients with homocystinurias, including cobalamin-related conditions, can occasionally present with isolated NDDs. However, these conditions are very rare, and those with time-sensitive treatments are detected by newborn screening. Creatine transporter disorder, which is X-linked, may rarely present with isolated NDD. Treatment does not alter clinical outcomes for this condition; however, diagnosis might be helpful for future family planning. Clinicians should be aware of the conditions tested for via newborn screening in their jurisdiction. Children who have not had newborn screening may be at increased risk for having an undiagnosed IMD, so clinicians should determine what newborn screening was done and, if limited, consider referring to a metabolic specialist. Recommendations for metabolic testing Metabolic testing is recommended as a first-tier diagnostic test for individuals presenting with: GDD, ID, or ASD and clinical features suggestive of an IMD. Metabolic testing should be tailored to the presentation (see ) and a referral made to a metabolic specialist promptly. Metabolic testing is not recommended for individuals presenting with ASD/GDD/ID without suggestive features unless newborn screening was not performed or the test panel was not comparable with standard provincial programmes (eg, newcomers to Canada). ES and multigene panels Massively parallel ‘next-generation’ sequencing technology has allowed for the simultaneous analysis of hundreds to thousands of genes from a single DNA sample. Currently, ES is widely available as a clinical diagnostic test. An alternative to ES is the use of comprehensive multigene panels, which are targeted to a specific phenotype. For NDDs, commercially available panels vary widely in the number of genes analysed; the largest ones include over 2500 genes. In future, GS is poised to replace both ES and CMA, but as it is not yet publicly funded in Canada, these recommendations consider the use of panels and ES only. The main advantage of ES and large panels is the ability to simultaneously interrogate large numbers of genes, which means that the clinician need not have a particular genetic condition in mind to direct the diagnosis. However, they have important limitations that means that a negative test does not rule out a genetic cause. Depending on the methodology used, all coding exons may not be completely sequenced and, thus, some variants may be missed. ES is less able to detect mosaicism or exon-level deletions compared with GS or panels that include deletion/duplication analysis. ES and panels do not reliably assess repetitive DNA sequences (such as trinucleotide repeats), intronic or non-coding variants, methylation, epigenetic or mitochondrial DNA variants or balanced chromosomal rearrangements. These tests can identify multiple rare variants in a patient’s sample, the clinical relevance of which can be challenging to decipher. They can identify misattributed parentage (when done as a ‘trio’ with both declared parents), as well as incidental and secondary findings (pathogenic variants in medically actionable genes unrelated to the indication for testing). Furthermore, they can identify misattributed parentage (when done, as they often are, as a ‘trio’ with both declared parents) and secondary findings (pathogenic variants in medically actionable genes unrelated to the indication for testing). Testing of the proband only (vs proband-parent

variants or balanced chromosomal rearrangements. These tests can identify multiple rare variants in a patient’s sample, the clinical relevance of which can be challenging to decipher. They can identify misattributed parentage (when done as a ‘trio’ with both declared parents), as well as incidental and secondary findings (pathogenic variants in medically actionable genes unrelated to the indication for testing). Furthermore, they can identify misattributed parentage (when done, as they often are, as a ‘trio’ with both declared parents) and secondary findings (pathogenic variants in medically actionable genes unrelated to the indication for testing). Testing of the proband only (vs proband-parent trio) results in a lower diagnostic yield and more labour-intensive downstream analysis and/or additional testing to resolve variants, so a ‘trio’ approach is the most useful, time-efficient and informative approach. Given these considerations, these tests require robust pretest and post-test genetic counselling and input from a clinical geneticist. ES and comprehensive multigene panels were not widely available as routine clinical tests when the practice guidelines for genetic testing for patients with NDDs were published by the American Association of Neurology in 2011 and the American Association of Pediatrics in 2014. However, a 2015 CCMG position statement recommended clinical GWS (either exome or genome sequencing) for patients with moderate-to-severe or syndromic ID, when appropriate first-tier genetic testing (such as CMA) is non-diagnostic. The 2021 ACMG practice guidelines strongly recommend that GWS be considered as a first-tier or second-tier test for paediatric patients with developmental delays and/or ID. Diagnostic yield of ES for patients with NDDs The reported diagnostic yield of ES for patients with GDD/ID demonstrates wide variation (8%–68%), likely owing to differences in cohort size and composition, whether ES was performed clinically or under a research protocol and whether a proband-parent trio or proband-only approach was used. When considering the largest studies from clinical laboratories, the diagnostic yield of ES is 26%–31%, consistent with results from a meta-analysis that showed pooled estimates of 29%. It is difficult to tease out the diagnostic yield in specific patient subgroups (such as ASD without GDD/ID, or GDD/ID without syndromic features). A few studies dedicated to patients with ASD, most of whom had ID (with or without other features), reported that ES had a diagnostic yield of 8%–25.8%. The few studies that have compared the diagnostic yield of ES for GDD/ID patients with and without syndromic features have not found statistically significant differences. Diagnostic yield of NGS panels for patients with NDDs A few studies have examined comprehensive panels for patients with NDDs, reporting a diagnostic yield of 11%–39%. Two studies directly compared a targeted NDD gene panel to ES, and both demonstrated slightly lower diagnostic yields for the panel Clinical utility of ES for individuals with NDDs The clinical utility of ES for the diagnosis of patients with suspected monogenic disorders has been well established. A 2020 Ontario Health Technology Assessment examined the clinical utility of ES in unexplained developmental disabilities and multiple congenital anomalies, concluding that ES allows for changes in clinical management, provides insight into the natural history of the patient’s condition, informs reproductive planning and optimises the patient’s ability to access disease-specific supports. Similar findings were reported in a 2020 ACMG systematic evidence review that examined the health, clinical, reproductive and psychosocial outcomes resulting from ES for the investigation of congenital anomalies, developmental delay or ID. It also considered possible negative impacts such as insurance discrimination, financial burden and psychological impact on patients and found that return of ES test results incur no clinically significant psychological harms with low levels of test-related distress and positive psychological effects. Genetic counselling and an appropriate consenting process can help mitigate any associated risks. Cost-effectiveness of ES The significant cost of ES has historically been a barrier to its implementation within the Canadian healthcare system as standard-of-care testing for NDDs. Recent evidence shows that performing ES early in the diagnostic testing pathway is cost-effective, although other studies have been inconclusive. In Ontario, a 2020 cost analysis of ES testing before or concurrently with CMA for patients with developmental disabilities supported ES as a second-tier test (when CMA is non-diagnostic) as the most cost-effective approach ; this study is based on ES analysis that does not include duplication/deletion analysis. In summary, the evidence strongly supports using ES as a diagnostic test for patients with ID/GDD due to its high diagnostic yield, cost-effectiveness and demonstrable clinical utility. The diagnostic yield for patients with GDD/ID is significant even in the absence of syndromic features. For patients with ASD without GDD/ID, there is insufficient data to make evidence-based recommendations, although evidence suggests a higher diagnostic yield for patients with syndromic features ( ). A trio-based testing approach is recommended. While ES provides a higher diagnostic yield, a comprehensive multigene panel for NDDs is a suitable substitute when ES

not include duplication/deletion analysis. In summary, the evidence strongly supports using ES as a diagnostic test for patients with ID/GDD due to its high diagnostic yield, cost-effectiveness and demonstrable clinical utility. The diagnostic yield for patients with GDD/ID is significant even in the absence of syndromic features. For patients with ASD without GDD/ID, there is insufficient data to make evidence-based recommendations, although evidence suggests a higher diagnostic yield for patients with syndromic features ( ). A trio-based testing approach is recommended. While ES provides a higher diagnostic yield, a comprehensive multigene panel for NDDs is a suitable substitute when ES is not available, especially when done as a trio-based test. When GS becomes a widely available clinical test, it is anticipated to replace fragile X, CMA and ES as a single test of choice for NDDs. In most cases ES is recommended as a second-tier test after CMA, as the latter has a high diagnostic yield, is more widely available, less costly and can be ordered by non-geneticists. However, it may be appropriate to do GWS before or concurrently with CMA; for example, when the proband is highly likely to have an autosomal recessive condition (based on parental consanguinity and/or affected siblings), or when a diagnosis must be rapidly obtained, such as to inform the management of an ongoing pregnancy (for a sibling of the proband), or to guide medical care in a patient who is acutely ill or whose clinical status is deteriorating (eg, neurological regression). Recommendations for ES or multigene panels Recommended as a second-tier diagnostic test for individuals presenting with: GDD or ID (with or without ASD). ASD and/or other NDD and clinical features suggestive of a syndrome (see ). Conclusions Patients with NDDs in Canada require a thorough evaluation for the underlying cause of their condition. The CCMG Neurodevelopmental Disorders working group recommends an approach to the diagnostic evaluation that is tailored to the patient and based on current evidence. These recommendations are based on best available evidence as of 2022 and may evolve as new evidence emerges. Therefore, they should be reviewed every 2–3 years. An overview of these recommendations are found in . We recommend a tiered testing strategy, such that first-tier testing is ordered by non-geneticists (family doctors, paediatricians, neurologists, etc), to allow patients faster access to testing and potentially a rapid diagnosis. The provision of genetic testing by non-specialists should be supported with enhanced genetics education at all levels of medical training. We provide guidelines for when a patient should be referred to a specialist in genetics or metabolics: specifically, anyone with GDD/ID (regardless of other features), as well as patients with ASD or other NDDs if they have syndromic features ( ) or features suggestive of an inherited metabolic disease ( ).

chunks.content: Nonstandard Abbreviations and Acronyms ACHD adult congenital heart disease CNOC Cardiac Neurodevelopmental Outcome Collaborative Adults with congenital heart disease (CHD) represent a growing and diverse patient population with challenges related to cardiovascular and neurological health. Advances in medical care have dramatically improved survival rates for individuals born with heart disease, and as a result, a growing number of individuals with CHD are living into adulthood. For those with CHD, risks for neurodevelopmental delays in childhood are high, and there is increasing recognition of the complex and often underaddressed neurocognitive and psychological challenges faced by this population. , In adulthood, challenges related to cognitive function, mental health, health literacy, and the ability to navigate health care systems can significantly impact education and employment, self‐care, quality of life, and well‐being. , Despite the multiple challenges this population faces, effective interventions to improve neurocognitive and psychological functioning remain largely unexplored in adult CHD (ACHD), whereas these efforts are growing for pediatric CHD. Heterogeneity in patients with ACHD, including varying disease severity, age of diagnosis and intervention, surgical era, medical comorbidities (eg, genetic disorder, cerebral palsy, epilepsy), and the long‐term effects of cardiac interventions, contributes to complex neurocognitive and psychological concerns that are often overlooked in ACHD care. There is a critical need for a systematic approach to identifying and addressing neurocognitive and psychological concerns for patients with ACHD. Available literature is, however, limited by small sample sizes, inconsistent methodologies, and a lack of longitudinal data, resulting in significant gaps that hinder the development of evidence‐based strategies to support and advance clinical care for patients with ACHD. Following monthly virtual meetings from December to March, multidisciplinary experts and patient partners (see Table ) convened at a 2‐day ACHD/Neuro Conference in April 2024 in Atlanta, Georgia, to evaluate current knowledge and identify critical gaps in neurocognitive and psychological research related to ACHD. The format for this project was modeled after a similar initiative within pediatric cardiology. Members included experts in adult and pediatric cardiology, cardiovascular surgery, nursing, psychiatry, psychology, neuropsychology, neonatology, neuroradiology, neurology, and neuroscience, as well as adults with CHD. Three working groups focused on genetics and brain health, characterizing outcomes, and interventions, to guide the next decade of research and clinical care with ACHD. Supported by the Meil Family Foundation Research Award, the initiative aimed to identify key research themes and 5 critical questions for future priorities. This article highlights the work of the Interventions Working Group (see companion consensus papers from the Genetics and Brain Health and Characterizing Outcomes Working Groups), offering a summary of existing knowledge, significant gaps, and proposed next steps regarding neurocognitive and psychological interventions (see Table ). These “next steps” aim to inspire dialogue, strengthen collaboration across the ACHD community, and drive meaningful improvements in care and outcomes. CRITICAL QUESTIONS Question 1: What Interventions Are Effective for Improving Neurocognitive Functioning in Patients With <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ACHD</styled-content>? Existing Knowledge Neurodevelopmental delays and disorders in children and adolescents with CHD have been widely recognized. More recently, it has become clear that concerns may not resolve and can still be evident in young‐ and middle‐aged adults with CHD. Neurocognitive difficulties vary on the basis of CHD complexity , including general cognition, academic achievement, executive functioning, visuospatial skills, memory, quality of life, social cognition, and psychological functioning, , , and affect education, employment, and disability status. For many, there is also an interplay between neurocognitive and psychological symptoms, such as when executive dysfunction and depression/anxiety exacerbate one another. Neuropsychological sequelae in patients with ACHD have been linked to structural brain abnormalities, including white matter injury and lower structural brain volumes. , Early neurological risks may interact with later cardiovascular morbidities, like heart failure and arrhythmia, further increasing neurocognitive decline. Early risk for dementia has been linked to ACHD, with studies suggesting that neurocognitive deficits, including impaired executive function and memory, may predispose patients with ACHD to accelerated cognitive decline and neurodegenerative processes later in life. In the general adult population without CHD, there is growing evidence that physical fitness and short‐ and long‐term exercise programs are associated with better neurocognitive and psychological health, as well as lower risk of neurodegenerative diseases. Modest improvements are shown for aspects of attention, executive functioning, and memory. Other efficacious interventions to address neurocognitive health in the general population include mind–body exercises, such as meditation. Multimodal interventions that couple physical activity with neurocognitive intervention may have greater efficacy and sustained effects. Among individuals with mild to moderate dementia in the general population, a growing number of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving cognitive rehabilitation show substantial variability in methodology that limits generalizability. For example, a recent review in the general population with mild to moderate dementia suggests weak evidence for improvement in specific cognitive processes (eg, attention, memory), but stronger support for improved functional abilities and perceived well‐being

memory. Other efficacious interventions to address neurocognitive health in the general population include mind–body exercises, such as meditation. Multimodal interventions that couple physical activity with neurocognitive intervention may have greater efficacy and sustained effects. Among individuals with mild to moderate dementia in the general population, a growing number of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving cognitive rehabilitation show substantial variability in methodology that limits generalizability. For example, a recent review in the general population with mild to moderate dementia suggests weak evidence for improvement in specific cognitive processes (eg, attention, memory), but stronger support for improved functional abilities and perceived well‐being following cognitive remediation. As for the CHD population specifically, a limited number of studies in pediatric CHD and other types of heart disease provide inconclusive evidence about how cardiac rehabilitation or physical exercise improves cognition, executive functioning, or quality of life. Studies have shown that remission from depression is associated with improvements in exercise capacity and lifestyle factors, mental health, and quality of life. In contrast, nonremitters continued to report low mental well‐being and quality of life, alongside a decline in exercise capacity, a well‐established prognostic marker in patients with ACHD. , Exercise capacity in CHD varies on the basis of disease severity and coexisting conditions, with prevalent concerns about reduced physical activity and exercise‐related fear that often begins in childhood. These factors significantly impact overall health and physical function in patients with ACHD. , Significant Gaps The effectiveness of interventions to address neurocognitive concerns in ACHD remains insufficiently evaluated. While physical exercise and mind–body exercises show promise for improving mild neurocognitive concerns in the general population, their applicability to ACHD is uncertain, as is the role of exercise fear and intolerance. Similarly, cognitive rehabilitation for mild to moderate dementia has not been studied in patients with ACHD. The feasibility of these interventions in acute or outpatient settings is unknown. Additionally, it is unclear how these interventions might impact the interaction between neurocognitive and psychological symptoms, such as how anxiety reduction could improve decision making. Next Steps ACHD centers offering neurocognitive interventions should publish descriptive or retrospective data on patients who have undergone neurocognitive training, rehabilitation, or physical exercise, including lessons learned. This information could help inform new service delivery. Clinical scientists working with patients with ACHD should adapt and implement empirically supported neurocognitive interventions used with other medical populations. This includes consideration of exercise limitations and fears that are common in patients with ACHD. ACHD centers should consider RCTs with control conditions when evaluating the efficacy of neurocognitive interventions. Outcome measurement could include cognitive processes, neurological correlates, functional capabilities, and well‐being. To inform clinical referrals and risk stratification, patient‐specific factors (eg, cognitive reserve, family) and risks (eg, medical, surgical) should be considered. Researchers should partner to leverage existing outcome registries. For example, the CNOC (Cardiac Neurodevelopmental Outcome Collaborative) registry could be used to recruit young adult participants for targeted neurocognitive interventions and track longitudinal changes. Question 2: What Interventions Are Effective for Improving Psychological Well‐Being in Patients With <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ACHD</styled-content>? Existing Knowledge A growing literature demonstrates the high prevalence of psychological symptoms and disorders (eg, anxiety, depression, posttraumatic stress) in patients with ACHD, with symptoms affecting quality of life, , , , health‐related self‐management, and retention in care. While the stressful and sometimes traumatic effects of living with a complex chronic medical condition are among the risks for the development of psychological symptoms/disorders, it is further understood that many individuals with CHD were raised in families that also experience high rates of psychological symptoms (eg, anxiety, depression, posttraumatic stress) and life stressors (eg, financial strain due to medical expenses). , Data on the efficacy of psychological interventions in patients with ACHD are sparse and methodologically weak. A recent review of 4 intervention‐based studies (mindfulness‐based stress reduction, resilience training, cardiac rehabilitation) that combined adolescents and adults with CHD with other types of cardiovascular disease found no significant improvements. This review article discusses how interventions without a theoretical framework and reliance on symptom‐based assessment without diagnostic cutoff or clinical corroboration are factors that limited efficacy. A later RCT with group‐based cognitive behavioral therapy in patients with ACHD reported a reduction in depressive symptoms with a moderate effect size for the intervention group compared with the control group. Integrating psychological care into routine ACHD care has also been found to facilitate feasible and timely psychological intervention. Given the paucity of interventions for patients with ACHD, extrapolation from other populations may be informative, especially given that evidence‐based psychological interventions exist for symptoms also occurring in patients with ACHD. In 2021, the American Heart Association published a scientific statement about the mind–heart–body connection, emphasizing the need for psychological interventions for adults with cardiovascular disease. A Cochrane systematic review and meta‐analysis found that psychological interventions, such as relaxation techniques, self‐awareness and self‐monitoring, cognitive restructuring,

intervention group compared with the control group. Integrating psychological care into routine ACHD care has also been found to facilitate feasible and timely psychological intervention. Given the paucity of interventions for patients with ACHD, extrapolation from other populations may be informative, especially given that evidence‐based psychological interventions exist for symptoms also occurring in patients with ACHD. In 2021, the American Heart Association published a scientific statement about the mind–heart–body connection, emphasizing the need for psychological interventions for adults with cardiovascular disease. A Cochrane systematic review and meta‐analysis found that psychological interventions, such as relaxation techniques, self‐awareness and self‐monitoring, cognitive restructuring, or emotional support, significantly reduced depressive symptoms, anxiety, stress, and cardiovascular death in adults with coronary artery disease. More broadly, in adults with and without medical conditions, there are decades of research to support the efficacy of various psychological approaches. Cognitive behavioral therapy, which involves restructuring patterns in one’s thinking and behavior, has been shown to improve symptoms of depression, anxiety, and trauma‐related disorders. For posttraumatic stress, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing has shown efficacy for symptom reduction. Mindfulness‐based interventions have also shown effectiveness for reducing stress, depression, and anxiety in those with cardiovascular disease, and neurological changes (eg, neural connectivity, functional activity) are also being explored. Acceptance and commitment therapy, which helps individuals accept their thoughts and feelings and commit to personally meaningful goals consistent with their values despite psychological difficulties, has demonstrated efficacy for reducing depression, anxiety, and other psychological symptoms associated with heart disease and diabetes. There is growing evidence to support a center‐level approach to the prevention or reduction in health‐related stress and psychological symptoms, including trauma‐informed care. Significant Gaps Existing psychological intervention studies in patients with ACHD have methodological limitations, such as retrospective designs, nonrandomized approaches, provider training, low response and high attrition rates, short follow‐up, and limited sample diversity. Additionally, it’s unclear how empirically supported interventions (eg, cognitive behavioral therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing) may need to be adapted for ACHD. There are also limited data on the prevalence of substance abuse, eating disorders, suicide, self‐harm behaviors, and psychotic symptoms in patients with ACHD, limiting the ability to prioritize intervention. Next Steps Psychological intervention studies should consider multicenter RCTs with clear procedures, validated outcome measures, and diverse participant demographics when assessing the efficacy in patients with ACHD. These trials should monitor outcomes for at least 6 to 12 months following intervention. Clinicians designing psychological interventions are encouraged to follow a community‐based participatory research approach involving individuals with lived experience (patients, peer mentors, family members) to understand the unique needs of patients with ACHD. Research is needed about the prevalence of substance abuse, suicidality, self‐harm, psychotic symptoms, and eating disorders in patients with ACHD, and how this information should inform intervention priorities. Clinical scientists should examine the effectiveness of existing models of integrated, patient‐centered, trauma‐informed care for ACHD centers. These data are necessary for broader implementation across centers. Question 3: What Evidence Do We Have for the Safety and Efficacy of Psychotropic Medications in Patients With <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ACHD</styled-content>? Existing Knowledge Psychotropic medications (eg, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, stimulants) can be used to support psychiatric symptoms (eg, anxiety, depression, attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder) commonly experienced in patients with ACHD. , , , Yet only 1 study has examined the effectiveness of such medications in patients with ACHD, focusing on the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for depression. Given this absence of evidence to inform the use of psychotropics in patients with ACHD, providers rely on research and clinical guidelines from other populations, including pediatric CHD, , , , , adults with acquired cardiovascular conditions (eg, heart failure, coronary artery disease), , , and the general population. , , , , In adults with acquired heart disease, selected selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (ie, escitalopram and sertraline), have been found effective in treating depression without significant adverse cardiovascular events. , , There are also robust data on the efficacy of stimulants (eg, amphetamine salts, methylphenidate) in reducing attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptoms in the general population and their short‐term cardiovascular safety in the CHD population. , , , , , However, the long‐term cardiovascular safety of stimulants in CHD has yet to be examined, especially for those who were prescribed stimulants since childhood. A recent meta‐analysis in a Swedish national cohort reported that medications for attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder, including stimulants and nonstimulants (eg, guanfacine, atomoxetine), were associated with increased risk of hypertension and arterial disease, especially in the first 3 years of treatment. While no stimulant‐prescribing guidelines exist for ACHD, guidelines for pediatric CHD recommend cautious use of stimulants in patients with hypertension, tachycardia, known risk of sudden cardiac death, or severe arrhythmia. , ECG monitoring is recommended at initiation and dose increase. One study on ACHD, a single‐center retrospective study, found no association between antidepressant

for those who were prescribed stimulants since childhood. A recent meta‐analysis in a Swedish national cohort reported that medications for attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder, including stimulants and nonstimulants (eg, guanfacine, atomoxetine), were associated with increased risk of hypertension and arterial disease, especially in the first 3 years of treatment. While no stimulant‐prescribing guidelines exist for ACHD, guidelines for pediatric CHD recommend cautious use of stimulants in patients with hypertension, tachycardia, known risk of sudden cardiac death, or severe arrhythmia. , ECG monitoring is recommended at initiation and dose increase. One study on ACHD, a single‐center retrospective study, found no association between antidepressant use and increased death ; however, the study did not stratify risk by medication or CHD type. Significant Gaps At the time of writing, no published clinical trials or large prospective studies have examined the efficacy and safety of psychotropic medications in patients with ACHD. This lack of research vastly limits our understanding of their effectiveness for reducing psychiatric symptoms, as well as any potential adverse outcomes. There is a notable absence of retrospective or cross‐sectional studies that could begin to establish the presence and strength of such associations. Existing literature does not analyze medications within subgroups of patients with ACHD, each with potentially unique cardiovascular or other medical risks. Consequently, evidence‐based prescribing and monitoring guidelines for psychotropic medications are nonexistent in patients with ACHD. Finally, it remains unknown how ACHD prescribing providers are currently practicing and managing these challenges within the context of growing needs. Next Steps Providers from ACHD centers should complete a survey study to describe current prescribing patterns for common psychiatric symptoms (eg, depression, anxiety, posttraumatic stress, attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder), factors that influence decision making (eg, peer consultation, clinical experience, pediatric studies), and provider priorities for unmet needs in patients with ACHD. Research should involve multicenter, demographically diverse longitudinal cohort outcome studies to examine associations between specific medications and longitudinal symptom profiles using empirically supported psychological or neuropsychological measures. Clinical scientists should conduct both prospective longitudinal studies and RCTs regarding psychotropic medication across different forms of ACHD. This is key to understanding benefits, risks, and adverse outcomes. Study design should also inform providers about individual‐level risk stratification for interactions between medications, other treatments, and noncardiac comorbidities. Prescribing providers should partner to develop and publish clinical practice guidelines for psychiatric medications in patients with ACHD. These are urgently needed to inform cardiologists, psychiatrists, and internists working with patients with ACHD. Question 4: What Interventions Can Improve Health Literacy in Patients With <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ACHD</styled-content>? Existing Knowledge Between 36% and 88% of adults in the United States have health literacy insufficient to navigate the health care system and promote wellness. A recent American Heart Association Scientific Statement addressed the critical role of health literacy in adult cardiovascular outcomes, including how it contributes to morbidity, death, health care costs, health disparities, and self‐care (eg, treatment adherence, managing symptoms). The definition of health literacy has evolved to integrate multiple dimensions, antecedents, and consequences, culminating in separate definitions for personal and organizational health literacy adopted by the Healthy People 2030 initiative of the US Department of Health and Human Services : Personal health literacy is the degree to which individuals can find, understand, and use information and services to inform health‐related decisions and actions for themselves and others. Organizational health literacy is the degree to which organizations equitably enable individuals to find, understand, and use information and services to inform health‐related decisions and actions for themselves and others (p. 259) Assessment of personal health literacy using self‐report measures is challenging, with considerations based on time constraints (eg, 1–22 minutes to complete), setting (inpatient versus outpatient), patient population, language, and modality (eg, verbal, paper, or digital). The online Health Literacy Tool Shed from Tufts Medicine shares different health literacy measures, with the ability to filter by patient population, administration time, language(s), and more. Interventions to address health literacy have grown in recent years. A review of 22 intervention studies between 2018 and 2020 across 9 countries and spanning multiple health conditions (eg, cancer, heart failure) identified 12 interventions that improved health literacy and 13 that improved health behaviors (eg, self‐care). Examples of interventions included standardized patient education, strengthening self‐management or health behaviors, improving patient–provider interactions (e.g., summarizing and teaching back techniques), technologies or resources to improve sharing of health information (eg, Adult Congenital Heart Association, Personal Health Passport). , Intervention approaches varied widely on the basis of content, time commitment, group or individual sessions, in‐person versus online format, and use of technology or social media as well as outcome measures. , In addition to addressing personal health literacy, key attributes of a health‐literate organization help guide interventions to address the role of providers and health systems. Both personal and organizational health literacy interventions have the potential to reduce the impact of low socioeconomic

patient–provider interactions (e.g., summarizing and teaching back techniques), technologies or resources to improve sharing of health information (eg, Adult Congenital Heart Association, Personal Health Passport). , Intervention approaches varied widely on the basis of content, time commitment, group or individual sessions, in‐person versus online format, and use of technology or social media as well as outcome measures. , In addition to addressing personal health literacy, key attributes of a health‐literate organization help guide interventions to address the role of providers and health systems. Both personal and organizational health literacy interventions have the potential to reduce the impact of low socioeconomic status on poor health outcomes, with extensive research supporting health literacy as a complex mediator of health outcomes. , Health literacy interventions specific to adult cardiology populations have focused on cardiac disease prevention, heart failure, cardiac rehabilitation, and coronary artery disease. Among CHD, high rates of neurodevelopmental delays, along with complex long‐term self‐care demands, suggest that health literacy should be an intervention focus. An assessment of needs among parents of children with CHD indicated gaps in preparedness, and parent‐focused interventions for pediatric CHD have since emerged to address caregiver education. , Health literacy interventions for patients with ACHD are extremely limited. One study focused solely on standardized education, but the target goal was not met for 9 of 10 patients. Multiple factors, including modifiable elements like self‐efficacy, depressive symptoms, and perceived family support, influence self‐care and should be considered when designing interventions. , Significant Gaps Health literacy priorities for patients with ACHD and their providers are largely unknown due to the lack of needs assessment. It is unclear if existing health literacy interventions can be effectively generalized to patients with ACHD. Patient‐specific factors, such as CHD type, co‐occurring conditions (eg, genetic conditions, heart transplant, stroke, intellectual disability), and the timing of diagnosis, may influence the effectiveness of health literacy interventions. Additionally, risk and protective factors related to caregivers, siblings, and communities are also unclear, especially for those treated during childhood. The connection between health literacy and social drivers of health (eg, economic stability, access to care, neighborhood and environment, racism and discrimination) is unknown for patients with ACHD, which limits the approaches that organizations can take to improve health literacy. Next Steps Research should examine the validity and reliability of health literacy and eHealth literacy measures for patients with ACHD, incorporating input from patients, providers, and family. Studies should explore how health literacy changes with age and care setting using standardized surveys, focus groups, and crowdsourcing to ensure diverse representation in measure development. Studies should explore patient‐specific factors in patients with ACHD that may affect health literacy intervention effectiveness, including disease type, co‐occurring conditions, family dynamics, sociocultural factors, mental health, and neurocognitive abilities. Use surveys, interviews, and focus groups to assess the fit of existing interventions. Clinical scientists are encouraged to partner with patients, providers, and administrators to pilot a CHD‐oriented health literacy intervention, tailored to specific settings and literacy levels, and prioritizing feasibility and sustainability. A subsequent RCT with pre‐ and post‐intervention assessments should then be conducted to more definitively determine intervention efficacy. Pediatric and adult health care system collaborations for research and clinical care are critical to understand the longitudinal nature of health literacy, the impact of family and community, and the role of pediatric transition programs. Improved knowledge in these areas can help inform future directions. Question 5: What Are Key Modifiable Facilitators and Barriers to Accessing High‐Quality Neurocognitive and Psychological Interventions in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ACHD</styled-content> Care? Existing Knowledge An estimated 39% of young adults with CHD are lost to follow‐up between pediatric and adult health care systems, with rates varying by disease severity, geographic region, and other factors. , Patients with ACHD report many barriers to follow‐up, including insufficient knowledge and education from cardiology providers about follow‐up, psychological concerns or symptoms, and poor accessibility (eg, high cost, transportation issues, limited providers). , Social factors exacerbate these barriers, and the number of patients with ACHD far exceeds the low number of providers and centers who provide care for patients with ACHD. A limited number of institutions have begun navigating these obstacles to provide psychological and neurocognitive services for patients with ACHD, and from them we can learn about patient‐specific barriers. Physical factors such as CHD severity, surgical history, medications, and associated conditions like pain or fatigue can impact engagement in exercise and rehabilitation programs., , , as well as use of psychotropic medications. These physical factors interact with psychological factors , such as mood, anxiety, posttraumatic stress, health anxiety, and social supports to influence a patient’s openness to and engagement with intervention. , Other relevant patient factors not specific to CHD include negative perspectives and stigma associated with mental illness and accessing mental health services. , Provider ‐ and organization ‐ specific barriers to psychological and neurocognitive

about patient‐specific barriers. Physical factors such as CHD severity, surgical history, medications, and associated conditions like pain or fatigue can impact engagement in exercise and rehabilitation programs., , , as well as use of psychotropic medications. These physical factors interact with psychological factors , such as mood, anxiety, posttraumatic stress, health anxiety, and social supports to influence a patient’s openness to and engagement with intervention. , Other relevant patient factors not specific to CHD include negative perspectives and stigma associated with mental illness and accessing mental health services. , Provider ‐ and organization ‐ specific barriers to psychological and neurocognitive interventions identified in other populations include inadequate resources, insufficient professional training, lack of intervention materials, provider shortages, and system fragmentation. Limited patient education about how to recognize symptoms (eg, of depression, anxiety, and stress), when and how to seek help, how services could be helpful, and how to gain access were all reported as barriers, , many of which are related to health literacy. In contrast, facilitators to implementing psychological services for at‐risk adult populations include engaging relevant stakeholders and evaluating the progress and quality of services. Quality of patient–clinician communication is critical to facilitating engagement, and technology (eg, telehealth) has improved access. Addressing health literacy can reduce the barriers associated with lower socioeconomic status and thereby facilitate access ; however, implementing organizational health literacy programs are a challenge due to barriers associated with culture and leadership, program planning and design, and provider/staff resources. , Attending to the perspectives of patients with ACHD about their priorities could serve as a facilitator. , Significant Gaps Beyond patient‐specific physical and psychological factors, limited data are available about provider and organizational barriers to accessing psychological and neurocognitive interventions. Anecdotal information from professional collaborations across institutions suggests that most ACHD programs are not providing integrated psychological and neurocognitive services. Thus, it is paramount that we share lessons learned from successful ACHD programs about how to facilitate access to high‐quality interventions. Next Steps ACHD centers should partner to conduct a multicenter standardized program survey to inform the cardiology community about existing intervention services, including resources, training, leadership, and funding. Identifying provider and organizational barriers and enablers would inform program development and quality improvement. Model programs could also partner with new programs. Clinical scientists should collect information about facilitators and barriers from patients who have previously accessed, are currently accessing, or have never used intervention services. Methods could include surveys, interviews, focus groups, and crowdsourcing in partnership with ACHD patient organizations. Institutions should implement alternative intervention service delivery methods (eg, telemedicine and asynchronous online intervention) to address barriers to care. Economic and process evaluations must also be conducted to ensure feasible/sustainable implementation. Clinical providers should explore potential partnerships between ACHD national organizations and programs to support online resources (eg, exemplar models and clinical processes; patient resources) that may address barriers. CONCLUSIONS Compared with other life‐limiting medical conditions, lifesaving cardiac surgical interventions are a relatively recent advancement in CHD, resulting in a comparatively young ACHD patient population that is continuing to evolve. However, the limited clinical research available and the fragmented nature of health care, marked by shortages of specialized ACHD providers, dedicated programs, expertise, and patient support services, pose substantial challenges to the effective implementation of psychological and neurocognitive interventions in this growing patient population. Addressing these barriers is essential to improving comprehensive care for individuals with ACHD. The pediatric CHD population faced similar challenges just 2 decades ago but has since developed a robust international collaboration that has catapulted the field forward to improve the quality care for pediatric CHD and their families. Valuable insights from the pediatric CHD community could be adapted and expanded to inform the ACHD community, encompassing a diverse group of stakeholders—including clinical and research professionals as well as patients and their advocates, leveraging systems and data that already exist (eg, neurodevelopmental data in the CNOC registry; also see the ). One critical lesson learned from interventions in pediatric CHD is that collaborations need to go beyond professional stakeholders to include community‐based participatory research with patients and families. These unique collaborations inform intervention design and goals, as well as strategies to address accessibility issues associated with social determinants of health. While this article focused on interventions for patients with ACHD, the relation between assessment and intervention for psychological and neurocognitive concerns is bidirectional. Neuropsychological assessment can identify concerns needing intervention, and intervention requires ongoing assessment to monitor progress. Additionally, interventions may reveal findings requiring further assessment. Readers are referred to the recommendations by the Characterizing Outcomes ACHD/Neuro 2024 working group to appreciate the role of assessment. The dynamic association between assessment and intervention also needs to be addressed in the future of clinical care. Readers are referred to the recommendations by the Characterizing Outcomes ACHD/Neuro 2024 working group to appreciate the role of assessment. The dynamic association between assessment and intervention also needs to be addressed in the future of clinical care. Neurocognitive and psychological interventions are costly and resource intensive, with limited funding and provider shortages hindering implementation across ACHD care systems. However, the costs of neglecting the needs of the ACHD population are much greater. Poor psychological health, neurocognitive impairments, and reduced health literacy can lead to lower quality of life and higher health care and societal costs. While existing knowledge on interventions is limited, there are opportunities to make significant improvements. By shifting toward early intervention and moving beyond the traditional medical model focused solely on treatment of problems, the ACHD community could develop more effective models of care that support long‐term well‐being and functional outcomes for individuals living with ACHD.
