Background The human epidermal growth factor-2 (HER2) receptor is a member of receptor tyrosine kinase family that regulates the signaling pathways of cell growth and differentiation. HER2 overexpression is significantly correlated with pathogenesis and progression of some epithelial solid tumors, including breast, ovarian, and gastric neoplasms, and is associated with poor prognosis, tolerance to chemotherapeutic agents, metastasis, and a lower survival rate ( - ). Thus, this receptor is considered as a promising target for cancer treatment ( ). Different strategies have been used to manage HER-2-positive breast cancers, including monoclonal antibodies, drug-conjugated antibodies, and tyrosine kinase inhibitors ( - ). However, the high resistance level to anti-HER2 drugs has lowered their efficacy and led to the search for novel treatment agents ( , ). Immunotoxins are among the novel therapeutic agents against cancer cells that can benefit from the targeting mechanism of monoclonal antibodies and improve their efficacy. Immunotoxins are molecules of two segments: a targeting moiety ( e.g., antibodies) and a toxic moiety ( e.g., bacterial toxins) ( ). Currently, immunotoxins are manufactured via a DNA recombinant technique with a more homogenous structure and more specific performance ( , ). Protein synthesis inhibitors are one of the main toxins used for construction of immunotoxins, which have similar characteristics and performance. Diphtheria toxin (DT) and Pseudomonas exotoxin (PE) are among the most popular recombinant immunotoxins that have been successfully evaluated in clinic ( ). These immunotoxins can be easily expressed and purified in bacterial hosts such as Escherichia coli ( ). PE has three main domains: binding, internalizing, and functional moieties ( ). Various studies have used PE as a toxic moiety in immunotoxins to target cancer cells ( , , ). A PE38-based immunotoxin was created by removing some amino acid residues in the binding domain of PE, eliminating one disulfide bond, and improving the in vivo tolerance of the immunotoxins ( , ). Similar to PE38, in the PE35 subtype, more amino acid domains were eliminated from the internalizing domain. Meanwhile, its toxicity against cancer cells was preserved, and immunotoxin tolerance improved ( ). In our previous study ( ), we developed a novel anti-HER2 immunotoxin consisting of a truncated and modified form of PE (PE35KDEL) and anti-HER2-scFv derived from pertuzumab. In vitro evaluation suggested that this immunotoxin showed significantly higher binding to and toxicity against HER2-overexpressing cells ( i.e., BT-474) than against low-expressing HER2 cells ( i.e., MDA-MB-23) ( ). However, in vivo safety was not evaluated. The present study aimed to evaluate in vivo acute toxicity of the scFv-PE35KDEL immunotoxin in a BALB/c mouse model. Furthermore, the histopathological effects of the immunotoxin in mice were evaluated. 2. Objective The objective of this research was to express and purify the recombinant scFv-PE35KDEL protein and remove its endotoxin content, as well as to evaluate its toxicity profile by determining the LD50 and monitoring body weight changes in BALB/c mice following injection. 3. Materials and Methods 3.1. Expression of Scfv-PE35KDEL Recombinant pTrc99a plasmid containing the scFv-PE35KDEL gene ( ) was transferred to E. coli BL21 DE3 cells using the heat shock method. Lauria-Bertani (LB) medium with suitable antibiotic (100 µg.mL -1 amoxicillin) was used to grow a positive colony. The overnight-grown seed culture of BL21(DE3) harboring recombinant plasmid was transferred to fresh LB medium at an inoculation ratio of 10% v/v. The sample was incubated at 37 ºC until the logarithmic phase was reached. Protein expression was induced by adding 0.5 mM isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG). After incubation at 180 rpm at 37 ºC for 3 h, the bacterial cells were harvested by centrifugation at 5000×g for 5 min at 4 ºC. 3.2. Purification of ScFv-PE35KDEL The immunotoxin was purified using hybrid method according to the instruction of the Ni–NTA Purification System (Invitrogen, USA), with some modifications. Briefly, bacterial cell disruption was performed by sonication and separation of soluble and insoluble fractions. The pellet ( i.e., insoluble fraction) was dissolved in denaturing binding buffer. The sample was then transferred to a Ni-NTA agarose chromatography column and gently shaken for 60 min at room temperature. The column was washed three times with denaturing wash buffer and three times with native wash buffer containing 10 mM imidazole and eluted with native elation buffer and stepwise increase in imidazole concentrations. The purified immunotoxin was subjected to Triton X-114 based endotoxin extraction as previously explained ( ). To exchange the buffer with phosphate buffered saline (PBS) and concentrate the immunotoxin, ultrafiltration using an Amicon filter (cutoff 50000 Da) was performed. Sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) was carried out to confirm the expression of the immunotoxin and to determine the purity of the protein. Briefly, 20 µL of each sample was electrophoresed (80 V for the stacking gel and 150 V for separating gel) on a 12% polyacrylamide gel. The gels were

native elation buffer and stepwise increase in imidazole concentrations. The purified immunotoxin was subjected to Triton X-114 based endotoxin extraction as previously explained ( ). To exchange the buffer with phosphate buffered saline (PBS) and concentrate the immunotoxin, ultrafiltration using an Amicon filter (cutoff 50000 Da) was performed. Sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) was carried out to confirm the expression of the immunotoxin and to determine the purity of the protein. Briefly, 20 µL of each sample was electrophoresed (80 V for the stacking gel and 150 V for separating gel) on a 12% polyacrylamide gel. The gels were stained with 0.125 % Coomassie Blue R-250 (catalog no. 20278, Thermo Scientific, USA) for 10 min and destained in 40% ethanol (v/v)-10% acetic acid (v/v) in water. The concentration of the immunotoxin was estimated using Bradford method ( ). 3.3. In Vivo Acute Toxicity Thirty BALB/c mice (25-30 g) were purchased from the animal house of Isfahan Pharmacy School, Isfahan. All animals were kept in polypropylene cages (every six animals per cage) under standard conditions of temperature and humidity. The animals had free access to diet pellets and tap water. All interventions were performed according to the animal care guidelines issued by Isfahan University of Medical Sciences. (Ethics Code: IR.MUI.AEC.1402.025). Mice were randomly divided into five groups (n = 6) according to immunotoxin dose as follows: Four groups (3 mice of each sex) were injected intraperitoneally with doses of 250, 500, 1000 and 2000 µg.kg -1 of scFv-PE35KDEL under the same conditions and time. Six mice were also injected intraperitoneally with PBS as a control group. Mice were weighed using a digital scale before injection and for 15 days after injection. The final weight of the animals was measured just before their sacrifice. All groups were monitored for mortality, behavioral symptoms and body temperature at 1, 2, 3, 5, and 24 h after injection. The behavioral reactions of the mice were recorded, and the number of deaths within 24 h was determined. In addition, the animals that remained in each group were checked for two weeks for signs of poisoning (including examination of hair and skin, eyes and mucous membranes, respiratory and cardiac conditions, autonomic and CNS symptoms, behavioral symptoms, tremors, seizures, salivation, diarrhea, lethargy, drowsiness and coma). A digital thermometer was used to determine the body temperature of mice. Every other day, the thermometer was placed on the skin under the abdomen, and the body temperature was measured accordingly. All groups were housed in the same environment with the same temperature and nutritional conditions during the study period. After 15 days, all the animals were euthanized in the carbon dioxide chamber, and the liver, kidney, and lung tissues were collected for further examination. These samples were kept in 10% formalin and stained with the hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining. Finally, the slides were examined and compared to those of the control group using a light microscope. 3.4. Statistical Analysis The results were presented as mean ± standard deviation of the groups and were subjected to analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey ´s test. Results were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05. 4. Results 4.1. Expression and Purification of Immunotoxin After protein expression, the total protein content of the samples was analyzed by 12% SDS-PAGE ( ). SDS-PAGE analysis suggested that the full-length immunotoxin was successfully expressed, with a molecular weight of approximately 62 kDa. Following purification using a Ni-NTA column under hybrid condition ( ), the sample was subjected to endotoxin removal and ultrafiltration. The final concentration of the purified immunotoxin was measured by Bradford method and found to be 520 µg.mL -1 . 4.2. In Vivo Toxicity Studies To estimate the lethal dose, two groups of three mice (male and female) were injected intraperitoneally with a single dose of 250 µg.kg -1 of scFv-PE35KDEL. After 15 days, all the mice survived. In the second step, we increased the injection dose to 500 µg.kg -1 and 1000 µg.kg -1 . Despite severe side effects, especially at a dose of 1000 µg.kg -1 ), all the mice survived for 15 days after the injection of immunotoxin. However, a single dose of 2000 µg.kg -1 of immunotoxin was lethal for all mice. Therefor the LD50 of immunotoxin was estimated to be approximately 1300 µg.kg -1 . To check the body temperature of BALB/c mice after injection, a digital thermometer was used to record the temperature every alternate day. Analysis of variance and Tukey’s test showed no significant differences between the groups receiving scFv-PE35KDEL protein and the control group (PBS injection) ( ). The body weight of BALB/c mice was recorded using a digital scale before immunotoxin injection. Then, their weights were measured every two days. Analysis of variance and Tukey’s test showed a significant (P = 0.01) weight loss between the

mice. Therefor the LD50 of immunotoxin was estimated to be approximately 1300 µg.kg -1 . To check the body temperature of BALB/c mice after injection, a digital thermometer was used to record the temperature every alternate day. Analysis of variance and Tukey’s test showed no significant differences between the groups receiving scFv-PE35KDEL protein and the control group (PBS injection) ( ). The body weight of BALB/c mice was recorded using a digital scale before immunotoxin injection. Then, their weights were measured every two days. Analysis of variance and Tukey’s test showed a significant (P = 0.01) weight loss between the groups receiving 500 and 1000 µg.kg -1 scFv-PE35KDEL immunotoxin and the group receiving PBS (control group) until the third day, and no significant weight loss was observed after thereafter ( ). To investigate the side effects after injection, the symptoms of poisoning in BALB-C mice were carefully observed, recorded and compared to the control group at 1, 2, 3, 5 and 24 h after injection ( Supplementary Table 1-5 ). The results indicated that more severe complications were observed by increasing the dosage of immunotoxin to a dose of 1000 µg.kg -1 . In the control group, PBS was injected intraperitoneally and the mice were observed for two weeks. No symptoms were observed in either sex of the control group, but when the dose was increased from 250 µg.kg -1 to 500 µg.kg -1 , digestive symptoms such as twisting and diarrhea were observed. At 1000 µg.kg -1 , muscle tonicity and reflexes disappeared 24 h after injection, and the severity of digestive symptoms increased. However, digestive symptoms such as diarrhea were still observed. The histopathological evaluation of lung, liver and kidney sections of mice is presented in . No significant histological damage was observed after analysis of H&E-stained sections of kidney, lung and liver of the mice after treatment with 250 µg.kg -1 and 500 µg.kg -1 of immunotoxin compared with PBS. In the liver, mild-to-moderate lobular inflammation and slight spotty necrosis were observed in mice treated with 1000 and 2000 µg.kg -1 ( ). Slight cortical hyperemia was observed in the kidneys of mice treated with doses of 1000 and 2000 µg.kg -1 ( ). In the lungs, a mild increase in alveolar dilation and focal hemorrhage was observed in mice treated with 1000 and 2000 µg.kg -1 body weight compared with control ( ). 5. Discussion Pseudomonas exotoxin-based immunotoxins usually target specific antigens or receptors overexpressed on cancer cells, thereby minimizing damage to normal cells. Several PE-based immunotoxins have been used in clinical trials, and some have received FDA approval. For example, moxetumomab psudotox, which targets CD22, has been approved for treatment of hairy cell leukemia ( ). In this study, we evaluated the acute toxicity of a novel anti-HER2 immunotoxin, scFv-PE35KDEL, in mice. Preliminary studies on in vitro cytotoxicity of scFv-PE35KDEL showed its selective toxicity toward cancer cells overexpressing HER2 ( i.e., BT-474). The IC50 obtained for the BT-474 strain was 52.95 nM, which is 17.5 times lower than the IC50 obtained for the MDA-MB-231 cell ( i.e., low expressing HER2) ( ). The findings of current study showed that BALB/c mice survived after single intraperitoneal injection of immunotoxin scFv-PE35KDEL up to a dose of 1000 µg.kg -1 . The LD50 of this immunotoxin was higher than 1000 µg.kg -1 and lower than 2000 µg.kg -1 . Similar to our results, Tsutsumi et al , injected native and mutant anti-Tac (Fv)-PE38 (LMB-2) intravenously into BALB/c mice and reported that LD50 of the immunotoxins was approximately 500 µg.kg -1 ( ). However, PEGylation of the immunotoxin improved its safety and LD50 of 3000 µg.kg -1 was reported for PEG5K-LMB-2 and PEG20K-LMB-2 ( ). In the present study, based on pathological evaluation of liver, kidney and lung and comparison with the control group, no specific toxicity was observed in liver and kidney tissues up to a dose of 1000 µg.kg -1 . Slight lung damage ( e.g., increase in alveolar dilation and focal hemorrhage) was observed in mice treated with 1000 µg.kg -1 of scFv-PE35KDEL, which may be due to vascular leak syndrome (VLS). VLS is the main dose-limiting toxic effect of immunotoxins including PE. Wang et al . constructed a PE-based immunotoxin ( i.e., SMFv-PE38KDEL) and investigated the effect of amino acid modifications of PE38 on VLS induced by the immunotoxin ( ). Single doses of SMFv-PE38KDEL or SMFv-PE38KDEL mutants were injected into the tail vein of the mice and in agreement with our findings, the LD50 of wild type PE and mutant PE was found to be 1290 and 1156 µg.kg -1 , respectively. Furthermore, they harvested the lungs and performed pulmonary vascular leak assay. No mortality or VLS were observed up to 500 and 5000 µg.kg -1 of SMFv-PE38KDEL and SMFv-PE38KDEL mutants, respectively ( ).

. constructed a PE-based immunotoxin ( i.e., SMFv-PE38KDEL) and investigated the effect of amino acid modifications of PE38 on VLS induced by the immunotoxin ( ). Single doses of SMFv-PE38KDEL or SMFv-PE38KDEL mutants were injected into the tail vein of the mice and in agreement with our findings, the LD50 of wild type PE and mutant PE was found to be 1290 and 1156 µg.kg -1 , respectively. Furthermore, they harvested the lungs and performed pulmonary vascular leak assay. No mortality or VLS were observed up to 500 and 5000 µg.kg -1 of SMFv-PE38KDEL and SMFv-PE38KDEL mutants, respectively ( ). Bang et al . evaluated the toxicity of a recombinant anti-CD22 PE-immunotoxin, HA22, and reported a single-dose LD50 of 1330 µg.kg -1 ( ). The main mechanisms through which most of PE-immunotoxins are internalized into the cell are receptor-mediated endocytosis. Then, they enter acidic lysosomes that contain proteolytic enzymes. Subsequently, immunotoxins are transferred to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and then into the cytosol. Another research group removed lysosomal protease-susceptible sites of HA22 and evaluated in vivo toxicity of a protease-resistant version of this immunotoxin, HA22-LR ( ). They found that a single intravenous dose of 2000 µg.kg -1 of HA22 killed all five mice; however, HA22-LR did not kill any of animals up to 20000 µg.kg -1 , and pathological evaluation showed less hepatotoxicity than HA22 ( ). Ding et al . Evaluated the effect of the targeting moiety on toxicity, and in vivo biodistribution of anti-HER2-PE25 immunotoxins ( ). They found that compared with ADAPT6 ( i.e., albumin binding domain-derived anti-HER2 affinity protein) as targeting domain, ZHER2:2891 ( i.e., HER2-binding affibody molecule) exhibited more plasma half-life and also shifted the elimination route of the immunotoxin from the liver to the kidneys ( ). Shapira et al . studied the in vivo toxicity of immunoconjugate of PE and anti-CD24 ( i.e., SWA11-ZZ-PE38) and its non-specific IgG control ( i.e., IgG-ZZ-PE38) and they reported LD50 of 750-1000 µg.kg -1 for both ( ). It could be concluded that the toxic moiety (PE38) mainly contributed to mortality induced by PE-immunotoxin. In addition to mortality, the effect of scFv-PE35KDEL on body temperature and weight was monitored according to a method used in previous studies ( ). Our results did not show a significant increase in temperature over two weeks. Therefore, it can be concluded that intraperitoneal injection of the immunotoxin into mice has no febrile effects. However, three days after intraperitoneal injection of 500 µg.kg -1 and 1000 µg.kg -1 doses, BALB/c mice experienced a significant weight loss. Subsequently, they returned to their average weight (day 6) until the end of the study, suggesting that the treatment had some toxic effects but was tolerable. Liu et al . developed a novel anti-GPC3 immunotoxin ( i.e., scFv-mPE24) by using PE24 a truncated version of PE38 to reduce the immunogenicity of the PE toxin and improve its efficacy and safety ( ). They reported only moderate body weight loss in mice treated with 5000 µg.kg -1 or 2500 µg.kg -1 of immunotoxin ( ). We also monitored the behavioral symptoms of mice for 24 h after treatment with scFv-PE35KDEL. By increasing the injection dose from 250 µg.kg -1 to 1000 µg.kg -1 and comparing them with the PBS control group, more severe behavioral symptoms, such as pallor, drooping eyelids, and diarrhea, were observed. In addition, the pain became more intense, and immobility was recorded longer. Muscle tonicity was lost at a dose of 1000 µg.kg -1 , and sometimes convulsion symptoms were recorded. These symptoms were resolved within 24h of injection. Hall et al . evaluated efficacy and safety of intrathecal transferrin-PE immunotoxin against LOX melanoma. They reported that a dose of 1 μg of intrathecal immunotoxin was not neurotoxic and all animals survived. However, significant neurotoxicity was observed with doses of 2.5 and 5 μg of intrathecal transferrin-PE immunotoxin, and 8 of 10 mice were killed within 24 h ( ). Li et al developed an immunotoxin, A1-PE24X7, con-sisting of an anti- mesothelin single domain antibody and a truncated form of PE ( ). They reported that this immuntoxin has a relatively broad therapeutic window as its therapeutic dose was 3000 µg.kg -1 and its maximum tolerable dose (to mice was higher than 15000 µg.kg -1 ( ). Recently, another research group developed an engineered E. coli Nissle 1917 to deliver an αPD-L1-PE38 immunotoxin to tumor tissue ( ). The bacteria could colonize to solid tumors and upon induction by L-arabinose produce and release the immunotoxin. They suggested that application of live engineered bacteria to deliver the immunotoxins could improve safety and efficacy of these molecules in cancer treatment ( ). 6. Conclusion In summary, in vivo acute toxicity evaluation suggested that the novel immunotoxin was safe and well-tolerated up to doses of 1000

its maximum tolerable dose (to mice was higher than 15000 µg.kg -1 ( ). Recently, another research group developed an engineered E. coli Nissle 1917 to deliver an αPD-L1-PE38 immunotoxin to tumor tissue ( ). The bacteria could colonize to solid tumors and upon induction by L-arabinose produce and release the immunotoxin. They suggested that application of live engineered bacteria to deliver the immunotoxins could improve safety and efficacy of these molecules in cancer treatment ( ). 6. Conclusion In summary, in vivo acute toxicity evaluation suggested that the novel immunotoxin was safe and well-tolerated up to doses of 1000 µg.kg -1 . At a dose of 2000 µg.kg -1 , scFv-PE35KDEL caused death in all mice. These findings suggest that this immunotoxin is a promising anti-HER2 drug candidate for further efficacy and safety in vivo evaluation. Furthermore, in the future studies, the safety of the immunotoxin may improve by PEGylation or amino acid modification.

chunks.content: Background Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe eating disorder that is associated with considerable physical, mental, and social impairments. With a lifetime prevalence of 1.4% for women, 0.2% for men, and a point prevalence of 5.7% in adolescents [ ], AN is widely recognized as a major public health threat. According to the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study, the prevalence increases around the age of 15 years, especially in females [ ]. During the first wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, a higher number of new diagnoses and hospitalizations in children and adolescents was observed [ ]. In addition, a landmark meta-analysis [ ] found a standardized mortality ratio for AN of 5.9 deaths per 1000 person-years, an almost sixfold increased risk, highlighting the need for effective treatments. Several evidence-based guidelines have been developed to inform the treatment of different eating disorders, including AN [e.g., – ]. For children and adolescents, these guidelines consistently recommend the involvement of near caregivers, mostly in the form of family-based treatment or therapy (FBT) [ ]. For adults, the main treatment recommendation is individual psychotherapy, with no superiority of one approach over another [ , , ]. All guidelines highlight the lack of evidence concerning pharmacotherapy for AN, especially as the sole treatment [ ]. Previous international guidelines were developed using literature searches from 2013 to 2022, with the World Federation of Societies of Biological Psychiatry (WFSBP) guideline [ ] currently being the most recent one. To the best of our knowledge, there are five relevant published systematic reviews with and without network meta-analysis (NMA) [ , , – ] and one umbrella review [ ] evaluating the efficacy of different treatments for AN in adolescents and adults in inpatient and outpatient settings (see Additional file 1). These reviews [e.g., [ ] informed clinical guidelines on the treatment of AN [e.g., ], but have some methodological limitations. First, except for Himmerich et al. [ ] and Zhu et al. [ ], who searched until January or July 2022, literature searches of previous reviews were mostly conducted until the end of 2020. Therefore, these reviews did not consider several new randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with large samples and/or long-term follow-up on (non-)pharmacological interventions for adolescents and adults that have been published in recent years [e.g., – ]. In addition, RCTs on newer treatment options like neurostimulation, which are still in its infancy [e.g., – ], were also not considered. Second, there is no information on the comparative efficacy of pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions, partly due to a different focus of the reviews [ , , ], inaccurate reporting of eligible studies in the reviews [ , ], or insufficient data to investigate those types of interventions in an NMA [ ]. Third, previous reviews have mostly focused on weight outcomes, while a meta-review of 13 qualitative evidence syntheses found that patients prioritize psychological needs over physical recovery [ ], highlighting the need to investigate additional outcomes including mental health (e.g., depressive symptoms, health-related quality of life [HRQoL]). Lastly, an exploration of subgroup differences between patients (e.g., female and male patients, patients with and without comorbidities) is urgently needed as subgroup analyses were rarely performed. Overall, patients, their families and various interest holders like healthcare staff would benefit from an updated systematic review to inform the revision of guidelines regarding the treatment of AN. Therefore, this systematic review with NMA aims to examine the comparative efficacy and safety of various pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions in the treatment of AN in adolescents and adults, and to obtain a clinically meaningful ranking of different treatment alternatives compared to each other and to relevant control groups, such as no treatment, treatment as usual and waiting list. To prevent problems encountered by other reviews [ , ], we will perform a component network meta-analysis (CNMA), allowing us to estimate the effects of individual components of complex (i.e., multicomponent) interventions. Methods This protocol for a systematic review with network meta-analysis is reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses for Protocols (PRISMA-P) [ ]. The PRISMA-P checklist can be found in Additional file 2. The NMA will be reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items of Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses for Network Meta-Analyses (PRISMA-NMA) [ ]. The protocol has been registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) database on 24th February 2025 (CRD420250654515). Eligibility criteria The eligibility criteria are defined according to the Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome, Study design (PICOS) framework. A detailed description of the eligibility criteria is provided in Table . Population We will include studies that assessed adolescents (≥ 10 years) and/or adults (≥ 18 years) diagnosed with AN. Mixed populations (i.e., AN and other eating disorders) will be considered if outcomes for the defined populations are analyzed and reported separately.

The protocol has been registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) database on 24th February 2025 (CRD420250654515). Eligibility criteria The eligibility criteria are defined according to the Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome, Study design (PICOS) framework. A detailed description of the eligibility criteria is provided in Table . Population We will include studies that assessed adolescents (≥ 10 years) and/or adults (≥ 18 years) diagnosed with AN. Mixed populations (i.e., AN and other eating disorders) will be considered if outcomes for the defined populations are analyzed and reported separately. Intervention Studies evaluating pharmacological (e.g., antidepressants) and/or non-pharmacological treatments (e.g., psychotherapy) in any setting and of any intervention duration will be considered. As non-pharmacological interventions, we will also include trials evaluating neuromodulation, physical activity-related and exercise therapy interventions, nutritional supplements, and novel refeeding approaches. Complex (i.e., multicomponent) interventions will also be considered. Comparator In our NMA, interventions will be compared, where possible, to each other and to relevant control groups, such as no treatment, treatment as usual and waiting list. Outcomes We will include studies reporting outcomes that have been suggested by clinical experts involved in the current review (AZ, AH, CF, BHD, TB, UC, SE, AMM, MS) or that have been considered in previous systematic reviews and clinical guidelines. In addition, we plan to identify further potentially patient-relevant outcomes by involving patients with AN in the review development process using a peer-research format. Ideally, two workshops with adolescent and adult participants ( n = 8 each), currently in treatment for AN or former patients, will be held at the Medical Center, University of Freiburg. In these workshops, we will explain the importance of our evidence synthesis project to the participants. Subsequently, we plan to use discussions to obtain further information about the patients’ experiences. Patients will discuss relevant outcomes of interventions, which will be summarized. Overall, based on these sources, we will provide a Summary of findings table for the first seven prioritized outcomes based on the assessment of the certainty of evidence (see “ ” section). The first seven outcomes specified in Table were provisionally prioritized by the clinical experts in this review (AZ, AH, CF, BHD, TB, UC, SE, AMM, MS), comprising weight-related and psychological outcomes mapping the DSM-5 criteria for AN, as well as possible adverse events (for details, see Table ). This prioritization will be adjusted, if necessary, based on the results of the patient workshops. Study design We will include RCTs using a parallel-group or crossover design (see “ ”) to examine interventions of any duration. RCTs have to include a minimum follow-up period of 6 months or more after the intervention. If more than one article is published on the same study, we will identify the original publication and will extract multiple outcomes from different papers, including the largest number of participants and using data from intention-to-treat analysis (ITT; see “ ” section). We will use no restrictions concerning publication date or language. We will consider published RCTs and grey literature (e.g., unpublished theses). Information sources and literature search The following six databases will be searched: Ovid MEDLINE, Scopus, World Health Organization (WHO) Global Index Medicus, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Science Citation Index Expanded (Web of Science), and Ovid APA PsycInfo. We will not include Embase and Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) in our search, as RCTs indexed here are now prospectively added to CENTRAL via a highly sensitive screening process. As additional sources, we will screen the reference lists of systematic reviews and of included studies to identify further eligible trials. To retrieve grey literature, we will search the Bielefeld Academic Search Engine (BASE). Moreover, we will search two clinical trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform [ICTRP]) to identify planned, ongoing or completed but unpublished studies. The strategy was developed by an experienced information specialist (HJ) and quality checked by a second experienced information specialist (MIM). It includes three clusters of search terms: a) terms related to AN, b) different treatments, and c) study design. We will use validated search filters for RCTs, if possible [e.g., ]. We will use Cochrane’s Screen4Me workflow to help assess the search results [ ]. After excluding duplicates, the references will be uploaded to Covidence ( www.covidence.org ) for title–abstract and full-text screening. Two reviewers (i.e., FH, JS, EK, LS, and AMK in different dual combinations) will independently screen the titles and abstracts of the studies. If an abstract is not provided by the database from which it originated and the title appears potentially relevant, we will forward the record to the full-text review stage. At this stage, the full-text versions of potentially relevant studies will be retrieved or acquired, and will also be screened by two reviewers independently. At both levels of screening, the two reviewers will compare their lists of relevant studies that meet the inclusion criteria. Potential disagreements will be discussed. If no consensus can be found or reached, they will seek the opinion of a third author (AZ, JJM, or LS). We will present a PRISMA flow diagram to show the process of study selection [ ]. We will list all articles excluded after full-text assessment and will provide the reasons for exclusion [ ]. For identified planned or ongoing trials, we will provide a table to follow up on these trials. Data extraction and data collection process Two reviewers (i.e., FH, JS, EK, and AMK in different dual combinations) will independently extract the data for each included study using a pre-tested excel data extraction form. We will extract information on design/methods, participants, interventions/comparators, and outcomes (see Additional file 4). Any disagreements will be discussed and if no agreement can be reached, we will consult a third reviewer (AZ, JJM, or LS) to find a consensus. If relevant data are missing, we will contact the corresponding study authors to request missing information (e.g., to ask for post-intervention data if only change from baseline is reported). Risk of bias assessment The risk of bias (RoB) will be assessed by two independent reviewers (i.e., FH, JS, EK, and AMK in different dual combinations) for each outcome using the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2) [ ]. This tool enables a domain-level judgment about the risk of bias comprising the following domains: bias arising from the randomization, bias due to deviations from intended interventions, bias due to missing outcome data, bias in measurement of the outcome, and bias in selection of the reported results. For this review, we are mainly interested in the effects of assignment to intervention (i.e., intention-to-treat effects). Any disagreements in the risk of bias assessment will be resolved by discussion or by consulting a third reviewer (JJM or LS). The RoB for each domain will be judged as ‘low risk’, ‘high risk’, or ‘some concerns’ by applying the code of the RoB 2 tool and by using the available RoB 2 Excel sheet [ ]. Based on these results, we will establish an overall risk-of-bias judgment for each predefined outcome. A traffic light plot of the domain-level judgments for each individual study and weighted bar plots of the distribution of risk-of-bias judgments within each domain will be provided using the R package “robvis” [ ]. Synthesis of included studies The statistical analysis has been planned and will be conducted by an experienced statistician (MP). We will conduct an NMA with the aim of assessing several comparative interventions (e.g., psychotherapy, pharmacological treatments, TAU) by combining direct and indirect evidence from RCTs. A frequentist random-effects NMA will be performed in order to evaluate the summary effects of each intervention using the R package “netmeta” [ , ]. As effect measures, we will use the risk ratio (RR) for dichotomous outcomes (e.g., remission), the mean difference (MD) for continuous outcomes (e.g., BMI), or the standardized mean difference (SMD) for continuous outcomes reported on different scales (e.g., HRQoL, BMI). For crossover trials, we will only consider the pre-crossover endpoints for the main analyses to avoid carry-over effects, especially in trials on pharmacological interventions. Data from ITT will be preferred over completer or per-protocol analyses. We will not consider any post-hoc analyses. We will provide a network plot (Fig. ) [ ]; an example network plot for hypothetical data) to visually depict the direct comparisons between the different interventions and control groups for each outcome [ ]. To summarize NMA results, effect estimates with their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) will be presented in league tables and forest plots. Treatments will be ranked by P-scores that are a frequentist version of the Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking curve (SUCRA) [ ]. We will provide a network plot (Fig. ) [ ]; an example network plot for hypothetical data) to visually depict the direct comparisons between the different interventions and control groups for each outcome [ ]. To summarize NMA results, effect estimates with their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) will be presented in league tables and forest plots. Treatments will be ranked by P-scores that are a frequentist version of the Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking curve (SUCRA) [ ]. P -scores are values between 0 and 1, with 1 indicating that a treatment always ranks best and a value of 0 meaning that a treatment always ranks worst. If at least ten comparisons are available for a particular outcome, we will evaluate the presence of small-study effects for each outcome using comparison-adjusted funnel plots. Comparison-adjusted funnel plots will also allow detecting extreme study effects (i.e., outliers) [ ], which can be further explored with outlier analysis using the R package “NMAoutlier” [ ]. The fundamental assumption of NMA is transitivity, meaning that the distribution of potential effect modifiers is balanced across treatment comparisons. We will assess this empirically by comparing the distribution of a-priori defined potential effect modifiers across the direct comparisons. The statistical manifestation of transitivity is consistency, which requires that direct and indirect evidence is in agreement. We will assess inconsistency as a whole in each network using a random-effects design-by-treatment interaction model [ , ]. If the global test suggests inconsistency, we will assess inconsistency locally by splitting the direct and the indirect evidence using the loop-specific approach [ , ] and, visually, using the net-heat plot [ ]. A-priori defined potential effect modifiers are based on previous reviews [e.g., ] and include the following variables: the patients’ age (i.e., young adolescents [10–14 years] vs. adolescents [15–19 years] vs. young adults [20–24 years] vs. 25–29 years vs. 30–34 years vs. 35–39 years vs. ≥ 40 years) [ , ]; sex; the duration of disease (i.e., number of years since diagnosis); subtype of AN (e.g., restricting vs. binge-eating/purging type based on DSM-5 and ICD-11); chronicity of disease (i.e., below vs. over 7-year cut-off for severe and enduring AN) [ ]; severity of disease (i.e., weight status based on ICD-11: AN with significantly low body weight [BMI 14.0–18.5 kg/m 2 in adults; 0.3-5 th percentile for BMI-for-age in adolescents] vs. AN with dangerously low body weight [BMI < 14.0 kg/m 2 in adults; < 0.3 percentile for BMI-for-age in adolescents]; adapted to ethnicity, if possible); previous treatment (i.e., any previous eating disorder-specific pharmacological or non-pharmacological treatment vs. not); comorbidity of mental illness (i.e., with comorbid mental disorder vs. without); treatment setting (e.g., inpatient vs. day hospital vs. outpatient); modality of psychotherapeutic interventions (e.g., face-to-face vs. digital interventions, group vs. individual); duration of the intervention (in weeks); study design (i.e., parallel-group studies vs. crossover trials, where only pre-crossover data will be considered for crossover trials); duration of follow-up after the intervention (i.e., ≤ 6 months vs. > 6 months ≤ 1 year vs. > 1 year ≤ 3 years vs. > 3 years ≤ 5 years vs. > 5 years); risk of bias of included studies; the provision of ITT analyses by included studies; and the type of reported data (i.e., post-intervention vs. change-from-baseline data). If appropriate, these potential effect modifiers will be incorporated into the analyses by using meta-regression and subgroup analyses (i.e., for age, sex, subtype of AN, chronicity/severity of disease, previous treatment, comorbidity, treatment setting, modality of psychotherapeutic interventions, study design, duration of follow-up) to explore their impact on treatment effects. In addition, we will perform sensitivity analyses by excluding studies with different key characteristics that contribute to heterogeneity (i.e., only including studies rated as low RoB, only including studies providing ITT analyses, only including studies reporting post-intervention data). The complexity of the interventions is a major challenge, as this can lead to increased heterogeneity if not accounted for properly. As we expect to end up with a network including complex (i.e., multicomponent) interventions in AN, for example, of CBT and olanzapine, we plan to conduct a CNMA to estimate the effect of individual components of multicomponent interventions [ ]. We will perform the additive CNMA model if the additivity assumption is satisfied. Additionally, we will explore various interaction CNMA models to account for potential interactions (e.g., more efficient use of CBT interventions due to olanzapine-induced reduced motor unrest) among components [ , ]. We will follow the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach for NMA to assess the certainty of evidence in each of the direct, indirect and network estimates [ ]. Additionally, we will explore various interaction CNMA models to account for potential interactions (e.g., more efficient use of CBT interventions due to olanzapine-induced reduced motor unrest) among components [ , ]. We will follow the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach for NMA to assess the certainty of evidence in each of the direct, indirect and network estimates [ ]. Two review authors (i.e., FH, JS, EK, and AMK in different dual combinations) will independently rate the certainty of evidence for each of the seven outcomes prioritized above (see “ ” section and Table ). We will resolve any differences in assessment by discussion or by consultation with a third review author (JJM or LS). To evaluate direct evidence, we will consider the risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, and publication bias. If the certainty of direct evidence is high and its contribution (i.e., relative weight in the network estimate) to the network estimate is at least as much or more than that of the indirect evidence, we will not rate the indirect evidence [ ]. To assess the certainty of network estimates, we will compare the ratings of direct and indirect evidence. If we detect inconsistency in a specific pairwise comparison, we will rate down the network estimate and acknowledge its limitations. If NMA or pairwise meta‐analyses are not possible, we will present the results in a narrative format in the Summary of findings table. Discussion Given the ambivalence of patients with AN to engage in treatment [ ], the willingness of patients and, in the case of adolescents, also of their relatives to consider therapy may substantially depend on the advice provided by specialized staff (e.g., clinicians). Therefore, high-quality evidence on the various treatment alternatives and their comparative efficacy and safety is essential. This systematic review with NMA aims to examine the efficacy and safety of different pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions delivered in various settings and modalities, compared to each other, where possible, and to control groups. Supplementing previous systematic reviews, it will use extended eligibility criteria and consider new relevant RCTs in the field, involving patients and important interest holders to identify patient-relevant outcomes and to disseminate the results using appropriate forms to reach patients, their families, clinical decision-makers and further interest holders (e.g., self-help groups). The findings of this systematic review with NMA will inform the revision of the German clinical guideline [ ], which is currently being worked on and possibly further international guidelines that need to be revised. The NMA will allow comparing interventions that might have never been compared before as well as to rank interventions based on their efficacy and safety. Therefore, our results have the potential to play a crucial role in improving clinical care in inpatient, day-hospital and outpatient treatment settings and, thus, the quality of life of adolescent and adult patients with AN and their families. Based on previous research [e.g., , , ] and the importance of multidisciplinary treatment approaches highlighted by several clinical guidelines [ ], it can be expected that the included studies, especially those in inpatient care, often investigate complex (i.e., multicomponent) interventions in patients with AN. Such cases include a treatment consisting of several (possibly interacting) components like psychotherapy, pharmacotherapy (e.g., single or several medications), and further treatment elements (e.g., nutritional interventions). This makes it challenging to distinctly separate individual components, such as splitting treatment nodes to conduct separate systematic reviews on the efficacy of pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions. Furthermore, especially for emerging treatments (e.g., neuromodulation), it remains unclear if these treatments should be delivered as stand-alone or adjunctive interventions [e.g., ]. Therefore, we decided to examine both pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions in one review using an NMA and CNMA approach to analyze their effects and to assess not only which interventions do work, but also which components. Providing a ranking at both intervention and component levels may optimize the use of resources in clinical care and, thus, improve patient outcomes in the treatment of AN. Extant research shows that there is considerable overlap between tinnitus-related distress and PTSD, including sleep difficulty, irritability, hyperarousal, and concentration problems. However, no studies have prospectively examined the relationship between the two disorders. The purpose of this study was to examine that relationship. Methods: Participants ( N = 112) with posttraumatic headache completed measures of tinnitus and PTSD. Correlational analyses and analyses of variance were conducted to examine the associations with PTSD symptom clusters and factors of tinnitus-related distress. Results: Approximately, half of participants with tinnitus demonstrated severe impairment. Correlational analyses indicated that reexperiencing, avoidance, negative emotions and cognitions, and hyperarousal PTSD symptoms were significantly related to many factors of tinnitus-related distress, including intrusiveness of tinnitus, perceived loudness, awareness, and annoyance. Participants with severe tinnitus demonstrated significantly greater reexperiencing, negative mood/cognitions, hyperarousal, and PTSD total severity compared to those with mild or moderate tinnitus. Conclusions: Trauma therapists should assess for the presence of tinnitus in order to more fully conceptualize key health problems of help-seeking patients.
